articles.title: Renee Good's family sues U.S. government, ICE officer and others over Minneapolis killing
articles.summary: Lawsuits filed by Renee Good's family allege wrongful death, conspiracy and other violations in the 37-year-old's fatal shooting by a U.S. immigration officer during an immigration crackdown in…

image.caption: Renee Good was fatally shot by a U.S. ICE agent on Jan. 7, 2026, as protests against immigration raids flared across Minneapolis. (Tim Evans/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Lawsuits filed by Renee Good's family allege wrongful death, conspiracy and other violations in the 37-year-old's fatal shooting by a U.S. immigration officer during an immigration crackdown in January.
Lawsuits allege wrongful death, conspiracy in fatal January shooting by U.S. immigration officer

Renee Good's family sued the U.S. government and several immigration officials on Thursday, alleging wrongful death, conspiracy and other violations in the 37-year-old woman's killing by an immigration officer during a federal crackdown in Minneapolis.
The two lawsuits were filed by Good's partner, Becca Good, and Renee's brother, Brent Ganger.
The U.S. Justice Department didn't immediately respond to an email seeking comment on the lawsuits.

Renee Good, a mother of three, was fatally shot Jan. 7 as protests against immigration raids flared across the city. According to Becca Good, her partner stopped their car in a street to support neighbours during an immigration operation.

items: Renee Good's brothers mourn loss of 'beautiful American'
Investigating Renee Good's death is now up to the county — and no one else

blocks.text: Bystander video shows Renee Good in the driver's seat of a red SUV blocking part of the road and repeatedly honking her horn.

Two immigration officers get out of a truck, their faces covered, and one orders Good to get out of the car. She reverses briefly, then turns the steering wheel as the officer says again, "Get out of the car."
Almost simultaneously, Becca Good, standing in the street, shouts: "Drive, baby, drive!"
One officer standing in front of the vehicle pulls his weapon and fires into the windshield. He lurches back as the car turns away from him.
The officer, now very close to the open window on the driver's side, opens fire two more times, fatally shooting Renee Good, according to an analysis of the videos by The Associated Press and others.
Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defence and that Good had engaged in "an act of domestic terrorism."
Moment of silence held at scene of Renee Good’s death days after Minneapolis ICE shooting
Lawsuits allege wrongful death and conspiracy

The lawsuit against the United States seeks damages for Good's wrongful death and "the immense suffering Renee endured in the final moments of her life, and for the profound and permanent losses that her death has inflicted upon her family," according to a news release filed by lawyers for Becca Good and Ganger.
The lawsuit also alleges "intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligent infliction of emotional distress" on Becca Good.

Becca and Renee Good were not legally married, according to a family lawyer, but referred to one another as wives. They had only recently relocated to Minneapolis from Kansas City, Mo. It asks for a bench trial.
The other lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights and seeks a jury trial.

items: ICE nodding to far-right extremists in recruitment posts, experts say
ICE detains 5-year-old boy coming home from Minnesota preschool

blocks.text: It says the shots fired by Jonathan Ross, the immigration officer who killed Good, "were the predictable and intended product of the operation," which the lawsuit describes as a "carefully planned, co-ordinated effort between senior federal officials and private actors to make two ethnic communities — Minnesotans of Somali and Hispanic descent and origin — the object of aggression and abduction, and to silence by intimidation, arrest and violence the neighbours and allies of those targeted communities who observed, documented and warned of that campaign."

The lawsuit also alleges "collaboration of federal agencies and individuals with private entities for an operation with discriminatory design, racially targeted pursuit and seizure of individuals without regard to their legal status, and each defendant's participation in the conspiracy."

It names Ross as a defendant, as well as White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security head Kristi Noem, former U.S. Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino, former campaign manager Corey Lewandowski and others.

The killing of Good and another U.S. citizen, Alex Pretti, in Minneapolis just weeks later sparked outrage across the country and calls to rein in immigration enforcement. At least 10 people have died in encounters with immigration officers during U.S. President Donald Trump's second term.
'Should never happen to any family'

In social media accounts, Renee Good described herself as a poet, writer, wife and mom. On Pinterest, a profile picture shows her smiling and holding a young child, alongside posts about tattoos, hairstyles and home decorating.

In an interview shortly after her death, Renee Good's mother, Donna Ganger, told The Associated Press: "She had this way of making you feel special and loved that I didn't even understand … until we lost her."
"As we have tried to navigate our own massive loss, I am also devastated by how many other lives have been destroyed in this darkest of times," Becca Good said in the news release on Thursday.

"So many other families are dealing with the loss of their loved ones; to everyone who has had to witness it — the pain of this moment extends far beyond our family. What happened to us should never happen to any family."

articles.title: Crude oil exports from strait of Hormuz largely return to pre-war levels
articles.summary:
Alternative ways being used to move fuel out of Gulf region, but flows of refined products such as diesel still constrained

Exports of crude from the strait of Hormuz have largely returned…

blocks.text: Exports of crude from the strait of Hormuz have largely returned to levels seen before the outbreak of the Iran war, as oil producers and the shipping industry have found alternative ways of transporting crucial fuel out of the Middle East.

Pipeline exports and ship-to-ship transfers are among the methods being used, according to analysts tracking the situation, while the US military continues to escort some vessels. However, flows of refined products such as diesel remain constrained, pushing prices higher.

At least 16.5m barrels per day (bpd) left the region in September, according to figures from the global trade intelligence firm Kpler, equalling the pre-war average, excluding Iran. The figure is 10.5m bpd higher than the monthly average for March, during the first weeks of the Iran war.

Since the conflict began on 28 February with US and Israeli strikes on Iran, Tehran has sought to exert its authority on the strait of Hormuz and has at times even declared the strategic waterway closed.
However, Iran’s control appears to have declined in recent weeks, as oil exporters have found workarounds to address the disruption.

About 40% of the region’s crude is now transported without transiting the strait, compared with just 17% before the war, through Saudi and Emirati pipelines, according to Kpler analysis. Saudi Arabia was able to restart operations on its east-west pipeline in late September, after it was damaged during drone attacks, allowing exports from resume from the Red Sea port of Yanbu.

In a sign of the other adaptations, the majority of crude transported through the strait of Hormuz is carried on a shuttle fleet mostly comprising very large crude carriers, sailing with their satellite transponders turned off. The cargo is moved on to different tankers in open water, usually off the coast of Oman or Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates.

blocks.caption: Tankers and merchant vessels anchor off Fujairah. Ship-to-ship transfers are among the methods being used to transport oil. Photograph: Barry Iverson/Alamy

blocks.text: More than 70% of the crude that passed through the strait in August changed tankers, whereas before the war almost no Gulf crude changed ships in the Gulf of Oman.
However, the recovery in exports from the region remains unbalanced, and supplies of refined products remain constrained.
This poses a problem for businesses and households that depend on refined products such as diesel to run their cars, vans and lorries.
The average diesel price in the UK hit an all-time high of 199.18p a litre on Monday, with many motorists already reporting prices above £2 on some forecourts.
“Diesel carries the sharpest risk,” said Kpler analysts, who found that less than 20% of pre-war levels of refined products shipped through Hormuz were being transported.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: The average diesel price in the UK hit an all-time high of 199.18p a litre on Monday. Photograph: Jacob King/PA

blocks.text: They recorded a seven-day average of 677,000 bpd of refined products as of Monday, compared with 3.6m before the conflict.
Even as oil exports from the region have increased, the level of threat to ships operating around the strait of Hormuz has not disappeared.

“New routes emerge, cargos are rerouted, risk is priced in and absorbed. The danger is assuming that resilience equals security. It doesn’t,” said Richard Meade, the editor in chief of shipping publication Lloyd’s List. “Oil flows have recovered because the market participants have accepted greater operational complexity and higher costs. The underlying threat remains.”
The danger to vessels and their crew was highlighted on Tuesday, when three Liberian-flagged tankers were hit by projectiles while transiting the strait.

The price of crude remains at elevated levels and moved higher again on Thursday, as traders balanced the recovery in some Middle East exports with uncertainty over a long-term solution to the conflict and reopening of the strait.
The price of Brent crude briefly was back above $100 a barrel on Thursday, up 3% to $101.

The rise came after reports that China had suspended exports of oil products to regions beyond Hong Kong and Macau, a move that would add further pressure to oil markets. Oil analysts said China’s decision could suggest it was concerned about the availability of domestic products.

articles.title: Burnham’s reopening of Brexit debate is ‘biggest boost in my career’, says Farage
articles.summary: Reform UK leader tells supporters PM’s move has ‘opened up a huge flank to us’

blocks.text: Nigel Farage has claimed that Andy Burnham has given him “the biggest boost in my career” by reviving the Brexit debate, which the Reform UK leader said had reopened a “huge flank” to his party.
The prime minister’s pledges to the Labour conference and admission on Wednesday that rejoining the EU was among options the government would look at had put “put me back into the debate”, he said.

Looking tanned and relaxed before his party’s first major rally since its conference last month, Farage indicated to reporters that he was relishing a return to the playbook that he and others deployed during the 2016 referendum.

Dismissing polls showing that as much as 59% of the public favoured rejoining the EU, Farage told the Guardian: “Of course they do, until you tell them it’ll cost 25bn quid a year, until you tell him it’ll mean joining Schengen [the area of Europe that has open borders], until he tells them it will mean actually having to recommit to joining the euro.

“Remember that the leavers haven’t made their arguments since 2016. The ‘remoaners’ have made their arguments every single week. I mean, do you know what? I actually think that Burnham has made a very big political mistake here.”

Farage was speaking before a rally in the South Yorkshire city of Doncaster, the first of a series Reform is holding around Britain on the theme of what the party would do in its first 100 days of government.

While the Reform UK leader said he believed Burnham had calculated that new language on the EU might help win back voters from the Greens in big cities, Farage added: “Here in Doncaster and across the ‘red wall’ in the north and Midlands, I think he’s opened up a huge flank to us.”

To cheers from hundreds of Reform supporters who gathered inside an event space at Doncaster racecourse, Farage said: “Today I’m back on the road and today is when our general election campaign starts.”
There were even bigger cheers when Farage said he would relish – “Bring it on, I say” – the prospect of fighting Burnham in red wall areas such as Doncaster on the issue of rejoining the EU.
“He might just have given me the biggest boost in my career I’ve ever had. Thank you, Andy, if you’re watching.”

The focus of the rally – “100 days to save Britain” – had been planned before Burnham’s announcement about UK-EU relations. However, Reform sources claim that the prime minister’s intervention has energised them and that specific donors are already discussing how they can fund a rerun of the 2016 campaign.

Meanwhile, Farage strongly hinted that Reform’s internal inquiry into the donations controversy that has overshadowed the party this year would absolve two key aides and that legal action would be launched against journalists involved.
Indicating that he had already seen the report and knew its conclusions, Farage said its release was “imminent”.

“It’s been done. It’ll be out in public very soon and I think some of your co-conspirators might find themselves with one or two legal challenges,” he told a Channel 4 journalist among reporters who questioned him.

Reform was rocked on the eve of its party conference after some of Farage’s team were filmed appearing to plot to avoid electoral laws on foreign donations in an undercover investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News.

A group of investigative journalists called Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party.

In Channel 4 News’s investigation, footage showed that the fake UK-based supporter also had conversations with Reform’s head of policy, James Orr, who talked about commissioning polling that would be paid for by the US-based father.

In footage of another meeting, a senior adviser to Farage, Dan Jukes, appeared to suggest to the fake UK-based supporter that his US-based father could make a substantial donation by channelling it through the son.
Jukes has denied “any wrongdoing” while Orr has said he would cooperate with the party’s internal investigation “fully”.
The Metropolitan police are carrying out a criminal investigation into Reform over allegations it broke foreign funding laws.

articles.title: Canada Malting plant could collapse at any moment, engineering report says
articles.summary: According to an engineering firm's report, the Canada Malting plant in Montreal's Sud-Ouest borough could collapse at any moment. The report states “controlled demolition is the only possible, safe…

image.caption: The Canada Malting company site along the Lachine Canal in St-Henri was built in 1902. It was sold in 1980 and has been abandoned for 30 years. (Elias Abboud/CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal·New

According to an engineering firm's report, the Canada Malting plant in Montreal's Sud-Ouest borough could collapse at any moment. The report states “controlled demolition is the only possible, safe and rational solution to eliminate the critical danger that this building represents.”
Report recommends demolition, threat of falling debris forces street closure near plant
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 01, 2026 11:42 AM EDT | Last Updated: 19 minutes ago
The Canada malting plant, which looms over Montreal’s Sud-Ouest borough and is notably home to the mysterious “pink house,” could collapse at any moment, according to a new engineering report.

The report, commissioned by the City of Montreal, says the structure — a mass of brick and concrete silos towering over the Lachine Canal to its south and Saint-Ambroise Street to its north — represents an “imminent danger” to public safety.

“Controlled demolition is the only possible, safe and rational solution to eliminate the critical danger that this building represents,” wrote the report’s authors, from the engineering firm STP ING inc.

Engineer André Houle, who wrote the report, is especially concerned about a facade wall, which he says has detached from the roof and is “hanging by a thread.” He’s worried about this brick facade falling onto Saint-Ambroise Street, where people walk and cars are currently parked.
“The only way to protect the public with this project right now is to close the street, there’s no other way,” Houle said in an interview with CBC.
The danger of collapse could worsen in the winter or spring, his report says. Freeze-thaw cycles could contribute to the collapse, as could vibrations from an earthquake.
Private developer ready to build
The engineering report is the latest development weighing on the future of the structure, which has lain vacant since 1985.
In a media release, La Malterie inc., a subsidiary of Renwick, the company that owns and plans to develop the site, said a demolition request had been submitted to the city.
Part of Saint-Ambroise Street will be closed in the meantime.
"The former Canada Malting site occupies a unique place in the history of Saint-Henri and in Montreal's industrial legacy,” Noam Schnitzer, the president of Renwick, said in a statement.
“We remain fully committed to ensuring that the identity of this iconic site can be live on through the future La Malterie project.”

La Malterie Inc. said its plan for the site includes 685 housing units, 20 per cent of which would be social housing. The plan also includes community spaces, businesses and community services. The company says it will also preserve the “pink house.”
The developer, the city and the community group À nous la Malting have clashed over the future of the site for years.
The group wants to turn the building into a collectively owned complex with 200 affordable rental units, a rooftop garden, a bike repair shop, a public daycare, a community kitchen and a museum.
Members of the group camped outside the plant in 2023 to protest Renwick’s development plan. They had pushed for the site to be used exclusively for social housing.
The malting plant and elevators were built in 1905 by the Canada Malting Co. Large cement silos were added in the 1940s to store barley.

The company exported the malt along the Lachine Canal, and when the canal closed to commercial navigation in 1970, the transportation cost rose to the point that the company abandoned the site in the 1980s.
Since then, it has fallen into disrepair. Windows are boarded up, brick walls are crumbling, and the facade is covered in graffiti.

And, though Renwick has set up barriers to prevent people from entering the building, it is popular with “urban explorers” and is home to the “pink house” — a small shack, painted pink and well maintained, which sits atop the crumbling plant.
Engineer says street should have closed earlier
Houle says he’s amazed people are still going into the building, given how dangerous it is. He described arches, made of bricks and steel, that have become especially hazardous.
“When that structure is rusted, it doesn’t hold the brick anymore and the brick falls on the ground,” he explained. “Left and right, the bricks are falling on the ground.”
The STP ING inc. report released Thursday warns that anyone entering the building risks death. In images, the report shows falling bricks and floors that are worn through.
Houle believes the area should’ve been closed one week ago. CBC News has reached out to the City of Montreal for comment.

“Anywhere else it would be, ‘we’ll close off the street and we’ll do the paperwork after. Because the safety is an issue,’” he said. “Here, we’re saying to the owner, ‘no… you need to go through the approval process.’”
“When it’s an urgent matter, there’s a safety issue, why do you have to work for the paperwork to be able to act?”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Matthew Lapierre is a journalist at CBC Montreal. He previously worked for the Montreal Gazette and the Globe and Mail. He can be reached at matthew.lapierre@cbc.ca and at mlapierre.07 on Signal.

articles.title: Netanyahu says flight attacker 'underwent Islamist radical indoctrination'
articles.summary: Israel's prime minister says the pilot who tried to take over the Flydubai plane clearly intended to "down the plane".

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".
The Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two hours into its journey on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control to land safely.
Speaking to Fox News, Netanyahu also said it was looking "very likely" that the attacker, who he said was an Omani national, "was going to down the plane".
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) state news agency reports investigations have begun there to determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose".
Passenger Almog Itali said it felt like a "rollercoaster" as Flight FZ1073 fell 17,000ft in less than two minutes

The co-pilot is currently being questioned in Saudi Arabia, where the plane made an emergency landing. However UAE officials say they have jurisdiction over the incident because the aircraft on which the attack took place is registered there and flies under its flag.

Netanyahu told Fox that once the attacker had been subdued and tied up by passengers and crew, he was "calling out to the aircrew 'kill me, kill me', so it's clear he was suicidal that's not a question".

"And with all the passengers in there, and if you couple that with what I just told you about the Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that were found in his background, I think ... that'll give us a pretty good clue but again I don't make final conclusions yet but that's the indications we have now."
The prime minister was also asked earlier on the same network whether there was an indication if Iran was involved, he replied: "It's too early to say".
The attacker was arrested in Saudi Arabia and is expected to be transferred to the UAE, Netanyahu said.
Both Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the stabbed pilot, Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar was a "hero".
India's ambassador to the UAE Deepak Mittal visited Captain Machhar in hospital on Thursday, the Indian Mission confirmed on social media, stating he was "in good health and recovering well".

blocks.caption: Image caption, The Indian government has praised Smit Machchhar for his "immense courage"

blocks.text: Image source, Embassy of India in Israel
The Indian government has praised Smit Machchhar for his "immense courage"
Preliminary findings from a separate Israeli investigation into the incident, suggest that the alleged attacker intended to crash the plane, an Israeli security source told BBC Arabic.
The source said the investigation - led by Israel's intelligence agency Mossad - interviewed passengers after they arrived in Tel Aviv to establish what had happened on the plane.
Flydubai's flight FZ1073, with more than 170 people on board, took off from Dubai International Airport in the UAE at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time), en route to Ben Gurion Airport.
Two hours later, the 17,000ft drop in altitude was reported on the plane tracking website Flightradar24 and minutes later the plane signalled an emergency code.

blocks.caption: Map showing the route of Flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The plane departed Dubai at 03:05 GMT and flew northwest across Saudi Arabia towards Israel. Near the Israel-Jordan border, the aircraft declared a general emergency at 05:31 and a hijacking alert at 05:38 before turning away…

blocks.text: At about 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent, landing safely at Tabuk Airport in the north west of Saudi.
Flydubai has since suspended flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv as it carried out its own investigation into the incident.
Israel's Transportation Ministry said the suspension aligns with Netanyahu's directive.
Israeli airlines including El Al, Israir and Arkia said plans were in place to operate rescue flights from Dubai starting on Friday to bring back stranded passengers.
The Transportation Ministry also said it sent an urgent request to Etihad Airlines to increase the number of flights between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv.

articles.title: Finland probes suspected break-ins at politicians' homes
articles.summary: The Finnish prime minister has not ruled out the possibility of foreign involvement in the suspected break-ins at the homes of members of parliament.

image.caption: Officials are speaking of a "significant" number of break-ins and attempted intrusions at the homes of several MPs [FILE: March 2023]Image: Heikki Saukkomaa/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Finnish police are investigating a series of suspected break-ins at the homes of members of parliament, officials announced on Thursday.
Finland's Prime Minister Petteri Orpo was asked by a reporter if a foreign power could be behind the suspected intrusions, and he replied that it was "very possible... quite possible in these times."
"If someone tries to destabilize Finland, our sense of security, or our support for example for Ukraine, it has the opposite effect. It strengthens our unity," he added.
Meanwhile, Finnish President Alexander Stubb stated, "An attack against a member of parliament is an attack against democracy."
What do we know about break-ins?

After the media reported on the alleged intrusions, speaker of parliament Jussi Halla-aho confirmed that parliament had been made aware of a "significant" number of break-ins and attempted intrusions at the homes of several politicians.
"I cannot comment precisely on the number of suspected cases known to us, but in any event, it is significant," Halla-aho said at a press conference.
He added, however, that the known cases had occurred over a longer period of time, with the first believed to have taken place about a year ago.
Halla-aho also emphasized that, at this point, no information is available about the motive or the perpetrator.
Paula Risikko, the deputy speaker who leads the parliamentary security group, said she was informed of the suspicions last week.
She added that the Helsinki police had been tasked with the initial stage of the investigation.
A night in Finland's largest underground defense bunker
MPs advised to keep an eye out
Earlier this week, newspaper Ilta-Sanomat reported that MPs had been warned of potential break-ins and that the newspaper was aware of at least two home intrusions.
All members of parliament were told to keep an eye out, report any suspicious activity, and file police reports if necessary.
Helsinki police confirmed that a preliminary inquiry had been opened. "The inquiry is at an early stage, and the police have nothing further to comment on at this time," it said.

Since the Kremlin began its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Finland has been on high alert. The Nordic country, which shares a 1,340-kilometer (830-mile) border with Russia, abandoned its decades-long policy of military non-alignment and joined NATO in April 2023.
Finland previously accused Moscow of "hybrid warfare" and orchestrating a surge of migrants at their shared border in 2023. The Kremlin denied the allegations.
Edited by Zac Crellin

articles.title: This is how fast Swiss glaciers, the 'water tower of Europe,' are melting away
articles.summary: Glaciers in Switzerland lost 5.5 per cent of their ice volume this year, the second-biggest percentage drop on record. It's part of a trend that could have big impacts in a country reliant on…

image.caption: Tourists gather at the glacier-feed Oeschinensee lake near Kandersteg, Switzerland, on Aug. 4. The country's glacier-monitoring service says Switzerland lost the second-highest percentage of glacier ice on record this year. (Hernan Munoz/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Science·New

Glaciers in Switzerland lost 5.5 per cent of their ice volume this year, the second-biggest percentage drop on record. It's part of a trend that could have big impacts in a country reliant on hydropower and which acts as the 'water tower of Europe,' feeding its major rivers.
Water lost so far this year is 4 times Switzerland's annual consumption

Glaciers in Switzerland — the home to the most in the Alps — lost 5.5 per cent of their ice volume this year, the second-biggest percentage drop on record due to heat waves and low winter snowfall, experts report.
"Alpine glaciers have no chance of surviving in the long term under such conditions," the GLAMOS Swiss glacier monitoring service and Swiss Academy of Sciences said in a statement Thursday.
The trend has worsened in recent years. Over the past five years alone, the volume of ice in Switzerland has declined by nearly a fifth, the experts say.
The report testifies to the latest concerns that global warming is wreaking havoc on Europe, the world's fastest-warming continent.

"The warming that we are experiencing now can be attributed 100 per cent to anthropogenic climate change. It's as simple as that," said Matthias Huss, who heads GLAMOS. "Without human emissions or fossil fuels we wouldn't have any warming at the moment."
Why low snowfall was a big problem

The record retreat of glacier ice in Switzerland came in 2022, when summer heat, low winter snowfall and an unusual smattering of reddish dust blown in from the Sahara darkened the glaciers and caused them to absorb more heat.
Huss said the snow cover in winter was important for two reasons.

"On the one hand, it protects the bare ice from melting. The longer you have snow, the longer you avoid the loss of old ice," said Huss in an interview at the Federal Polytechnic Institute ETHZ, where he is a glaciology professor.

"On the other hand, the snow is important also for generating new food for the glacier. The more snow you have, the higher the potential to keep some of the snow at high elevation and to form new ice."
Satellite images show glacier collapse that triggered flooding at Nepal-China border

The great thaw in Europe's legendary Alps is not alone: Experts say global warming helped to destabilize a Himalayan slope that collapsed in August and unleashed catastrophic and deadly flooding across Nepal. Satellites have shown vast shrinkage of glaciers in places like Greenland and Antarctica over the last half-century or so.

In Switzerland, in absolute terms, volume lost has been less than that in 2003, but the percentage decline this year is greater. That's because the total volume today is roughly a third of that 23 years ago. Back then, the relative loss was 3.5 per cent of total ice volume in Swiss glaciers.
What happens if Canada's thickest glaciers disappear?

Such accelerated ice melt has had an impact in Switzerland — the loss of 2.2 trillion litres from July to September amounts to four times the annual consumption of water in the country of about 9.1 million people. Switzerland gets more than half of its electricity from hydropower.
But the impact of accelerated glacier melt ripples far beyond: Switzerland is the water tower of Europe, and feeds some of the continent's most important rivers: the Danube, Po, Rhine and Rhone.

The experts say the "extreme melting" faced by Switzerland's glaciers this year included a decline in the average thickness of individual glaciers between two and half and four metres — and a reduction of up to 10 metres on the tongue of some glaciers.
Which glaciers saw the biggest melt
The expert teams have fanned out to assess runoff and crevices caused by the running water through the glaciers, in part by dumping red dye into the streams to track the water flows.
The Allalin, Clarident, Rhone and Aletsch glaciers — Aletsch being the largest in the Alps — were among the glaciers to experience their biggest melt on record this year.
"We just need to stabilize the climate by reducing CO2 emissions and this will help the glaciers," said Huss, of GLAMOS, though he added that it is "almost too late" to save those in the Swiss Alps.

"For the ice in the polar regions like the ice sheets, there it's not yet too late," he said. "There, we can make a difference and we need to make a difference in order to limit sea level rise, for example, a factor that is a fundamental threat to billions of people living along the coast."

articles.title: Canadian Olympian Claire Thompson retires from PWHL to pursue medical career
articles.summary: Defender Claire Thompson, one of Canada's top women's hockey players, is retiring from the sport to become a doctor. The 28-year-old played with the PWHL's Vancouver Goldeneyes last season.

image.caption: Former Goldeneyes defender Claire Thompson set an Olympic record for points by a defender with 13 at the 2022 Beijing Games and finished with 17 points in 14 career Olympic games. (Ethan Cairns/Canadian Press/File)

blocks.text: PWHL·Updated
Defender Claire Thompson, one of Canada's top women's hockey players, is retiring from the sport to become a doctor. The 28-year-old played with the PWHL's Vancouver Goldeneyes last season.
28-year-old defender played 2 seasons in league with Frost, Goldeneyes
One of Canada's top women's hockey players is retiring from the sport to become a doctor.
Defender Claire Thompson announced her retirement Thursday on Instagram and in an exclusive interview with The Athletic.
The 28-year-old Toronto native won Olympic gold with Canada at the 2022 Beijing Games and silver earlier this year in Milan after putting her medical career on hold for two years.
Thompson set an Olympic record for points by a defender with 13 in Beijing and finished with 17 points in 14 career Olympic games.
She also won the Walter Cup with the PWHL’s Minnesota Frost in 2025 before spending last season with the expansion Vancouver Goldeneyes.

“A career in medicine has always been an overarching goal of mine and I feel that now is the best time in my life to step away from hockey,” Thompson told The Athletic. “I have achieved far more than I could have ever hoped for and I feel like I’m ready to step away and continue on the long road ahead of becoming an orthopedic surgeon.”
Thompson has returned to medical school at New York University.

In 2024, she had started school and hoped to also practice with the PWHL New York franchise (now known as the Sirens) when the league officially began play. But it wasn't a viable option, so Thompson chose hockey.
Helped Frost to second straight title
She declared for the 2024 PWHL draft and was selected third overall by the reigning champion Frost.
Thompson adjusted quickly following her time away from the game and was one of the PWHL's top defenders, helping Minnesota to a second consecutive title.

“That was such a fun run,” she recalled to The Athletic. “I feel so lucky to have been drafted by Minnesota … I really feel like it was just a fortunate happenstance that they took a chance on me after the year off."

items: Goldeneyes sign No. 1 PWHL draft pick Caroline Harvey to 3-year deal
PWHL hires hockey attorney Alison Izzi to be Goldeneyes GM

blocks.text: Thompson joined the Goldeneyes for the 2025-26 campaign, becoming the first player in franchise history and an alternate captain.
She scored and added an assist in Vancouver’s first game, played in front of a deafening crowd of 14,958 at Pacific Coliseum.

"Getting to play in front of Canadians and living back in Canada was something that was also really special,” said Thompson. “To be able to play my last season in Canada, in front of Canadian fans, was amazing.
She also represented Canada at the 2025 world championships and captured a silver medal.

articles.title: Underlying causes of recurrent bacterial vaginosis identified by Australian scientists
articles.summary:
Melbourne researchers behind previous BV transmission breakthrough turn attention to understanding why some cases are harder to cure

Australian scientists have identified two contributors…
articles.byline: Donna Lu Assistant editor, climate, environment and science

blocks.text: Australian scientists have identified two contributors to recurrent bacterial vaginosis infections, a common sexual health condition that affects about one in four women globally.

The condition, commonly called BV, is characterised by an imbalance of naturally occurring bacteria in the vagina, in which there is a reduction of “good” bacteria and an overgrowth of other mixed bacteria.
In March last year, researchers published a landmark study which found that BV can be sexually transmitted to women by male partners.
Concurrently treating women with the condition and their male sexual partners with antibiotics reduced BV recurrence rates by more than 60%, they found.
In new research, the same group of scientists set out to understand why about 20% of women treated concurrently with their partners were not cured of BV.

The study, published in The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology & Women’s Health, involved 188 couples: the women were given a weeklong course of oral antibiotics, while the men were treated with both oral and topical antimicrobials.
It identified two distinct pathways to recurring BV: persistence of the condition despite a weeklong course of antibiotics, and re-infection.

Study lead author Dr Lenka Vodstrcil, a senior research fellow at Monash University and Bayside Health’s Melbourne Sexual Health Centre, said: “For about two-thirds of women, the day after they finish treatment, they return to … an optimal vaginal microbiome”, which is characterised by an abundance of healthy Lactobacilli bacteria.

The other third of women had microbiomes suggesting “they may not have cleared their BV” before couples resumed sex after treatment, and were nearly three times more likely to get the condition again within four weeks.
A better understanding of “persistence of infection … helps us develop new strategies to cure more women from BV,” Vodstrcil said.

BV can be asymptomatic or can cause vaginal itching, burning and discomfort. Treatment is essential as the condition can increase susceptibility to other infections and is linked to complications in pregnancy and childbirth.

The study – which the researchers believe is the largest to date involving heterosexual couples receiving concurrent BV treatment – found that persistence and reinfection from partners were “distinct, but not mutually exclusive, pathways”.

Of the female participants, 30% used an intrauterine device, which the study found “could enhance the persistence of bacterial vaginosis following treatment in some women” but noted that further research was needed.
The scientists now plan to trial longer treatment lengths and combinations of multiple antibiotics.
“Our aim is to stop women from having two, three, four courses of antibiotics throughout the year, which was happening previously,” Vodstrcil said.

Study senior author Prof Catriona Bradshaw, head of research translation and mentorship at Monash University and the Melbourne Sexual Health Centre, said: “Using partner-treatment to mitigate re-infection and more intensive strategies that target persistence of BV-bacteria, we hope to create more effective treatment approaches that can be tailored to an individual and achieve higher levels of cure.”

Though the ethnicities of participants were “representative of urban Australia”, the study noted that its results “might not be generalisable to other global populations, including those in low-income and middle-income countries and in other settings with a high burden of bacterial vaginosis”.

articles.title: Million-dollar public servants: 11 staff at Australia’s Future Fund paid significantly more than the PM
articles.summary:
One executive received a $1.5m package last year, while 10 other staff received remuneration exceeding $1m each

  • Get our

blocks.text: Nearly a dozen federal public servants were paid more than $1m last year, with one receiving a $1.5m package worth more than double Anthony Albanese’s base salary.
The generous remuneration – which includes bonuses and allowances – has been criticised as insulting during a cost-of-living crisis and amid job cuts across the public service.
The 11 staff are employed by Australia’s sovereign wealth fund, the Future Fund, and have direct oversight and responsibility for its investments, worth $350bn.
One Future Fund manager employed at an “executive level 2” rank was paid $1.5m of taxpayer money last year, which is significantly more than the prime minister’s $622,000 salary.
All 11 staff are paid more than federal cabinet ministers and all but one department secretary, including the heads of Australia’s domestic intelligence agency and the federal police.
Their pay emerged after Greens senator Barbara Pocock asked the minister for the public service, Katy Gallagher, to justify the high remuneration in a question on notice in August.

A response from Gallagher’s office, tabled in parliament this week, said the fund operated in a “highly competitive global market” and the generous wages were needed to attract the best possible talent.
“The Future Fund delivered a return of 14.8% in the 12 months to June 2026, adding $37.4bn to increase the value of the investment portfolio to over $350bn,” the spokesperson said.
In the private sector, senior managers at major Australian banks commonly receive annual bonuses of more than $1m. But these salaries remain controversial with shareholders.
The spokesperson said the salaries were within government rules that state performance bonuses can only be used in limited circumstances.

“This includes positions that involve significant, at-risk investment outcomes and for Commonwealth entities and companies whose primary purpose is to operate in commercial markets – both of which apply to the Future Fund.”
Pocock was not satisfied by the response, and said “most taxpayers would be questioning if these payments are good value for money”.

“In a cost-of-living crisis, Australians are suffering and many would be outraged to learn that a dozen public servants are earning over a million dollars, and in some cases double what the prime minister earns,” said Pocock.
“What kind of public service work warrants a salary of $1m or 1.5m dollars? We’re not talking about secretaries running government departments but employees. How can the government justify this?”
The Future Fund declined to comment.
It comes amid budget pressures that last month resulted in the National Disability Insurance Agency announcing voluntary redundancies for the first time since its 2013 creation.

Several other government departments have also announced job cuts in recent months, including in the prime minister’s own department, home affairs and the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water.
In December, the Future Fund was criticised for spending $20,000 to send the chief executive’s then-assistanct on a scoping trop to assess hotels in the US and negotiate rates.
The fund told a Senate estimates hearing the trip led to annual savings of $30,000. The executive assistant and another person flew business class to the US.

articles.title: Matt Kean warns climate crisis ‘isn’t someone else’s problem’ as largest coal project in NSW history greenlit
articles.summary: Exclusive: Climate Change Authority chair says planning commission did not account for climate-related economic damage in NSW
articles.byline: Adam Morton, Graham Readfearn and Penry Buckley

blocks.text: A senior Albanese government climate adviser has challenged the state approval of the largest coalmining development in New South Wales’ history, arguing “climate change isn’t someone else’s problem”.

Matt Kean, the chair of the Climate Change Authority and a former NSW treasurer and energy minister, questioned why the state Independent Planning Commission had not weighed the economic cost of climate change caused by burning the coal from the Hunter Valley Operations mine before giving it the green light to run until 2045.

The commission said greenhouse gases from the coal mined near Singleton would contribute to climate change impacts that affected the “people, economy and environment of the Hunter region, NSW and globally”, but said those impacts were outweighed by local benefits, including “employment, economic activity, support for local business, ongoing royalties and taxation revenue”.

The decision was applauded by the NSW Labor premier, Chris Minns. In an interview on 2GB radio on Thursday, he said it was “the right decision” and “hugely important” for the state economy. “It props up, and is responsible for, literally thousands of direct and indirect jobs,” he said. “It also produces billions of dollars of royalties for the NSW government.”

Minns did not mention in the interview the development’s projected climate impact. The mine’s owners, Yancoal and Glencore, forecast it could lead to 809m tonnes of carbon dioxide – nearly double Australia’s annual climate pollution – being released into the atmosphere once the coal is exported and burned.

Kean said the commission had acknowledged the project would contribute to climate change, and evidence that found climate-related disasters could cost Australians at least $73bn a year by 2060. But he said it had not estimated the climate-related economic damage in NSW as it weighed the local costs and benefits of the mine expansion.

He pointed to a recent report by the UN Environment Programme that found the world was heading beyond 1.5C in global heating – a goal agreed in the 2015 Paris agreement – and stressed that costs would increase with “every fraction of a degree of warming”.

“Climate change isn’t someone else’s problem. Australians pay through it through high food prices, damaged infrastructure, disrupted businesses, and lower incomes. The hotter the planet gets, the bigger that bill becomes,” he said.

“This isn’t an abstract environmental issue. Climate change is already imposing economic costs on NSW households and businesses, and those costs rise as the planet gets hotter. For regional NSW, that means greater risks from extreme heat, drought, fire, and other extreme weather, alongside pressure on food production, infrastructure, and household incomes.”

The approval decision follows a protracted assessment that drew more than 10,000 public submissions. Without it, the export mine could have been forced to close in December. The approval was welcomed by Coal Australia and the NSW Minerals Council. The latter urged the Minns government to pass legislation to prevent climate activists challenging it in court.
after newsletter promotion
The mine expansion still needs approval under federal environment law before the end of the year. Climate impacts are not considered grounds to block a development under national legislation.

The Greens called on the Albanese government to rule out approving the extension before the November Cop31 climate summit in Turkey, where the federal climate change minister, Chris Bowen, will lead the negotiations. Anthony Albanese and Bowen will intend a Cop31 preparatory meeting in Fiji next week.

The Greens’ deputy leader, Steph Hodgins-May, said Australia had supported a global transition away from fossil fuels at previous summits but was “contemplating walking into the next summit having just approved a massive fossil fuel project”. “The prime minister should be listening to the Pacific communities on the frontline of the climate crisis,” she said.

Jacynta Fa’amau, a Pacific campaigner with the global organisation 350.org, said the decision was horrifying. “It’s not just the Pacific that will suffer. The science has made it very clear that whether Australia burns its coal at home or overseas, the wildfires, floods and droughts will remain at their front door,” she said.

articles.title: Anthropic pushes for opt-out model for Australian content as ABC warns of ‘cannibalisation’ of news
articles.summary:
Maker of Claude claims AI could transform economy but ABC and SBS say the technology should be subject to media regulations

  • Get our

blocks.text: AI giant Anthropic has urged the Albanese government to consider giving “conditional approval” for big tech to train its models on Australian copyrighted works under an opt-out model, after conceding it won’t secure a blanket copyright exemption.

But Australia’s public broadcasters, the ABC and SBS, have strongly criticised AI firms, calling on the government to enact strict new rules to compensate media organisations and protect public interest journalism.

In submissions to a federal parliamentary inquiry, the ABC demanded AI companies be subject to the same copyright, defamation and privacy rules as media outlets, warning of a “cannibalisation” of mainstream news.
The ABC and SBS also suggested the government include AI companies in the news bargaining incentive, which would require them to make commercial deals with large media outlets to support journalism.

“As publishers, AI-based services are currently unregulated and receive more favourable treatment than established Australian media. This unequal treatment will accelerate the cannibalisation of the Australian news industry,” the ABC said in its submission.

SBS said AI-powered large language models – such as ChatGPT or Claude – were “challenges to the sustainability of the Australian news industry and the erosion of information integrity and public trust through their use of news content without permission, attribution or compensation”.

The joint select committee on AI will hold a series of hearings in Sydney next week, with executives from Anthropic to attend along with those from OpenAI, after it admitted one of its AI agents had accessed Services Australia data in June.

In a newly published submission, Anthropic said there was “light and shade” to be considered around the development of AI. It claimed the technology could “transform the Australian economy, drive a new wave of productivity” and “solve some of the nation’s biggest challenges”, but also warned of “serious implications for Australia’s national security, the resilience of its critical infrastructure and the safety of its people”.

The company talked up its plans for investing billions in Australia, including large new datacentres, and urged the government to support “frontier model training”. But one sticking point raised by AI companies has been access to Australian copyrighted works – such as news, books, music and other written material – to help train AI models.

The Labor government has ruled out a so-called text and data mining exemption, with the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, promising “the strongest possible protection” for Australian creatives. But questions have lingered about other possible copyright changes and the suggestion of an opt-out measure, allowing copyright holders to choose whether their content can be accessed by AI companies.
Anthropic’s submission called on Australia to “provide legal certainty under copyright that brings AI developers to the table while advancing its national cultural interests”.
after newsletter promotion

“Anthropic accepts that broad exceptions from copyright, such as a text and data mining exception, have not received widespread support and have been ruled out by the Government. As an alternative, we believe that the Government could permit AI model training through a narrow form of conditional approval,” the company submitted.

It suggested the implementation of “do not crawl” signals through robots.txt files – which tell bots what they may and may not access – and said the company was “open” to supporting Australian creators.
However SBS said that such an opt-out measure may not work.

“Robots.txt mechanisms are routinely ignored or bypassed, and the blocking of ever-evolving training bots increases the burden on rightsholders to monitor and update protections, when the onus should be on AI companies to avoid wrongdoing,” the broadcaster said in its submission.
The ABC complained that AI companies did not abide by the same rules as media outlets, calling the current system “anti-competitive”.
Both broadcasters called for AI to be included in the news bargaining incentive – with which big tech platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, Google, TikTok and Snapchat have been forced to comply.

articles.title: Global bond sell-off intensifies, as UK long-term borrowing costs pass 6%
articles.summary: Fears that US deficit is unsustainable drive yields on Treasury bills and UK gilts to multi-decade highs

blocks.text: The turmoil in global bond markets has intensified amid fears the US deficit is reaching unsustainable levels, helping drive UK long-term borrowing costs to a 28-year high.

The threat of a renewed round of inflation from the persistently high cost of oil has spooked investors, who believe central banks will be forced to raise interest rates in the coming months to prevent price increases from becoming embedded.
In a morning of hectic trading on Thursday, the yield, which is a proxy for the interest rate, hit 6% on Britain’s 30-year bonds for the first time since 1998.
The yield on five- and 10-year UK bonds also rose, driving up the government’s borrowing costs and adding to the pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before the budget later this month.
The sell-off also drove US government borrowing costs to 24-year highs on Thursday, with 10-year Treasury bill yields hitting 5.34%.
Thirty-year US Treasury bond yields rose above 5.67%, hitting their highest level since May 2002.

Stock market investors also sold heavily, knocking 1.7% off the FTSE 100 in London during early trading. Bourses in other parts of Europe were also hit, with Germany’s Dax and France’s CAC 40 falling by 1.1%.

“There is carnage in the bond market which is hitting stocks hard,” said Neil Wilson, the investor strategist at Saxo UK. “It looks like the relentless rout in the bond market is sending investors running for cover.”
By midday in the UK, the sell-off had eased, pulling the 30-year bond yield back below 6% and lifting share prices off their lows.
But yields then pushed higher in afternoon trading, back over the 6% mark.
The bond sell-off around the world is being driven by fears of high inflation, as the Middle East conflict continues to restrict oil supplies from the region.
Japan’s 10-year yield rose towards the 30-year high set last month.
after newsletter promotion

US bonds weakened despite inflation data on Wednesday coming in lower than forecast, which was expected to calm investors’ nerves about the prospect of further increases in the cost of borrowing by the US Federal Reserve.
Traders remain anxious that the Fed will continue to raise interest rates to fight inflation, mainly in response to the strength of the US economy and the prospect of workers bidding up their wages.
Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies, said there was growing concern at the amount of debt being issued to fund government deficits, as well as inflation concerns.
“Inflation, deficit and issuance concerns continue to weigh on the bond market,” he said.

“There is also a buyers’ strike as investors do not want to step in till we get some form of stability. Hedge funds have suffered in the latest round of sell-off and do not have the risk appetite to fade the move. Real money, potentially has the risk appetite, but won’t step in till we get some stability.”

Axel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “While the latest data has reduced expectations of an October Fed rate hike, investors remain wary that persistent inflation and higher oil prices could keep rates elevated for longer.
“The dollar is benefiting from that caution, climbing to a three-month high, while the prospect of a December rate increase keeps pressure on bond markets.”

articles.title: Renee Good's family sues Trump admin over fatal ICE shooting
articles.summary: The family of Renee Good, one of two US citizens fatally shot by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis in January, has sued President Donald Trump's administration alleging negligence and civil…

image.caption: The deployment of federal border forces in Minneapolis in January led to protests, which were only amplified after the fatal shootings of Renee Good and another US citizen [FILE: January 11, 2026]Image: Lisi Niesner/REUTERS

blocks.text: Relatives of Renee Good, the 37-year-old woman shot dead in her car in Minneapolis by a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent on January 7 this year, are suing the US government in a civil lawsuit connected to her death that was filed on Thursday.

Good and her wife had been taking part in daily protests in the city against the deployment of armed and often masked federal agents deployed to Minnesota to arrest and identify undocumented migrants for deportation.

The lawsuit alleges "federal conspiracy with discriminatory design and authorized use of force against observers," saying that this resulted in "extreme and unconstitutional force" being exerted against "people exercising their rights under the [US] constitution's Bill of Rights."

Good's killing, followed two weeks later by the death of nurse Alex Pretti, intensified the already-sizeable protests against the deployment of ICE and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents in Minneapolis known as Operation Metro Surge.

blocks.caption: The deaths of Renee Good and later Alex Pretti led to widespread protests in Minneapolis, and a winding-down of Operation Metro Surge, which ceased entirely by mid-FebruaryImage: Stephen Maturen/Getty Images

blocks.text: What do the lawsuits allege?

The plaintiffs in the twin civil suits from the Romanucci Blandin Law firm, filed on October 1, are Good's brother Brent Ganger — acting as trustee for her other next of kin including her three children — and her partner Becca Good.
One names the United States of America as the sole defendant.

The other names a series of responsible government and border control officials, including but not limited to the ICE officer who shot Good in her car, White House Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy Stephen Miller, and the US Secretary of Homeland Security at the time of the shooting, Kristi Noem.

"Renee's death was not an accident," Romanucci Blandin Law wrote in a statement. "It was the predictable result of a coordinated campaign by senior officials in this administration to target Minnesotans of Somali or Hispanic origin and silence anyone who dared to raise their voice in protest."
Minnesota killing spurs backlash over ICE enforcement

They allege that Operation Metro Surge "was built on exaggerated fraud accusations that the White House embraced as a pretext for thousands of masked, unidentified federal agents to rove neighborhoods and stop people based on how they looked."
It said that government officials "told agents to force confrontations with observers like Renee and led agents to believe that they would face no consequences for using force."

The crackdown in Minneapolis, which has a large Somali population, came as part of President Donald Trump's tough stance on migration and border security, and amid his assertions that local authorities in some Democrat-run states do an inadequate job fighting crime and irregular migration.
More to follow...

articles.title: AMLC testimony on VP Sara, Mans' bank records moved to Monday, Oct. 5, 2026
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court has ruled that the presentation of the AMLC's reports on covered and suspicious transactions involving the Vice President and her husband will begin on Monday.

blocks.text: Published October 1, 2026 10:40pm

The Senate impeachment court has ruled that the presentation of the Anti-Money Laundering Council's (AMLC) reports on covered and suspicious transactions involving Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio will begin on Monday, October 5.

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero made the ruling after defense counsel Sheila Sison objected to the prosecution’s scheduled presentation on Thursday, saying they only got the summaries of AMLC reports around 11 a.m. on that day.

“I did not consider the sidebar of Attorney Sheila [Sison of the defense] as a motion for reconsideration [of an earlier ruling]. On the requested time of the respondent to prepare to adequately prepare for the AMLC…out of courtesy and equity, the chair grants the time requested by the counsel for the correspondent for time to prepare for the cross examination, rather, to prepare for the direct and cross examination of the AMLC witness on Monday,” Escudero added.

The earlier ruling being referred to by Escudero was issued by the impeachment court last July 20 wherein the court noted that while Section 8A of the Anti-Money Laundering Law regulates unauthorized and arbitrary disclosures by AMLC personnel, the provision “does not constitutionally and cannot nullify the lawful subpoena powers of the Senate sitting as an impeachment court.”

It was House prosecutor Chel Diokno of Akbayan party-list who invoked the ruling, saying the same court decision also states that a compliance with the lawful constitutional subpoena, including that of the Senate impeachment court, “is a justifying circumstance that, if at all, would extinguish any penal liability under Article 11, Paragraph 6 of the Revised Penal Code for any person acting in obedience to an order issued by a superior or some other lawful purpose.”
House lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro earlier told the Senate impeachment court that their witness, AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura, would testify on the following documents:

items: Summary of covered transaction reports (CTRs) and suspicious transaction reports (STRs) submitted by the Anti Money Laundering Council (AMLC) to the Senate Impeachment court
Summary of all CTRs and STRs involving 15 juridical persons from 2007 to 2025
Summary of all CTRs and STRs involving Vice President Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio from 2022 to 2025
Summary of CTRs and STRs involving the 15 juridical persons from 2022 to 2025
Summary of CTRs and STRs pertaining to inward remittances to Calle 88 Foods Corporations from China and other countries
Summary of CTRs and STRs involving insurance policies and investment-related transactions.

blocks.text: In a separate press conference, private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan argued that the laws are clear that the impeachment case is not covered by existing laws on confidentiality of bank records and bank transactions.

"The impeachment proceeding is an exception to the rules on Bank Secrecy and AMLA [Anti-Money Laundering Act] and the rules on confidentiality. The defense's argument [against it] will not hold," Kapunan said.
House hearings

During the House justice panel hearings on the impeachment complaints against Vice President Sara Duterte, Buenaventura testified that bank transactions totaling P6.7 billion—classified as covered and suspicious—were recorded under the names of the Vice President and her husband, Manases Carpio.
Of the total amount, P3.7 billion was attributed to the Vice President, while P2.998 billion was linked to Carpio.
The report also identified P791 million in transactions as having undetermined inflows and outflows.

“Vice President Sara Duterte’s accounts generated a total of 371 large transactions and 30 suspicious transactions from Oct. 13, 2005 to Jan. 28, 2026, with transaction amounts reaching as high as P55.158 million,” Buenaventura said, reading from the report submitted to the House justice panel.

“A review of the identified inflow transactions shows total inflows of approximately P1.51 billion, recorded only from 2006 to 2022. These inflows are largely dominated by credit memo transactions amounting to P1.41 billion, which account for the majority of recorded inflows. Other notable sources include check deposits totaling P48.33 million, deposit transactions amounting to P45.73 million, and cash deposits of P4.95 million,” the AMLC report added. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: SILG Remulla urges Velasco couple to return to PH, take polygraph test over alleged cash delivery to Duterte family
articles.summary: Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Thursday urged former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco and his wife to return to the Philippines amid allegations linking them to cash deliveries to members of…

blocks.text: Published October 1, 2026 10:35pm

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Thursday urged former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco and his wife to return to the Philippines amid allegations linking them to cash deliveries to members of the Duterte family.
In an ambush interview, Remulla challenged the Velasco couple to undergo a polygraph test.
“I dare the Velasco couple to come home and take the same polygraph para makita natin kung sino talaga nagsasabi ng totoo,” he said.
(I dare the Velasco couple to come home and take the same polygraph so we can see who is really telling the truth.)
Remulla issued the call after former police officer Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. underwent a polygraph examination administered by the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI).

Gracioso surfaced last week and claimed that he delivered suitcases containing over P2 billion in cash to Vice President Sara Duterte, her father former president Rodrigo Duterte, and her brother Representative Paolo Duterte.
The ex-cop said he was ordered by Velasco while he was the lawmaker’s former security aide.

According to Remulla, the lie detector test indicated that Gracioso was telling the truth when asked about his alleged delivery of cash. However, Remulla acknowledged that polygraph results are not admissible in court.

Remulla also acknowledged that Gracioso has a problematic past including dismissal from the service, suspension, and administrative cases. But the DILG head said these do not necessarily invalidate the ex-cop’s allegations.
“But even a broken clock is correct twice a day,” Remulla said.
Meanwhile, Remulla said that Velasco and his wife, Rowena, are currently in Niseko, one of the most exclusive vacation spots in Japan.

“They are in Niseko, Japan. Meron silang bahay roon na the most exclusive vacation spot sa buong Japan. Mahal doon sa Niseko, mayayaman lang nakakapunta doon. So far, to our information, nandoon silang mag-asawa,” he said.

(They are in Niseko, Japan. They have a house there, which is the most exclusive vacation spot in Japan. It's expensive in Niseko, only the rich can go there. So far, to our information, they are there.)
Earlier, the Bureau of Immigration (BI) confirmed that Velasco is currently not in the Philippines, saying there is no derogatory record preventing his departure from the country.
The BI also noted that there is no existing hold departure order against Velasco.

GMA News Online is attempting to reach out to the former lawmaker for comment. His camp on Saturday released a statement on what it called “fabricated attacks” against him, saying the allegations have “no basis.”
Vice President Sara Duterte on Saturday said she does not know Gracioso and refuted his claims she received money from him.

articles.title: Alto high-speed rail project likely to cost more than originally thought: budget watchdog
articles.summary: Building the proposed high‑speed rail project between Toronto-Quebec City could cost between $75 billion and $113 billion — higher than the official initial estimates, according to a new report from…

image.caption: This 3D rendering shows what an Alto high-speed train could look like. The Crown corporation is overseeing a project exploring a potential high-speed corridor between Toronto and Quebec City. (Alto)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Building the proposed high‑speed rail project between Toronto-Quebec City could cost between $75 billion and $113 billion — higher than the official initial estimates, according to a new report from the Parliamentary Budget Office.
New report says Toronto-Quebec City corridor project could between $75B to $113B

Building the proposed high‑speed rail project between Toronto and Quebec City could cost between $75 billion and $113 billion — higher than the official initial estimates, according to a new report from the Parliamentary Budget Office.

Following a request from the Senate finance committee, the federal budget watchdog released a report on Thursday trying to put a dollar figure on the government's controversial Alto high-speed rail corridor, which promises to connect Toronto and Montreal in about three hours.
Alto, the Crown corporation responsible for the major infrastructure project, is also looking at a potential stop in Kingston, Ont.

The Parliamentary Budget Office said based on analysis of international construction experience and assumed characteristics of the proposed Canadian route, the baseline route, excluding Kingston, could cost between approximately $75 billion and $113 billion to construct.
"This range reflects the considerable uncertainty inherent in large-scale rail infrastructure projects," said the report.

items: Could the Alto high speed rail plan be derailed?
Kingston probably getting high-speed rail stop, says Alto CEO

blocks.text: That's billions more than the official estimates of between $60 billion and $90 billion.

The main drivers of the cost are the tunnels and elevated structures used in the project. The budget watchdog said international evidence indicates that each additional kilometre of tunnel will add $169 million to the total cost of this project, while an additional kilometre of elevated structures will add $153 million.

Adding a stop in Kingston, Ont., is expected to increase uncertainty, the report notes, "due to the counter-balancing effects of easier geography for construction, but higher density of regional populations and greater ecological sensitivity."
Liberal Transport Minister Steve MacKinnon has defended the project as a way to "build a strong economy and create new opportunities for Canadians."
Conservatives call the proposal a costly "boondoggle." The project has also received vocal opposition from Eastern Ontario residents living along the proposed route.

articles.title: Rick Ross arrested on domestic battery and strangulation charges
articles.summary: The rapper was arrested in Miami Beach on Thursday, days after an ex-girlfriend accused him of physical abuse

blocks.text: Rick Ross has been arrested on domestic violence charges in Miami Beach, according to local police.
The rapper was booked at Turner Guilford Knight correctional center at 6.10am local time on Thursday and faces one felony count of battery by strangulation as well as a misdemeanor count of battery.
Bond has been listed at $6,000, according to Miami-Dade jail and court records.
Local authorities have not specified the circumstances that led to Ross’s arrest or details of the alleged incident. They also do not identify the alleged victim of the charges.
The Guardian has reached out to the musician’s representative for comment.
The arrest comes days after Rick Ross’s ex-girlfriend Jazzma Kendrick alleged that the rapper was physically abusive to her, People magazine reported.

“He saw a punching bag,” she wrote on an Instagram story after sharing images of a swollen lip that she said was caused by Ross. Alongside the picture she wrote: “The day Rick busted my lip and the day I left.”
“I don’t know a lot of things, but I do know that a man that puts his hands on me, is a man that never loved me and never will,” Kendrick posted over another image.
“It’s always good until it isn’t,” she said. “If a man hits you one time, he will do it again. Don’t give him the opportunity. Value your life and leave.”

Rick Ross, born William Leonard Roberts, is a longtime Miami resident with five No 1 albums and hit collaborations with Drake, DJ Khaled and Nicki Minaj, among many others. In July he released his 12th studio album, Set In Stone, which featured Gucci Mane, The-Dream and Yung Miami.
Local court records say that Ross has retained attorney Bradley Horenstein. His arraignment is set for 22 October.
