articles.title: Naomi Campbell wins legal challenge over charity trustee ban
articles.summary:
Supermodel was disqualified from role in 2024 after Charity Commission accused her of misusing funds and abdicating responsibilities

Naomi Campbell has won a legal challenge to overturn a…

blocks.text: Naomi Campbell has won a legal challenge to overturn a five-year ban on being a charity trustee after judges found she was unaware of serious misconduct at the charity she set up and helped oversee for several years.

In 2024, the 56-year-old supermodel was disqualified from being a charity trustee for five years after the Charity Commission – which regulates charities in England and Wales – found mismanagement of funds at Fashion for Relief, which she founded.

Campbell brought a case to the first tier tribunal to overturn the ban earlier this year, saying she had been “deceived” by fellow trustee Bianka Hellmich, who had forged documents and lied about her credentials as a charity lawyer.
The commission argued Campbell had “completely abdicated” her responsibilities as a trustee and was “highly culpable” for failures of governance and misuse of funds.

This included use of charity funds to pay for Campbell’s stay at a five-star hotel in Cannes, France, as well as spa treatments, room service and cigarettes, and paying a trustee £316,000 in unauthorised fees and travel expenses.

However, in a judgment on Thursday a tribunal ruled in the supermodel’s favour. The judges Joe Neville and James Armstrong-Holmes, sitting with a third member, said: “There was serious misconduct and mismanagement in the administration of the charity she founded, Fashion for Relief.

“The tribunal has found, however, that its most serious features, including unauthorised payments to Ms Campbell’s co-trustee, Bianka Hellmich, failures in the management of the charity’s finances and the misuse of its funds, resulted from Ms Hellmich’s conduct and were concealed from Ms Campbell.”
Campbell was one of three of the charity’s trustees to be disqualified as a result of the investigation, with Hellmich disqualified for nine years, and Veronica Chou for four years.
The judges said Hellmich “used forged documents” and also deceived professional advisers and the Charity Commission.
They added: “Ms Campbell was not involved in, and did not know of, that conduct.”

The judges also said while Campbell shared responsibility for the charity failing to file its accounts on time, this did not mean she was unfit to be a charity trustee in the circumstances of the case “including the sustained deception” she had faced.
It is understood to be the second time a court has overturned a trustee disqualification order made by the commission.
During a four-day hearing in June, Campbell said her “only mistake” was trusting Hellmich, whom she alleged forged her signature and lied about her credentials.

“I don’t look at it as a failure, I look at it as me trusting someone that I knew, someone that was a lawyer,” Campbell said, telling the London tribunal that she and the Charity Commission had been deceived.
Speaking to the Guardian, Hellmich previously said there was “absolutely no truth” to Campbell’s claims.
The judges rejected criticisms made by lawyers for the commission about Campbell’s evidence, including that the supermodel was focused on “controlling the media narrative”.

They said: “In our assessment none of Ms Campbell’s answers were capable of being taken as doing any such thing,” adding that her evidence and conduct while the charity operated “was entirely honest”.

A probe into Fashion for Relief was opened by the commission in 2021, after partner charities, including Save the Children and the Mayor’s Fund for London, received just a tiny fraction of the proceeds of events organised by Fashion for Relief for their benefit.
The charity was dissolved and removed from the register of charities in 2024.

It had been set up with the aim of uniting the fashion industry to relieve poverty and advance health and education by providing grants to other organisations and giving resources towards global disasters.

A Charity Commission spokesperson said its intervention had ensured £250,000 of funds raised for charities including Save the Children and The Mayor’s Fund for London was passed on to the organisations.
They added: “We made the disqualification order for Ms Campbell based on the evidence available to us at the time.

“The court recognised that Ms Campbell, the commission and the law firm concerned were subject to sophisticated deception by one of the other trustees. This was referred to the Metropolitan police when we became aware.
“We acknowledge and will reflect on the court’s decision and are considering any wider implications for our work.”

articles.title: Finnish PM says suspected break-ins at MPs’ homes could be work of foreign power
articles.summary:
Police investigating reports of politicians’ homes being broken into in last year with nothing being stolen

The Finnish prime minister, Petteri Orpo, has said a foreign power could be…

blocks.text: The Finnish prime minister, Petteri Orpo, has said a foreign power could be responsible for a series of suspected break-ins at the homes of several members of parliament.

Police said on Thursday they were investigating multiple reports of MPs’ homes being broken into in the Helsinki area in the last year in which nothing was stolen but subtle signs of breaking and entering were left.
When asked by a reporter if a foreign power could be behind the alleged intrusions, Orpo said: “It is very possible. Quite possible in this day and age.
“If someone tries to destabilise Finland, our sense of security, or our support for example for Ukraine, it has the opposite effect. It strengthens our unity.”
He said the incidents would be investigated by police and within government and would be “taken very seriously”.

With the Finnish parliamentary elections just six months away, Orpo said the risk of election interference must be taken seriously. “We see in several European countries that Russia has sought to influence elections,” he said.
Finland shares a long border with Russia that has been closed for years amid a rapid deterioration of relations since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and Finland joining Nato.
The Finnish president, Alexander Stubb, said when asked about the suspected incidents: “An attack on a member of parliament is an attack on democracy.
“It should not be allowed or accepted in any form … I stand in support of every member of parliament.”

At a press conference in parliament, the speaker, Jussi Halla-aho, said he did not have an exact number of suspected cases but that it was “significant”. He said it was the kind of behaviour associated with state actors.

“It is known that state actors sometimes engage in activities that resemble suspected cases, but we have no information to comment on at this time and there is no point in speculating,” Halla-aho said.
Observations had been made “drop by drop”, he said. “It is possible that the marks were left visible on purpose.”
According to the broadcaster Yle, suspected cases include doors being left open to homes and lights being left on.

Helsinki police said they had received information from parliament about suspected intrusions at the homes of MPs and had begun a preliminary inquiry. The force said in a statement: “The Helsinki police department is working closely with the national bureau of investigation in clarifying the matter. The inquiry is at an early stage, and the police have nothing further to comment on at this time.”

articles.title: West Coast oil pipeline becomes 1st project designated in national interest

image.caption: Workers lay pipe during construction of the Trans Mountain pipeline expansion on farmland, in Abbotsford, B.C., on May 3, 2023. A new West Coast pipeline will ship one million barrels of oil from Alberta to the B.C. coast once it opens in 2032-33. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·Breaking

The federal and Alberta governments have announced that a proposed pipeline carrying one million barrels of oil a day from Alberta to the B.C. coast has become the first project designated in the national interest.
Classification under Building Canada Act will fast-track approval process, environmental assessments

A proposed pipeline carrying one million barrels of oil a day from Alberta to the B.C. coast has become the first project designated in the national interest, the federal and Alberta governments have announced.
Listing the West Coast oil pipeline on Schedule One of the Building Canada Act means the federal government has moved from considering whether it should be built to how it will be built.

A senior government official told reporters in advance of the announcement that the pipeline is expected to boost Canada's GDP by up to $30 billion annually — $20 billion of that coming from the pipeline itself.

By diversifying Canada's exports away from the U.S., officials said Canada will be able to charge a higher price for the oil it currently ships south of the border, providing what could be an additional $10 billion a year in revenues.
The federal government also said that once approved, the project once will create up to 140,000 jobs.

articles.title: Germany expresses optimism over Montenegro's EU ambitions
articles.summary: Germany's top diplomat said Montenegro has made "remarkable progress" in the accession process. The small Balkan state is being seen as a frontrunner among six regional candidates.

image.caption: The EU has been conducting accession talks with Montenegro and Serbia since 2012 and 2014 respectivelyImage: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany on Thursday expressed optimism regarding Montenegro's bid to become part of the European Union.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said that the Western Balkans country's ambition to join the bloc was being "heard in Brussels and in all European capitals."
Wadephul made the comments after traveling to Montenegro on Wednesday to attend the annual meeting of European foreign ministers as part of the so-called Berlin Process.
Montenegro has its sights on the EU
What did Wadephul say?
"Montenegro has made remarkable progress towards EU membership – it thus sets an example for the Western Balkans," Wadephul said in a post on X.

He posted up a picture of himself embracing Ibrahimovic and thanked him for hosting the Berlin Process Foreign Minister's meeting, adding that there had been agreement to "foster regional cooperation on reconciliation and reforms."
"Those who are willing and able to join the European Union and meet the criteria can succeed in the coming years," said Wadephul at the meeting with his Montenegrin counterpart Ervin Ibrahimovic.
EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos was also at the talks held in the coastal city of Budva.
EU candidate countries in the Western Balkans are Montenegro, Albania, Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and North Macedonia. Kosovo is also a potential candidate for membership.
Montenegro's EU ambition not just a pipe dream
Of the six Western Balkan candidates, Montenegro is seen as the frontrunner, having been pursuing membership for 22 years.
The small, mountainous nation of 623,000 people adopted the euro as its de facto currency as early as 2002, declared independence from the union with Serbia in 2006, and joined NATO in 2017.
With public support for accession reportedly at around 80%, Montenegro is aiming to become the EU's 28th member state by 2028.
Montenegro: Crackdown on crime and clans

Progress on economic and democratic reforms previously prompted the EU's enlargement commissioner to flag the possibility of completing technical negotiations by the end of the year, making the 2028 timeline appear realistic.

Among the other Western Balkan countries, Albania is also seen as a promising candidate, but Kosovo's path to EU membership remains the most complicated, with five EU member states still refusing to recognize its independence from Serbia.

articles.title: Canadian Joshua Kutryk and Crew-13 astronauts set to launch to International Space Station

image.caption: The crew for the upcoming NASA-SpaceX launch, from left: Canada's Joshua Kutryk, Russia's Sergey Teteryatnikov, NASA commander Jessica Watkins and NASA pilot Luke Delaney at the Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Fla., on Saturday. (John Raoux/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Canada’s next astronaut in space has a big scheduling conflict
Canada's next astronaut to spend 6 months on the International Space Station — and miss the birth of his 3rd child
The Latest

items: Four astronauts, including Canadian Joshua Kutryk, are scheduled to launch to the International Space Station (ISS) today in a joint NASA-Space X mission.
NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins, Luke Delaney and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov make up the rest of the crew on board SpaceX's Dragon spacecraft.
The team will join several astronauts who are already on the ISS to conduct several experiments, some of which are Canadian.
The launch from Cape Canaveral, Fla., is set for 11:10 a.m. ET.

blocks.text: Pinned
Blast-off scheduled for 11:10 a.m. ET
I’m senior science reporter Nicole Mortillaro down here in Florida for Joshua Kutyrk's launch to the International Space Station (ISS) as part of NASA's Crew-13.
Not gonna lie: I'm a little sleep deprived after catching a shuttle from the press site to the New Center at 5:15 this morning, but the adrenaline is overriding everything else!
It's only been six months since Canada's Jeremy Hansen made history by flying around the moon. Now, it's Joshua Kutryk's turn to blast off into space.
Kutryk and three fellow astronauts are launching to the International Space Station (ISS) today in a joint NASA-Space X mission. The crew will be living and working on the ISS for roughly six months.

"I never, ever, ever, ever … thought that I would have this opportunity to go out on behalf of Canada and do a mission like this," Kutryk, the flight's Canadian astronaut, said during a media call on Wednesday.

The crew will blast off inside SpaceX's Crew Dragon from Cape Canaveral, Fla. The launch was postponed from Sept. 12 due to an issue with the spacecraft, but Kutryk has said he has faith the vehicle is ready to fly.
The Crew-13 launch, as it's called, also includes NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins, Luke Delaney and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteriatnikov.
The crew will join several astronauts who are already on station and will conduct several experiments, some of which are Canadian.

items: October 1A difficult jobNicole MortillaroHeather Kutryk at this morning's walkout. (Shawn Benjamin/CBC)Being an astronaut sounds pretty cool to some people (count me in!), but let’s not forget the challenges that come with that.You’re training for years, oftentimes with long hours and trips around the world. You also are waiting to find out when your mission will come up. It takes a lot of patience and drive.But then, finally, comes the day: Launch day. Imagine leaving everything you have ever known behind, especially your loved ones.Joshua Kutryk may be blasting off to live a dream, but he’s also leaving his wife — who is pregnant — and two children behind as he embarks on a dangerous mission.

Off to space, with a new baby on the wayVerity StevensonISS mission 'starting to feel real,' says wife of Canadian astronaut Joshua KutrykIt's t-minus two days before Alberta-born astronaut Joshua Kutryk heads to the International Space Station (ISS) in a joint NASA-SpaceX mission. Kutryk and his crew will join several astronauts who are already on the station and conduct experiments, some of which are Canadian.As the crew prepared for launch this week, they got to spend time with their families who were quarantining along with them in a hotel in Cape Canaveral, Fla. Heather Kutryk, Joshua Kutryk's wife, says she and the couple's two children, Anna, 5, and Peter, 7, have been enjoying trips to the beach with their dad before his six-month space odyssey. "It's just good quality family time leading up to the launch and I'm grateful for that," said Kutryk.Kutryk is pregnant and due to give birth in November during Joshua's mission. She said she isn't stressed about the delivery because of the strong community and support she has around her. "It was a bit of a surprise — not exactly planned, but you know, it's a great thing," she said, laughing. The family has lived in Houston since 2017, with Joshua training and preparing for this launch for years. He's undergone intense physical training, learned Russian and travelled to Los Angeles, Europe, Japan and Russia in preparation, his wife said.Anna and Peter also seem to be taking their father's departure in stride, although Peter has had his moments, his mother said. "Both Josh and Peter have a really special bond. So, I think it's hitting him a little bit harder. Anna, she's just independent. She's very strong-willed and she's just kind of like, 'All right, I'll see you later, Dad. We're good!'"Kutryk, too, says she feels OK about her husband's departure because it's been years in the making.Still, she said, "maybe it'll hit me when he's actually gone, but so far I feel like we're going to be great."

Who is Joshua Kutryk?Nicole MortillaroMeet Joshua Kutryk, the next Canadian to go to spaceNASA has announced that Expedition 75, the next crew to go to the International Space Station, will include Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk. Kutryk, NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov will spend several months aboard the ISS.Kutryk was born on March 21, 1982, in Fort Saskatchewan, Alta., where he was raised on a cattle farm. His interests include backcountry skiing, mountaineering, cycling and paragliding (sounds like he really likes being high up!).He's been a test pilot, a fighter pilot and is still a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force.In 2017, he was recruited by the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) alongside Jenni Gibbons, who served as Jeremy Hansen's backup for the Artemis II mission around the moon back in April.He graduated from astronaut training in 2020 and was certified for capcom (short for "capsule communication," a term left over from the old NASA days) for the ISS.He's trained in caves, which tests astronauts' physical and mental endurance needed for long-duration space missions, and participated in a lunar geology expedition at the Mistastin Lake Impact Crater in Labrador.He was supposed to fly on Boeing's CST-100 Starliner capsule to the ISS; however Boeing has suffered major setbacks to their spacecraft. That mission will now be uncrewed. Instead, he's flying on the much-tested SpaceX Crew Dragon where he sits right now.

Meet your crewNicole MortillaroCanadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, left, U.S. astronaut Luke Delaney, U.S. astronaut Jessica Watkins, and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov prepare to head to the SpaceX Dragon spacecraft in Cape Canaveral, Fla., this morning. (Marco Bello/AFP/Getty Images)Let's look at who makes up this Crew-13 launch.First, the name Crew-13 comes from the fact that it's SpaceX's 13th mission to be launched since NASA restarted flights from U.S. soil, following years of relying on the Russian space agency (Roscosmos) to get astronauts to the ISS. This happened after NASA cancelled its space shuttle program in 2011.While SpaceX and Boeing were both awarded contracts to build spacecraft to take astronauts to the ISS, so far only SpaceX has succeeded after Boeing suffered major setbacks.There are two NASA astronauts on this mission. Jessica Watkins is the spacecraft commander, and Luke Delaney is the pilot.Then there is Sergey Teteryatnikov from Roscosmos, who will be a mission specialist.And finally, we have our own Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency, who will also serve as a mission specialist.This will be the first flight for not only Kutryk, but also Delaney and Teteryatnikov.

Ready to goNicole MortillaroA Tesla vehicle awaits astronauts at the morning walkout. Three Teslas, including a Cybertruck, all had these same licence plates. (Shawn Benjamin/CBC)Before the crew head to their spacecraft for any mission, there is a traditional walkout from the quarantine building.Fences are put up around the area where the press gathers, but there’s a special area for the families and their astronaut escorts, who are all in quarantine. NASA administrator Jared Isaacman arrived and briefly went into the quarantine facility.There are a lot of photographers here, many of them old-timers who know the game and brought ladders to get the best view.Three Tesla cars were onsite to take the astronauts and others to the pad, all of which had licence plates that read "LUCKY 13." Because…you know.It was great to see Canadian astronaut David Saint-Jacques, who flew to the ISS in 2018, arrive with Kutyrk's daughter on his shoulders, while Kutryk's son and wife followed. His son pointed up towards the windows of the nearby building as NASA employees gathered at the windows. NASA employees don't seem to take these launches for granted.The Crew-13 astronauts soon walked out of the quarantine facility at 7:40 a.m., waving to the crowd and spending a few moments with their families.Kutryk's wife Heather was visibly moved, appearing to hold back tears and turn her face away. Eventually, the four astronauts entered their Teslas, and Joshua lowered his window as his son ran to give him a kiss.It was an emotional experience for us all.

Chances of favourable weather at launch: 40%John MazerolleA SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket with the company's Dragon spacecraft on top, on the launch pad at Space Launch Complex 40 yesterday at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. (Joel Kowsky/NASA/Getty Images)At last update, weather officials with the U.S. Space Force 45th Weather Squadron predicted a 40 per cent chance of favourable conditions at the launch pad for liftoff.There are a long list of weather criteria that must be met on launch day. NASA said this morning that the main concerns today are nearby cumulus clouds, cloud thickness and precipitation. Other non-weather related considerations need to be cleared before launch is ultimately given the green light.

articles.title: White House removes CNN from press pool for second time in a week
articles.summary:
Network was listed as primary TV pool covering Thursday’s presidential activities but then was abruptly removed

For a second time in a week, the White House has unilaterally removed CNN from…

blocks.text: For a second time in a week, the White House has unilaterally removed CNN from its assignment as the primary television pool representative covering Donald Trump.

CNN was excluded on Saturday from pool duty aboard Air Force One, despite a district judge’s ruling – two days earlier – overturning the White House’s ban on the network and two other media organizations.

But on Sunday, in what appeared to be a thawing of tensions, the White House published a pool assignment list that listed CNN as in-town pooler for Thursday’s activities, with the conservative network Real America’s Voice serving as secondary pooler.

Then, on Wednesday night, the White House abruptly removed CNN from pool duty for the following day, leaving Real America’s Voice as the only pooler as the president travels to Texas and Oklahoma. The country’s largest broadcast and cable television news networks have not aired Real America’s Voice footage, though the network has widely broadcast its availability.

The five networks that serve in the primary television pool have taken it day by day since the White House originally banned CNN on 18 September, initially suspending operation before tentatively kicking back into action this past Friday.
As they did on Saturday, none of the other four networks will take CNN’s place on Thursday, meaning there will be no primary pool footage, though networks could cover individual parts of his trip.
CNN did not comment on the network’s exclusion on Thursday.
A White House official sent a statement touting Trump’s accessibility and referring to television networks as “performative and dishonest”.

Earlier this week, lawyers for CNN, MS Now and Politico – the three outlets targeted by Trump’s ban – formally asked a judge to extend his ruling overturning the White House ban for a period of 14 days.

The judge in the case will soon hold a hearing to weigh arguments from both sides about whether the networks should be granted a preliminary injunction that would block the ban until the network’s 21 September lawsuit against the White House plays out.

articles.title: Tourette syndrome campaigner John Davidson to watch Bafta Scotland awards in separate ‘relaxed’ space
articles.summary:
Decision follows independent review into handling of February ceremony, where his involuntary tics caused a BBC crisis

John Davidson, the Tourette syndrome campaigner whose outburst at the…

blocks.text: John Davidson, the Tourette syndrome campaigner whose outburst at the British Academy film awards in February led to a crisis for Bafta (British Academy of Film and Television Arts) and the BBC, will attend the Bafta Scotland awards and watch the ceremony from a separate “relaxed” space.

In a letter sent to Bafta members on Thursday, the organisation’s chair Sara Putt and CEO Jane Millichip said that, after an independent review, Bafta had “strengthened and centralised our safeguarding, risk assessment and compliance processes” and had made arrangements in consultation with “safeguarding and inclusion experts” for Davidson’s attendance at the awards ceremony organised by Bafta’s Scottish branch, which is due to take place in November.

For the Bafta Scotland awards ceremony, Bafta says that, in accordance with Davidson’s own suggestion, he will “watch the ceremony via video link from a separate relaxed space within the venue with his family and friends”.

I Swear, the film based on Davidson’s life, is the leading contender with seven nominations at the Bafta Scotland awards, including all three nominations in the best film actor category, for Peter Mullan, Robert Aramayo and Scott Ellis Watson, and best film actress for Shirley Henderson. Aramayo unexpectedly won best actor at the national Bafta film awards in February.

As executive producer of I Swear, Davidson had been in attendance at the Baftas and was heard several times shouting during the ceremony, including using the N-word while actors Delroy Lindo and Michael B Jordan were on stage presenting the evening’s first prize. In a statement after the show, Davidson said he was “deeply mortified if anyone considers my involuntary tics to be intentional or to carry any meaning”. He added: “I have spent my life trying to support and empower the Tourette’s community and to teach empathy, kindness and understanding from others and I will continue to do so. I chose to leave the auditorium early into the ceremony as I was aware of the distress my tics were causing.”

The crisis became more acute after it emerged that Davidson’s outburst was audible during the BBC’s coverage of the event, despite the broadcast starting two hours later. The BBC apologised and suggested that producers overseeing the ceremony for the BBC were doing so from a truck and did not hear the slur.

articles.title: Russian dissident Garry Kasparov says US warned him of danger to his life
articles.summary: "My family and I will not truly be safe as long as Putin is in power," says the former chess world champion.

blocks.text: An exiled Russian opposition figure living in the US says he was warned by American and Lithuanian security services that his life was in danger.
Former chess world champion Garry Kasparov said he was one of two dissidents told to take precautions, which he had done.

His comments come after the US Justice Department unsealed an indictment earlier this month charging five people who allegedly work for a network linked to the Kremlin with plotting attacks and murders in countries including the US, focusing on Russian dissidents and defectors.

Kasparov wrote in his publication The Next Move that he had not been told explicitly that he and fellow Free Russia Forum co-founder Ivan Tyutrin were considered targets, but said both had been warned about their safety.

Spanish newspaper El Mundo reported that it had obtained information that Kasparov, along with another Russian opposition figure, Ilya Ponomarev, had been warned about the plot over the summer by US authorities.
Citing sources close to Kasparov, the paper said he had been placed under enhanced protection over the summer for the first time since he moved to the US.
Kasparov wrote separately: "I will not stop and I will not hide, even if I thought it was possible to do so.
"My family and I will not truly be safe as long as [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is in power in Russia - a circumstance shared by millions."
Kasparov retired from competitive chess in 2005 to pursue a career in politics, founding movements that openly opposed Putin before fleeing Russia in 2013.

He has not returned since. Russia classed him as a foreign agent following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and subsequently added him to a list of terrorists and extremists in 2024 - both categorisations he rejects.
The other reported target, Ponomarev, was the only Russian MP who voted against the illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014 and later went into exile in Ukraine.
He declined to confirm or deny to the Moscow Times whether he had been tipped off about the alleged plot but said the allegations marked "a new level of escalation" by Russia.
A network of individuals working for the Russian intelligence services has operated since at least 2024, the US Justice Department said.
It said the so-called RIS Network had been conspiring and conducting attacks and murders on Russian dissidents and defectors around the world.

Five alleged members of the network had been accused of operating "as part of a global assassination network that reached into the United States, attempting to recruit US citizens and foreigners to carry out killings at the behest of the Kremlin", Assistant Attorney General for national security John A Eisenberg said.
The five people alleged to be responsible for organising the plots are Yuri Khrameev, Kirill Khrameev, Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, Yaidel Delgado Suarez and Angel Eduardo Castro.
All five remain at large, the Justice Department said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said when the indictment was unsealed that he would not comment on the charges until he had heard or seen "any credible evidence" or "tangible facts".

articles.title: Ex-Sara Duterte aide, Jefry Tupas, denies receiving cash on behalf of VP
articles.summary: Former Davao City chief information officer Jefry Tupas on Thursday denied the claim of dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. that he received suitcases containing cash on behalf of Vice President…

blocks.text: Published October 1, 2026 10:01pm

Former Davao City chief information officer Jefry Tupas on Thursday denied the claim of dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. that he received suitcases containing cash on behalf of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Tupas said he believed that Gracioso was referring to him in his affidavit as he was the only one with the nickname “Jepoy” or “Jepoi” among Duterte’s closest aides at that time, despite incorrectly being referred to as “Tupaz” instead of “Tupas.”

“Sa simula pa lamang ay nais kong sabihing malinaw na ang mga pahayag at paratang na ito ni Gracioso ay pawang kasinungalingan lamang at madaling maipakita na sinungaling siya,” he said in an affidavit submitted to the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI).
(From the very beginning, I want to make it clear that these statements and allegations by Gracioso are all lies, and it can easily be shown that he is a liar.)

Gracioso previously said that he delivered cash to Vice President Sara Duterte, former President Rodrigo Duterte, and Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo Duterte on the instructions of former Speaker Lord Allan Velasco.
In his affidavit, Tupas denied Gracioso’s account that he was supposedly told by Duterte to hand over the cash to “Jepoy” at Marinduque in April 2019.
However, Tupas said that he has never been to Marinduque, nor was he in the country from April 18, 2019 to April 21, 2019. He said he was in Korea.
He also denied Gracioso’s claim that on September 21, 2019, he delivered two suitcases containing P50 million to Duterte. Gracioso said that Duterte again directed him to bring the cash to Jepoy.
Tupas said that he flew to Japan on September 19, 2019 and only returned to the Philippines on the evening of September 21, 2019.

Further, he belied Gracioso’s claim of delivering three suitcases to Duterte in 2020, during the height of the coronavirus pandemic, saying that Davao was strictly implementing the lockdown at that time.

“Ang masasabi ko lang ay puro kathang-isip at pawang kasinungalingan lamang. Kahit kailan, walang nangyari na may tinanggap akong maleta ng pera, regalo, o sasakyan para kay Sara Z. Duterte,” he said.
(All I can say is that it is all fabricated and completely untrue. At no time did it happen that I received a suitcase of money, a gift, or a vehicle for Sara Z. Duterte.)
“Kung hindi nga lang seryoso ang mga paratang niya, na halatang nagpakay ay sirain ang pangalan ni Ms. Sara Z. Duterte, ay nakakatawa ang mga kuwento niya,” he added.
(If only his allegations were not serious, as it is obvious that the purpose is to tarnish the name of Ms. Sara Z. Duterte, his stories would be laughable.)
According to Tupas, he has never been to the house of Velaco in Valle Verde or any other house. He also said that he did not know who Gracioso was.
This came after the NBI issued a subpoena for Tupas.
Tupas's legal counsel, lawyer Caesar Europa, said that though Tupas will be unable to comply with the subpoena due to its short notice, he will submit an affidavit to the bureau.
Europa also said they were surprised by the subpoena, as Tupas expected the NBI to offer to place him under protective custody due to information that he was under threat of abduction. —LDF, GMA News

Witnesses in the chamber said Christa Pike was still breathing despite receiving injections intended to kill her

When the prison warden asked Christa Pike if she had any last words, she said…

blocks.text: When the prison warden asked Christa Pike if she had any last words, she said she was going to leave this world “with love” for those on her side and also the ones angry with her.
What followed was the second botched execution in Tennessee this year, after two doses of the lethal injection failed to produce the desired effect.

Witnesses present in the chamber said Pike was still breathing despite the injections intended to kill her late on Wednesday, that nothing about the failed execution was normal and that it was unprecedented. For their part, officials said they followed every step of the approved protocol.

Pike was finally taken to the hospital after surviving the two attempts to execute her. The current status of the woman convicted of murdering a classmate in 1995 is unknown. John North, an investigative producer at WBIR television in Knoxville and also a witness at the Riverbend maximum security institution in Nashville, said when he left the building she was “probably still alive”.

“This event is the worst we’ve seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era. There is no precedent,” said Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, according to the New York Times.

“Nothing about today was normal, typical, at all,” said Tori Gessner, a reporter and anchor at WKRN of Nashville and one of the members of the media who served as witnesses in the execution, according to NBC.

“They went through two rounds, and she was still breathing at the end. She was very ragged,” said Catherine Sweeney, a reporter at the Nashville Public Radio WPLN, at a news conference after the execution attempt. “She lifted her head up and was looking around. At one point, she said … there was a spot that was burning and hurting, and asked if that was normal. None of it was normal.”
Gessner also said Pike was heard saying: “My arm feels like it’s about to burst open. Does this happen like that?”

Gessner described the victim as “inconsistently going in and out of snores and silence” after the injections. “When the curtains closed the final time at 8.05, we could consistently hear her snoring, and then it kind of developed into a snore squeak, and then a snore. And even at 8.53, when the microphone was cut off, we could still hear snoring.”

Pike, 50, was convicted of killing Colleen Slemmer, her 19-year-old classmate at Knoxville Job Corps. She had been scheduled for execution on Wednesday and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start, but hours later the US supreme court overturned that stay.

Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, described the failed execution attempt in a phone interview with NBC News on Thursday. “It was a mess,” she said. The Tennessee governor, Bill Lee, said he was suspending all executions this year and ordered “a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred”.

In a statement, the department of correction said the state “followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office” and that “the lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective.” In May, Tennessee also aborted attempts to execute a man convicted of murders after failing to find a suitable vein for his lethal injection.

articles.title: Trump and his allies credit deportations with record low crime. Experts disagree
articles.summary:
Administration says increased immigration enforcement led to fewer homicides, but they have been on the decline since Joe Biden’s term

Over the last year and a half, the US has seen a…

blocks.text: Over the last year and a half, the US has seen a historic drop in homicides. Researchers and reporters are still puzzling through the complex set of reasons why - from the easing of pandemic-era stressors and the Biden administration’s investments in community-based violence prevention to policing and other factors.

But for the Trump administration, there’s one easy explanation: increased immigration enforcement. As the midterm elections approach, the White House has been doubling down on this message, saying its crackdown against immigrants is why US crime rates are now falling.

“We have the most secure border in the world, nobody comes in, unless they’re invited. Unless they have permission,” Trump said during a speech to the UN general assembly last week. “As a result, last year we achieved the largest drop in violent crime ever recorded.”

JD Vance, the vice-president, made a similar claim at a rally in Iowa the week prior. “When you get the violent criminals out of your country you see the largest drop in violent crime in the history of the United States of America,” he said. “Murder rates, because we got the bad guys out.”
But experts say this simply isn’t true.

There’s no data that proves mass deportations or enhanced immigration enforcement leads to lower crime rates, and the research that does exist shows there is no relationship between immigrants – documented or not – and homicide rates in the US, experts say.

blocks.caption: ICE agents make an arrest during an early morning operation in Park Ridge, Illinois, on 19 September 2025. Photograph: Erin Hooley/AP

blocks.text: “It’s a specious claim if you’ve never attempted to verify anything with actual facts and are willing to believe what the administration will tell you,” said Pratheepan Gulasekaram, a law professor at the University of Colorado, Boulder. “If you live in a fact-free world this is the type of nonsensical data you’re willing to imbibe.”
In addition, the plummeting homicide rate the US is experiencing now didn’t start during Trump’s second term. It started in 2023, when Biden was president, researchers say.

Even though there’s no evidence to back up the Trump administration’s claims, Gulasekaram said xenophobia is one reason why they resonate with many Americans. “There’s an intuitive appeal to that claim if you start with the premise that foreigners are so different from us and are the source of economic and social ills,” he said. “That feeds into that underlying sentiment and it becomes extremely sticky.”

Other conservatives are echoing the White House’s unsubstantiated claims by making the same link between immigrants and crime. In a May Instagram video, Erich Pratt, vice-president of Gun Owners of America argued that Americans are “enjoying unprecedented safety”, because of the Trump administration’s aggressive approach to immigration enforcement.

“It didn’t come from new gun restrictions,” he said in an email to the Guardian of the plummeting homicide rates across the US. “It came from a shift in priorities. President Trump implemented measures aimed at deporting violent gang members, ending catch-and-release policies for illegal aliens, and getting repeat offenders off the streets.”

A Guardian analysis published in February showed that more than 75% of people who entered deportation proceedings for the first time had no criminal convictions. Only 34 of more than 18,400 people arrested by ICE between 2025 and June this year were convicted of killing someone, according to DHS data. The most common convictions were for illegal re-entry, driving under the influence and a category marked as “other.”

It’s unclear how many undocumented migrants are currently in prison for murder convictions or have been convicted for killing someone since Trump took office. State prisons track demographic information such as age, race and type of conviction but, with the exception of Texas, immigration status is not one of them.

And by the federal government’s own acknowledgement, there is no comprehensive or centralized data on the citizenship status of people incarcerated in local jails and state prisons, the government accountability office said in a 28 September report.

Still, Trump has spent a decade claiming, without evidence, that undocumented migrants pose a safety threat to US citizens. In his 2016 presidential run, he repeatedly talked about the killing of Kate Steinle, a 32-year-old woman who had been killed in San Francisco the year before. The man accused of killing her was undocumented, but he was eventually acquitted. And during his 2024 run, he often spoke of Laken Riley, a nursing student who was killed while she was jogging. Her killer was an undocumented immigrant, and was sentenced to life in prison.
Researchers say that stories like these have long been used to push for tougher immigration policies and more deportations.

blocks.caption: People protest against ICE in New York on 6 April 2026. Photograph: Melissa Bender/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “The argument in their tragic cases is that they should have never been at risk because this person should have never been able to commit these crimes,” said Michael Light, a sociology professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. “But that’s more of a political disagreement than an empirical one.”

Leaning on these kinds of anecdotes to determine immigration policy, and then claiming that they have led to public safety can cause misunderstandings of why homicides and other crimes have decreased, Light said.

“There’s no question that they’ve increased enforcement and we’ve seen a historic decrease in homicides,” he said. “But the idea that immigration policy is the only thing that’s changed is problematic. And if we misdiagnose what’s actually driving the homicide decline, that’s going to lead to bad public policy.”

This week, the Department of Justice announced a new $25m grant program to support people whose loved ones were killed or injured by undocumented migrants and fund law enforcement efforts to prevent future deaths.

The Guardian reached out to DHS and the White House to request any data or research that can prove a causal relationship between immigration enforcement and the declining homicide rate. Both agencies reiterated their claims that deportations are the reason homicides are down, but did not supply any evidence.

articles.title: Flydubai passenger describes hugging his children as plane nosedived during attack
articles.summary: Adam Polovincik tells the BBC he told his young children "everything is going to be all right" as flight plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m).

blocks.text: A man has described how he hugged and reassured his two young children as their plane suddenly descended after one pilot stabbed the other in an attempt to seize control of the flight.

A Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes around two hours into its journey from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered him and retook control to land safely.
Adam Polovincik told BBC Newshour that he hugged his six-year-old son and three-year-old daughter "really hard" and tried to stay calm for them as the attack unfolded.
He praised the pilot who was stabbed and passengers who fought off and subdued the attacker, saying they were "true heroes".
The stabbed pilot is in a stable condition in hospital, while the alleged attacker has been arrested.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said it was too early to say whether Iran was involved in the attack, but that the alleged attacker had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".
Polovincik, who was sitting in aisle 13, was flying home with his wife and children after an "amazing" holiday in Singapore and Thailand.
He said there had been a "huge degree of panic" on the plane as there was a "very, very, very sharp decrease in height".
He thought at first that this was simply because of an air pocket, but "it took a lot of time, almost a minute".
Everyone who had not been seated fell to the floor, the 40-year-old said.
"After a couple of seconds, we started to hear screams. 'There is blood, there is stabbing, we need help'," Polovincik said.
"At the end of the day, you understand very, very quickly that literally there is nothing that you can do at this point in time," he said.
Polovincik, a performance marketing analyst, said he tried to "be cool" for his children.

"You just tell them, yeah, everything's going to be all right. It's just a malfunction in the aeroplane, there is a crew under control, the passengers are helping them, [you] hug them really hard and try to keep your face so it doesn't look very panicked, try to keep your tone of voice."
But he said there was naturally a "high degree of panic" on the flight.
There were lots of families with children on the plane because the flight took place towards the end of a Jewish holiday period.
After about 10 to 15 minutes, he said a passenger in the cockpit told them the incident was "under control" and other staff were flying the plane.
In a video released by Netanyahu's office, passenger Yaniv Hayun described putting the attacker in a chokehold and pulling him out of the cockpit before other passengers helped pin him down.
Two other pilots who were onboard the flight then took over the controls and safely landed the plane, which had been carrying more than 150 passengers.

Polovincik said: "After they told us that the situation is, again, 'under control', then it was a bit harder to tell the kids that it's malfunctioned because people start to walk around the aeroplane covered with blood."
Polovincik was praised Indian pilot, Capt Smit Machchhar, who fought off his attacker and opened the door to the cockpit, allowing passengers to step in.
"Without him opening the door, we're probably not speaking here right now," he said, adding that he "can't even start saying our gratitude for this human being".
Polovincik said that, although he was not religious, he could not escape "the feeling that it was the hand of God yesterday" that had put "the pieces on the board in the way that they did".
"It's remarkable."
After the situation onboard was brought under control, the flight was diverted to Saudi Arabia, where Polovincik stressed the passengers, who were almost all Israeli, were treated well.
"They brought us water and food and coffee and even sweets for the kids - even though we don't have any diplomatic relationship between Israel and Saudi Arabia," he said.
The alleged attacker, who was arrested in Saudi Arabia, is expected to be transferred to the United Arab Emirates, from where the plane departed, Netanyahu told Fox News.
The passengers were taken to Tel Aviv on another flight later on Wednesday and were greeted at the airport by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags.
Polovincik said it had been "such a terrible ending" to an amazing family trip and that it would take some time for his family to come to terms with what had occurred.

articles.title: North and South Korea trade accusations over landmines that injured three soldiers
articles.summary: A mine blast that injured three South Korean soldiers has renewed scrutiny of North Korea's actions along the border and raised questions about its strategic goals.

image.caption: North Korea has been fortifying the border after a shift in policy against Seoul, calling it a 'foe' [FILE: June 2019]Image: Ahn Young-joon/AP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Pyongyang and Seoul are trading increasingly hostile accusations across the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that divides the peninsula, 10 days after three South Korean soldiers were injured by a land mine on the South's side of the border.

The latest tensions may reflect a broader North Korean effort to test South Korea's resolve while extending its control to the outer limits of its territory, including an area that has effectively been a no-man's land for more than 70 years, according to a professor of foreign policy at South Korea's Kyung Hee University's department of Chinese studies
"The North revised its constitution in March this year and officially stated that they intend to define the absolute geographical limits of the nation, and that includes within the DMZ," said Choo.
"They want to maximize their territory and it is my sense that they would like to push the Military Demarcation Line [MDL] — the half-way point in the DMZ — further south," he told DW.
"I see the placing of landmines on the South's side of the line as a purely political act by the North, an attempt to threaten and intimidate the South."
Why Seoul blames North Korea

The three men were part of an 18-strong patrol clearing a new route through the DMZ as part of an investigation into the activities of North Korean troops in the western sector of the zone. The 4-kilometer-wide strip of land has divided the peninsula since the Korean War ended in an armistice in 1953.

blocks.caption: The DMZ is a fortified buffer zone between the two Koreas that has been in place since 1953Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Shortly before 11 a.m. on September 21, the patrol was around 10 meters south of the MDL when a staff sergeant detonated a mine. A second mine went off as the unit commander approached to provide assistance. Both men were successfully evacuated and have undergone surgery, with a third soldier treated for minor wounds.

The South Korean military has conducted an investigation with the United Nations Command, which administers the armistice on the border, and concluded in a report released this week that the mine was of North Korean origin.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff on Wednesday accused the North of sowing mines to the south of the MDL, a breach of the armistice agreement, and demanded an apology from Pyongyang and a commitment to halt the construction of further fortifications along the border.

"This constitutes a blatant violation of the Armistice Agreement and undermines the spirit of existing inter-Korean agreements and must be halted immediately," Kang Hyun-woo, chief director of operations, said in a press briefing.

"North Korea must immediately cease activities that heighten tensions on the Korean Peninsula, such as its so-called 'border fortification.' We strongly demand an apology and responsible measures from the North," Kang added.
In a statement, the UN Command said it had "determined that an Armistice Agreement violation occurred. UNC is addressing the violation through established Armistice mechanisms."
Prisoner swap: From North to South Korea via Ukraine
Many in the South are demanding more resolute action on the grounds that failure to respond will be taken as a sign of weakness in Seoul.

Na Kyung-won, a politician from the conservative opposition People Power Party (PPP), has demanded that the South Korean military carry out exercises simulating a "decapitation attack" against North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
She has also called for the restart of propaganda broadcasts from loudspeakers on the border and for dissident groups to be allowed to launch balloons carrying propaganda into the North.
A pattern of border confrontations

Yu Yong-weon, also of the PPP, told reporters on Wednesday that North Korean troops had crossed the MDL around 20 times in August and on 30 occasions in September. On each occasion, South Korean troops fired warning shots when the incursions were detected.

An editorial in the Korea JoongAng Daily on Thursday said North Korea must be "held accountable" for the incident, arguing that Pyongyang's denial of responsibility "demands a firm response, clear accountability and stronger border enforcement."

blocks.caption: Kim Jong Un's sister Kim Yo Jong has accused Seoul of conspiracy after it blamed Pyongyang for the blast in the DMZImage: Yuri Smityuk/TASS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The North is not backing down, however, with Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, accusing the South of staging a provocation and threatening to retaliate.

In a statement published by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) on Wednesday, Kim Yo Jong dismissed the South's allegations as a "self-staged farce" and accused the "South Korean armed gangs" of using the incident to justify political and military provocations against Pyongyang.
Accident or calculated provocation?
Andrei Lankov, a professor of history and international relations at Seoul's Kookmin University, is more willing to view the landmine detonations as an accident.

"It makes no sense to me for North Korea to do this deliberately," he said. "At the moment, the North wants to keep a low profile and do nothing that could provoke the South. There is no gain in a deliberate attack like this."

Lankov believes a more likely scenario is that the mines were shifted from the northern side of the MDL in heavy rain or natural movements of the terrain, meaning that the North's protestations of innocence are genuine.

"I also do not think the South Korean government has any interest in escalating the situation further and that they will hope this is quickly forgotten," he said. "They will want to brush it under the carpet."
Choo, however, is less convinced and senses a growing anger in South Korean society that the government is not standing up to provocations from north of the border.

"I believe that resuming the propaganda broadcasts over the border would be an effective response, but I do not believe this government will do that," he said. "This government is trying very hard to connect with the North, but I see a failure to take a firm line this time being interpreted in the North as a sign of weakness in Seoul.

"Not responding would give Pyongyang a green light to push a little more and then a little more again," he said. "There is a lot of anger here that the government is not doing enough to protect soldiers who are serving on the DMZ, to protect the people and to protect our territory."

articles.title: Judge dismisses sexual assault case against Trailer Park Boys star Mike Smith
articles.summary: A sexual assault case against Trailer Park Boys actor Mike Smith was dropped in Dartmouth provincial court on Thursday. The complainant says the trial was dismissed because she was "unwilling to…

image.caption: Mike Smith, the actor behind the character Bubbles from the Trailer Park Boys, poses for photos in 2009. (Larry MacDougal/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·New

A sexual assault case against Trailer Park Boys actor Mike Smith was dropped in Dartmouth provincial court on Thursday. The complainant says the trial was dismissed because she was "unwilling to sacrifice" her mental health to go through the criminal justice process.
Complainant says trial dismissed because she was 'unwilling to sacrifice' mental health to proceed

A Nova Scotia judge dismissed a sexual assault case against Trailer Park Boys actor Mike Smith on Thursday, as the complainant tells CBC News she decided the emotional toll of testifying would be too difficult to endure.
The three-day trial of Smith, known for playing Bubbles on the comedy series, was set to begin on Thursday in provincial court in Dartmouth, N.S.
But the Crown offered no evidence in the case, so the defence requested the case be dismissed. Judge Jill Hartlen dismissed it.
Smith, 54, was charged in October 2025 with sexual assault in relation to an alleged assault on Dec. 30, 2017, in Dartmouth.
He pleaded not guilty to the charge in February.
CBC spoke with the complainant, who cannot be named due to a publication ban on her identity, on Wednesday.
In a statement, she said the trial was dismissed "because I am unwilling to sacrifice my mental health" by testifying.
The statement says evidence in sexual assault cases "hinges almost exclusively on the testimony of the victim."

"This process retraumatizes survivors, subjecting their experiences to dissecting public scrutiny. Meanwhile, the accused seldom speak; they are exempt from the pain of taking the stand, giving testimony, and facing cross-examination," the statement reads.

Since the burden of evidence relies so heavily on the character of the witness, victims face "character assassination" during cross-examinations, and defence lawyers can even "insinuate that victims played a part in the crime — or deserved it," the statement said.
"I am intimidated by a system, despite it being 2026, where defence attorneys still use tactics that blame victims for surviving and reporting sexual assaults," the statement continues.

"I know what happened that night in 2017. My stepping away from the case does not change the facts of that incident. Rather, it is a gesture of reclaiming my agency after investigating options within a system that strips me of my voice."

A statement issued Thursday morning by Trailer Park Boys Incorporated said now that the court matter has concluded, Smith is resuming his responsibilities with the company. He previously held the role of managing director.

articles.title: AI agents tried to hack Library and Archives Canada website, research firm says

image.caption: The Library and Archives Canada building is shown in Ottawa on April 17, 2026. AI agents tried to hack into a website belonging to the federal library, an artificial intelligence research firm said Wednesday, casting the effort as a failed hacking attempt. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Business·New
AI agents tried to hack into a Library and Archives Canada website, according to a report by artificial intelligence research firm Transluce.
Recent breaches by rogue AI agents are alarming governments and companies

AI agents tried to hack into a Canadian government website, an artificial intelligence research firm said Wednesday, casting the effort as a failed hacking attempt, while Canada said there were no indications its systems were compromised.

AI research firm Transluce said the attempts exhibited tactics "consistent with prior observed agent activity that we have attributed to OpenAI in a similar timeframe." But it added it was not confidently attributing these attempts to OpenAI.
The agents attempted to access Library and Archives Canada on May 28 and June 9, Transluce said in a blog post. Transluce said it disclosed the action to the Canadian government on Monday.

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security said Tuesday it was aware of reports of suspected AI agent activity. "There is no indication that government systems have been compromised at this time," it said in a statement.

OpenAI said it was "aware of reports of OpenAI models attempting to access publicly available information from Canadian government websites." A spokesperson said OpenAI was reviewing the reported findings and had provided an initial briefing to Canadian officials conducting the government’s review.
Will rogue AI development mean the end of humanity? Experts weigh in
Governments struggle to keep pace with AI advances

The ​world’s leading AI companies have warned ⁠of the risks posed by AI to ​humanity, appealing for governments to work together to ​manage the increasingly powerful technology. Governments around the world have struggled to keep pace with rapid advances in AI.

Free online service arquivo.pt, the national Portuguese web archive that is operated by the Portuguese Foundation for Science and Technology, captured 899 requests hitting the "collection-search" service of the Library and Archives Canada, including a series of apparently failed rudimentary hacking attempts, on May 28 and June 9, Transluce said.
Several recent breaches globally by rogue AI agents have alarmed governments and companies.

Last week, Australia said an OpenAI agent breached a government health data portal in June, gaining unauthorized access to files, in ​what was the first known instance of an AI agent hacking into a government website.
OpenAI apologized on Tuesday for the hack by the rogue AI agent.

articles.title: Water concessionaires told: Look for alternate sources due to stronger El Niño
articles.summary: Metro Manila"s water concessionaires have been instructed to look for alternative sources as a more severeNWRB El Niño looms across the country.

blocks.text: Published October 1, 2026 9:47pm
Metro Manila’s water concessionaires have been instructed to look for alternative sources as a more severe El Niño looms across the country.
In a 24 Oras report from Gabriel Gonzales on Thursday, the National Water Resources Board (NWRB) said that Metro Manila will have a reduced water supply in October due to a more severe El Niño.
The NWRB has advised the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS) and either water concessionaires to look for alternative water sources as to not deplete the Angat Dam.
While the Angat Dam has increased its reserves following the enhanced Southwest Monsoon, it is still slightly lower when compared to its high normal level.

“Sa ngayon po kasi ay pwede pong i-tap ng MWSS at mga konsesyonaryo 'yung mga other sources po nila 'no kagaya po dito sa may Laguna Lake, dito po sa may bandang Cavite at dito rin po sa may bandang Upper Wawa 'no. May mga pwede po silang mapagkunan ng karagdagang tubig para po matugunan 'no 'yung ibang pangangailangan ng mga kababayan po natin,” NWRB Executive Director Sevillo David Jr. said.

(For now the MWSS and other concessionaires could tap their other sources like the Laguna Lake, around in Cavite, and the Upper Wawa Dam. They have other water sources to be able to provide for the needs of our citizens.)
The NWRB said that there is a possibility that the MWSS water allocation will be lowered from 53 cubic meters per second to 44 cubic meters per second.
State weather bureau PAGASA has already forecast fewer rains, so the water conversation efforts needed to start now to make sure water supplies lasted until 2027, David said.

The MWSS said water concessionaires Manila Water and Maynilad have already signified preparations for the El Niño phenomenon. The agency is guarding the activities of the two firms to ensure continued supplies.

"Sa Manila Water, na-deliver na po nila ang phase 1 ng East Bay at 'yung pagma-maximize ng existing facilities nila katulad ng Cardona at Calawis…’Yung Maynilad naman, ang inutusan natin sa kanila ay magtayo po sila ng mga modular treatment plant po sa Cavite at pina-adjust po natin ang kanilang non-revenue water,” MWSS Chief Regulator Patrick Ty said.

(For Manila Water, they delivered phase 2 of the East Bay and the maximizing of the facilities in Cardona and Calawis… for Maynilad, we instructed them to put up a modular treatment plant in Cavite and we had them adjust their non-revenue water.)

The MWSS said that there were no expected widespread water outages. If there were, they would be localized and short-term. Consumers also do not need to worry about increased water prices, the agency said.
A few residents of Caloocan City have already started to save water.

At a carinderia in Barangay 12, Caloocan City, Thess Serdon was waiting for the dirty dishes to accumulate before she washed them. Resident Rodolfo Decena on the other hand was planning to reuse water.

“Yung mga pinaglabahan, itatabi para magamit sa ibang kwan, sa CR, ganun… mga drum mayroon na,” Decena said. (The water for laundry, we will just set it aside to use it for other things, for the toilet, like that… we have drums already.)
