articles.title: What we know so far about the midair FlyDubai incident

image.caption: A FlyDubai aircraft carrying Israelis who experienced an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia is shown arriving at Ben Gurion International Airport, near Tel Aviv, Israel, on Wednesday night. (Ariel Schalit/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

The motivations of a FlyDubai pilot, and what weapon was used, are among the foremost questions surrounding how a flight bound for Israel from the United Arab Emirates avoided disaster Wednesday after a cockpit incident.
Attacked pilot recovering in hospital, Indian official says, with alleged attacker reportedly from Oman

A co-pilot stabbed his captain in an apparent attempt to crash a flight bound for Israel from the United Arab Emirates on Wednesday that was carrying 174 people. The passengers, most of them Israelis, feared for their lives as the FlyDubai aircraft lost half its altitude in about a minute.

The wounded pilot managed to open the cockpit door, and a passenger and a crew member rushed in to subdue the attacker, according to Israeli officials and plane passengers. Other crew members gained control of the aircraft, which landed safely in Saudi Arabia.
Here's what we know, and what isn't known, so far:
The incident
The distress call came at 8:44 a.m. local time, about 2½ hours after Flight FZ1073 left Dubai, a hub of international business and tourism, heading to Tel Aviv in Israel.
Israeli officials later said that the co-pilot stabbed the pilot and tried to crash the aircraft.

The plane swiftly lost altitude — dropping from 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet (10,000 metres to 5,100 metres) in the span of about a minute. It then circled close to the Jordanian border before landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, about an hour later.
Aviation experts said they were surprised that the plane did not crash after a descent so extreme that most of the rudder was ripped off the aircraft's tail.
How the mid-air struggle aboard a FlyDubai flight unfolded | Hanomansing Live
Hours after the plane landed at Tabuk's Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport, replacement aircraft retrieved the passengers, who arrived in Israel on Wednesday night.

The wounded pilot, Capt. Smit Machchhar, from Mumbai, has been praised for opening the cockpit door so that others could subdue the attacker and take control of the Boeing 737, pulling it out of a risky dive. Other crew members were able to fly the plane to a safe landing.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on X that the pilot's opening of the cockpit door had "enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic midair disaster."
The alleged attacker

The United Arab Emirates government said an investigation team had begun its work, adding that it has jurisdiction because the plane is registered there. The state news agency said the probe will try and determine, in part, "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or ⁠purpose, or involved prior planning or direction."

Israeli intelligence and security officials were in Saudi Arabia to help investigate the suspect, according to a regional official who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media. Israel has requested that the suspect be sent to Israel for the investigation, though it is unclear if that request will be granted, the official said.

items: U.A.E. announces investigation into FlyDubai stabbing

blocks.text: Israeli officials have identified the attacker as an Omani national. Omani authorities have not commented.
Netanyahu said in an interview on Fox News on Thursday that the attacker had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination," but did not provide further details to support that allegation.
The security questions
One question surrounding the incident is what was used in the attack — and if it was a knife, how a pilot could transport it onto the aircraft without being detected.

Pilots, like passengers, must pass through metal detectors at airports. It's also standard for airlines to check their pilots' background for criminal and employment history, and their physical and mental health, as well as having them undergo intelligence and security screening.

Netanyahu brought up the possibility in the Fox News interview that an axe was used. Airlines are generally required to carry crash axes in the cockpit for use in an emergency to break open a window to escape or break open a panel to access a fire.

The cockpit door on all aircraft is locked during flight for security reasons — a measure that became the industry standard after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, in which hijackers broke into the cockpits of four domestic flights in the United States.

Israel, targeted in a series of hijackings decades ago, has some of the most stringent airline security measures worldwide. Passengers on Israel-bound flights regularly are taken aside for questioning and baggage searches after passing through normal airport security.
The attacked pilot
Machchhar was in ​"good health and recovering ​well," the Indian ⁠Embassy ⁠in ‌the U.A.E. said Thursday on X.
The ⁠embassy said the Indian ambassador there visited the pilot in hospital and ​it remained ⁠in close co-ordination ⁠with local authorities ⁠to ⁠ensure ​his continued medical care ​and well-being.
Speaking to the Times of Israel, a passenger named Dr. Shota Musaev, a dentist, said Machchhar was bleeding from the head and hands after the attack. Musaev said he helped stop the bleeding.

SpiceJet, a budget carrier in India, also praised Machchhar early Thursday. SpiceJet said he had been an employee of theirs for about a decade, with a LinkedIn profile attached to Machchhar indicating he started flying for FlyDubai in 2022.

Machchhar has logged nearly 9,750 flying hours over a career spanning about 15 years, according to a Reuters report. In a podcast interview published on YouTube last year, the captain said, "I always wanted to fly a Boeing. My first aircraft was a Boeing."
The airline and the plane

FlyDubai says it has more than 6,000 employees from 144 countries. While the airline doesn't break down those numbers by pilots, it said in 2024 that it was on a recruitment drive to hire 130 new pilots by the end of that year.

The airline, in operation for nearly 20 years, says it flies to more than 125 destinations in some 56 countries across Africa, Europe, Central Asia, the Gulf, the Middle East, the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia.

Its most tragic incident occurred in 2016, when all 62 passengers and crew aboard its Boeing 737-800 died in a nighttime crash on a second landing attempt in Russia. Pilot error was among the factors cited in the final report on the crash.
While the airline has ordered some Airbus planes for future use, its fleet at present includes dozens of Boeing 737 aircraft of various generations.
While Boeing has been under fire in the past decade regarding other aviation incidents, the American company was praised during this event by U.S. President Donald Trump on Truth Social.

"Congratulations to the GREAT Boeing company for producing a plane, the 737 Max, that was able to withstand the G Forces and Strain far beyond what it was designed and expected to. It was an amazing show of precise and powerful structural panning and design," he wrote.
With files from CBC News and Reuters

articles.title: Defense, prosecution debate AMLA's confidentiality provision in Duterte trial
articles.summary: The House prosecution and Vice President Sara Duterte"s defense counsel clashed over the Anti-Money Laundering Council"s (AMLC) confidentiality provision on the 32nd day of the trial.

blocks.text: Published October 1, 2026 9:35pm
The House prosecution and Vice President Sara Duterte’s defense counsel clashed over the Anti-Money Laundering Council’s (AMLC) confidentiality provision on the 32nd day of the trial.

On the day before the prosecution was meant to present AMLC Executive Director Ronell Buenaventura as a witness, Duterte’s lead defense counsel, Attorney Sheila Sison, requested to move his testimony to Monday, arguing that their camp was not given enough time to prepare for the voluminous records.
“In addition, of course, to our objection that we may raise on the confidentiality, absolute confidentiality, of these records,” Sison said.

Sison said that the summaries which were presented to them had a confidentiality mark. She cited Section 8-A of Republic Act 11521 or the amended Anti-Money Laundering Act, which mandated that AMLC employees should protect the information they learn.
She also argued that when the impeachment court ruled to subpoena the AMLC records in July, the ruling did not prohibit any further objection.

House prosecutor Diokno, however, stated that the defense already had access to all of the AMLC documents since September 2. Moreover, Diokno said that Section 8-A does not prevent the AMLC records from being discussed.

“It does not, and constitutionally cannot, nullify the lawful subpoena powers of the Senate sitting as an impeachment court where compliance with the lawful constitutional subpoena is a justifying circumstance that, if at all, would extinguish any penal liability under Article 11, Paragraph 6 of the Revised Penal Code, for any person acting in obedience to an order issued by a superior or some other lawful purpose,” Diokno said.

“I believe I have said this before, that Section 8-A was only intended to prevent leaks by officers or employees of the Anti-Money Laundering Council. It was never intended as a blanket shield for any lawful subpoenas issued by a proper court,” he added.
Diokno said that the Sandiganbayan has already issued subpoenas to AMLC officers before, where they presented documents. The Senate, as an impeachment court, was no different, Diokno said.
He further argued that the defense cannot move to reconsider the ruling of the impeachment court, and only a senator-judge could.

Impeachment court presiding officer Senator-Judge Francis Escudero said that out of an abundance of caution, he would prefer to have the defense review the documents again. This would also allow senator-judges to look at the materials as well.

“Out of courtesy and equity, the chair grants the time requested by the counsel for respondent for time to prepare for the cross-examination, rather, to prepare for the direct and cross-examination of the AMLC witness on Monday,” Escudero said. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Zimbabwe tycoon Wicknell Chivayo dies in helicopter crash
articles.summary: Zimbabwe's President Emmerson Mnangagwa has confirmed the death of businessman Wicknell Chivayo and his wife in a helicopter crash, calling the high-rollers with a lavish lifestyle "consummately…

image.caption: Wicknell Chivayo was well known in Zimbabwe and had close ties to several African leadersImage: Instagram/sir_wicknell

blocks.text: The family of Zimbabwean businessman Wicknell Chivayo and President Emmerson Mnangagwa have confirmed reports that he and his wife Lucy Muteke were involved in a fatal helicopter crash southeast of Harare on Wednesday evening.
Family spokesperson Herbert Chivayo told state broadcaster ZBC that the 43-year-old tycoon and his wife were killed in the crash, saying, "We are at a loss for words after the tragic news."
President Mnangagwa said the sudden and unexpected deaths "left our nation, my family, and me personally numbed and in deep shock and grief."
Chivayo was a prominent supporter of Mnangagwa who had secured a series of lucrative government contracts and was known for his lavish lifestyle and often-ostentatious gifts to allies and associates.
What do we know about the crash?
The helicopter crashed with six people on board in the rural Marondera district of Zimbabwe, not far southeast of Harare. There were no survivors.

Initially, as reports circulated that Chivayo was on board, a government spokesman said only that a "high-profile businessman" was one of four passengers. Police also said that they were conducting DNA tests and conducting other checks to confirm the identities of the victims, whose remains had been burned in a fire.
Mnangagwa published a tribute to Chivayo and his family the following day online.

"We are all shattered by this unexpected, sudden demise of so young a family," he wrote. "Consummately philanthropic, the Chivayo Family touches so many lives in our nation through its countless acts of charity and generosity which ran into millions of dollars, and which motivated and transformed countless lives."

"Tellingly, the Chivayos lost their lives on their way back from Gandami in rural Chikomba where they were putting up modern family and community structures, all in line with our policy on rural development through investments, industrialization, development and transformation," Mnangagwa wrote.
Who was Wicknell Chivayo?

Chivayo cultivated close ties both with Mnangagwa and the ruling ZANU-PF party, but also with other African leaders, including South Africa's Cyril Ramaphosa, Tanzania's Samia Suluhu Hassan, Eswatini's King Mswati III, and Kenyan President William Ruto.

"Wicknell was a dear friend whose warmth touched many people. I will remember him for his friendship, his energy and his deep conviction in the possibilities of our continent," Ruto wrote in a tribute online.

Going by the handle "Sir Wicknell" in his social media persona, Chivayo would often post images of himself with Zimbabwean and African leaders. He was also known for a lavish lifestyle with luxury cars, designer clothing, and often for giving high-value gifts to associates, business partners, religious leaders, or even social media followers voicing support for him or for Mnangagwa.

Critics would often point to these close ties and to Chivayo as a case study of Zimbabwe's small elite class benefitting from large government contracts in a country with estimated median wages of less than US $5 per day.

Chivayo always denied allegations of corruption but faced several legal investigations that never resulted in convictions, starting with a 2005 money laundering case. He was arrested in 2018 in connection with the alleged misuse of a large advance payment tied to a solar power project, but five years later a judge dismissed the case, citing delays by prosecutors.

blocks.caption: President Mnangagwa lauded Chivayo, saying it was telling that he died on his return from a visit to an impoverished area where he was coordinating a development projectImage: Tsvangirayi Mukwazh/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "His generous hand cut across sectors and reached many individuals: in politics, religion, public service, culture, sport and many different professions," Mnangagwa said of Chivayo.
"The late Wicknell Chivayo had a grand vision for his family, for our country, for the Southern African subregion and for our African continent."

articles.title: Trump unveils South Korean investment in US energy projects
articles.summary: Donald Trump said South Korea has agreed to invest in an LNG project in Alaska, but Seoul has said it will only proceed once certain conditions are met.

image.caption: South Korea's Lee pushed back against Trump's investment claimsImage: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has announced that South Korea will invest $200 billion (€177 billion) in energy projects in the United States.
The investments would include $54 billion for a liquefied natural gas (LNG) pipeline project in Alaska, Trump said late Wednesday.
But on Thursday, Seoul said the Alaska LNG pipeline project had not yet been decided on, and that it would only proceed with the project once certain conditions are met.
The South Korean government has reportedly told Washington that it regrets Trump's announcement.
What did Trump say about the Alaska LNG project?
"Thanks to the agreements my administration has secured with the Republic of Korea, they will invest up to $200 billion," Trump said in the Oval Office on Wednesday.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said, "The United States and Korea have agreed to commence working together on the $50 billion ALASKA LNG PROJECT."
Trump also said South Korea would back a $22.3 billion natural gas-fired power project in Texas. "This will bring tremendous new, reliable power capacity to Texas," the US president said.
How has South Korea reacted to Trump's announcement?

South Korea on Thursday confirmed that the plans for the Texas natural gas power facility, which will supply power to AI data centers, would proceed. It also confirmed plans to invest $120 billion to build eight nuclear reactors.

But it said it had not yet decided on the Alaska LNG project, which South Korea said would be "considered on the condition that it is commercially viable and subject to relevant domestic legal procedures."
"No decision has been made regarding whether to invest in the project or the scale of any potential investment," South Korea's trade ministry said in a statement.

South Korean Industry Minister Kim Jung Kwan said that he had spoken to US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to express his government's regret over Trump's announcement, South Korean news agency Yonhap reported.
In a post on X, President Lee Jae Myung also said that both the LNG project and the nuclear reactors' commercial viability must be confirmed before they can proceed.

Last month, Lee described negotiations on the projects as "very complex and difficult" and said that he had found some of Washington's terms "difficult to accept," although he did not elaborate further.
South Korea's Foreign Ministry, for its part, said it hoped the investment announcement would lead to progress in ​discussions in other areas, namely security.
During his tour of Asia this summer, Trump announced that the US would be "substantially reducing" its joint annual military exercises in South Korea.
The US leader cited what he considered insufficient support from Seoul for the war with Iran and his "very good relationship" with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un.
What do we know about the South Korea-US trade agreement?

Under a trade deal signed in July 2025, South Korea had agreed to invest $350 billion in the US and increase purchases of US energy products, with the US setting a 15% tariff on South Korean imports to the US.
Trump's announcement was the first set of major projects under that trade agreement, which included $200 billion for strategic investments and $150 billion for shipbuilding.

The announcement is the latest in a series of economic deals Trump is touting in the run-up to November's midterm elections, which are expected to reflect voter concerns over high gasoline prices and the US-Israeli war with Iran.

If it goes forward, the Alaska LNG project will see an 800-mile (1,300 kilometer) pipeline carry natural gas from the North Slope to a liquefaction facility near Anchorage on Alaska's southern coast for shipping to Asian markets.

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial suspended until October 5
articles.summary: Duterte's defense counsel requests to defer the testimony of an Anti-Money Laundering Council witness over confidentiality issues, drawing mixed reactions from senator-judges

blocks.text: HUDDLE. Senator-judges huddle during a break on Day 31 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on September 29, 2026.
Senate Social Media Unit
Duterte's defense counsel requests to defer the testimony of an Anti-Money Laundering Council witness over confidentiality issues, drawing mixed reactions from senator-judges

items: The Senate impeachment court suspended the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte until October 5, allowing the defense more time to review confidential financial records from the Anti-Money Laundering Council.
Defense counsel Sheila Sison argued that the defense needed to examine the 11-page summaries and 23 to 24 boxes of documents to prepare for cross-examination.
While some senator-judges expressed reservations about the postponement, the court ultimately granted the defense's request, emphasizing the importance of a fair process in the trial.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Senate impeachment court suspended proceedings in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte until Monday, October 5, amid the defense’s appeal for the deferment of the testimony of an Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) witness over confidentiality issues.

Impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero on Thursday, October 1, granted the request of Duterte’s defense counsel to defer the testimony of AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura, initially scheduled for October 1, to allow them more time to study the financial records.

Lead defense counsel Sheila Sison said the defense received summaries submitted by Buenaventura only on Thursday morning and noted the 11-page submissions and their annexes were marked “strictly confidential.” She also said an attached cover letter stated the AMLC was “not waiving the confidentiality” of the records.
The defense would also need to review 23 to 24 boxes of documents to prepare for cross-examination, Sison added.

“Without a review of that, we cannot imagine how we would be able to intelligently respond to the questioning of the prosecution to their intended witness — should it come to that — and raise the proper grounds therefore, without examination of the documents that we need to do to appreciate the so-called summaries here,” she said.
“In addition, of course, to our objection that we may raise on the absolute confidentiality of these records,” Sison added.
The defense’s request drew mixed reactions from senator-judges.
Senator-judge Vicente “Tito” Sotto III expressed “strong reservations” about the postponement, noting that the defense had access to the AMLC records since September 2.
“All this time, I thought that the prosecution and the defense [had] been ready with this since July,” Sotto said.
“I don’t think many would enjoy a postponement only because they were not given proper time. This was since July, and, as I understand, September 2, the defense was given access,” he said.
Senator-judge Alan Peter Cayetano said he shared Sotto’s view but nevertheless urged the court to grant the defense’s request.

“If I can use the word ‘main event,’ one of the, if not the, main events of this trial, the same as the Corona trial, is actually the questions about financial impropriety or graft and corruption and about the actual finances of the respondent accused,” Cayetano said.

“In a democracy, the result is important, but the process is as important…. I don’t think the defense is asking for a month, a week. They’re asking for this afternoon and tomorrow, so, meaning, on Monday,” he said.

Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros addressed the confidentiality issue, saying the confidentiality requirement under the law is intended to prevent indiscriminate or voluntary disclosure of information and does not necessarily prevent compliance with subpoenas issued by courts, including an impeachment court.
“Ang isang absolute reading ay magiging kabaligtaran dahil hindi na po magagawa ng AMLC ang mismong trabaho niya, kung bakit siya nilikha ng ating batas,” Hontiveros said.
(An absolute reading of the law will oppose the reason and essence of the creation of the AMLC.)
House prosecutor Chel Diokno urged the court to reject the defense’s request, saying the subpoenaed AMLC records had been made available to the defense since September 2.
Diokno also argued that the confidentiality issue had already been addressed when the impeachment court issued subpoenas for Duterte’s bank and financial records in July.

In granting the request, Escudero said the court would furnish senator-judges with copies of relevant provisions, particularly sections 9(c) and 14(d) of Republic Act No. 9160, as amended by Republic Act No. 11521, or the AMLC law, as well as Section 8-A of the same.
Senator-judges may raise questions on the issue during a caucus or open session on October 5.

“I believe this is only the first time that this is being done in excess of the day. So, ex comitate, ex aequo, out of courtesy and equity, the chair grants the time requested by the counsel for respondent for time to prepare for the cross-examination, rather, to prepare for the direct and cross-examination of the AMLC witness on Monday,” Escudero said.
The Senate clerk of court was directed to amend Buenaventura’s subpoena.

The impeachment court was supposed to begin its new two-week, whole-day trial schedule on October 1. But the ruling cut short Thursday’s proceedings and suspended the trial scheduled for Friday, October 2.

articles.title: What happened in failed execution of Christa Pike - and what next?
articles.summary: The convicted killer is in hospital in Tennessee after surviving two lethal injections, in a case that has raised many questions.

blocks.text: What we know after Christa Pike survived two lethal injections
US convicted murderer Christa Pike is in hospital and being given "life-saving measures" after Tennessee authorities failed in their attempt to execute her by lethal injection.
The case of Pike, whose attempted execution had already been the subject of a high-profile legal battle, has raised a number of questions.
These include what went went wrong, what happens next, and - for opponents of the death penalty - fresh concerns around the suffering of an inmate when an execution does not go to plan.
What happened?
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, an attack that was perpetrated alongside her then-boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp.
She was scheduled to be put to death on Wednesday evening, local time. The injections were allowed by the US Supreme Court at the eleventh hour after the legal battle.
Pike was given two syringes of the drug pentobarbital, though her legal team said these failed to stop her heartbeat and that she could still be heard snoring.
The Tennessee Department of Correction defended the method it used, and said "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening".
The state protocol does not clearly specify what should happen if an inmate remains alive after a second dose, according to the AP news agency.
Authorities have yet to provide their explanation of why the dosage given to Pike proved to be non-fatal, although medical experts have provided theories of their own.

Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine who told the BBC he had been retained by Pike's legal team as a medical expert, said she probably never achieved a sufficient blood level of pentobarbital to cause apnoea and cardiovascular failure.
What happens next?
The state correction department added that Pike had been taken to an off-site medical facility.
One of her lawyers said she was "being provided life-saving measures" in hospital.
Her health status is unclear as of Thursday morning.
In his emailed comments to the BBC, Zivot said: "It's very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she will have a brain injury."
A third-party review has been ordered by the state governor, Bill Lee, who also says the year's last remaining execution will not go ahead as planned.
May Martinez, the mother of Colleen Slemmer who had pushed for Pike's execution to take place, told NBC News the events had been "a mess".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and her boyfriend

blocks.text: Image source, Family handout
Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and her boyfriend
Opponents of the death penalty have similarly been quick to react.

Maya Foa, the chief executive of international legal organisation Reprieve, said: "We cannot know exactly what went wrong, because so much happened behind a curtain – lethal injection relies on secrecy at every stage, to hide the violence of the state taking a human life."
Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike. There is a historical precedent of authorities making a second attempt to execute those on death row.
Meanwhile Shipp, Pike's boyfriend and co-defendant, remains in prison, having been spared the death penalty under state law. He was 17 at the time that Slemmer was killed.
What is the drug pentobarbital?

Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.

Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review - which took place under the presidency of Joe Biden - raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".
His government banned its use in federal executions but that did not bind individual states such as Tennessee, which can choose their own methods.
In recent years, states have found some drugs needed for lethal injections harder to come by, because pharmaceutical companies have opposed the use of their products for such purposes.

The Tennessee Department of Correction has not specifically addressed an allegation from Pike's legal team that the pentobarbital it used was "degraded". Drugs may degrade for a number of reasons, including if it has aged beyond its use-by date and its potency has decreased.
The department issued a broader defence of its method, writing in a statement: "The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective."
Has this happened before?
The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.

The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal injection. He was given a one-year reprieve by Governor Bill Lee.
More widely across the US, the issue of botched executions continues to cause alarm.

In 2022, more than a third of executions in the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center (DPI) - an organisation that provides statistics and research on the death penalty but does not take a stance on it morally.
The DPI says lethal injection has the high­est rate of botched exe­cu­tions.

An incident in Oklahoma in 2014 gained particular notoriety. The execution of Clayton Lockett was postponed after 20 minutes because the lethal injection of three drugs failed to work properly when one of his veins ruptured, and he went on to writhe and shake uncontrollably.

In the US, 27 of the 50 states have the death penalty under state law. The federal government can also carry out executions after President Donald Trump, a supporter of capital punishment, ended a moratorium last year, However, it is yet to actually carry out any executions since then.

articles.title: A brutal assault reignites fears over women's safety in India
articles.summary: A string of sexual assault cases has revived questions about women's safety in India, fuelling fear, protests and demands for action.

image.caption: Sexual violence is a ​major issue across India, ‌with more than 80 rapes reported to police every dayImage: Sajjad Hussain/AFP

blocks.text: This article includes accounts of rape and physical assault
Reports of the gang rape of a 17-year-old girl in New Delhi earlier this week has thrust the issue of women's safety in India back into the spotlight.
Three men who posed as police officers took the girl away at gunpoint to a secluded part of the Aastha Kunj Park, according to local media.
Security around New Delhi's parks has been stepped up since the incident, with a focus on improved lighting, increased security and more frequent patrols.
New Delhi park rape sparks fear across India
Anita Kunwar, a 18-year-old college student from city's East Delhi district said a lot has changed after what happened at Aastha Kunj Park.

"Women and girls across the city are incredibly wary, anxious, and deeply concerned about their safety said Kunwar. "An incident like this, especially in a public space where people go to relax, shatters your sense of security."
"Reports of these ghastly sexual assaults seem to have risen in recent years," said Deepika Singh, a university student in New Delhi. "It is as if these crimes are being normalized. It is sickening."

blocks.caption: Hundreds of students, many of them women, marched in New Delhi a few days after the alleged assaultImage: Sajjad Hussain/AFP

blocks.text: "The assaults have also become more brutal and aggressive," the 19-year-old told DW. "But I am not going to change the way I live my life because of them."
Hundreds of students, many of them women, marched in New Delhi a few days after the alleged assault, demanding greater safety in public spaces.
"Our body is our own," some placards said, while others demanded ​freedom to go out at night without fear.
Students at nearby Lady Shri Ram College have also highlighted poorly lit roads, limited police presence and gaps in surveillance around the campus.
Sexual violence across India
The concerns are not confined to one neighborhood or one city.

In Bihar state's Jamui district, a video showing the sexual assault of a teenage girl and the beating of her male friend triggered widespread anger last month. Police arrested three minors and formed a special investigation team.

blocks.caption: The fatal gang rape of a student on a bus in Delhi in 2012 sparked national outrage and demands for stricter lawsImage: Reuters

blocks.text: Elsewhere in Bihar, a woman was allegedly raped and brutally assaulted in a hotel room on Sunday after travelling to the Begusarai district for work. A video of the assault later circulated on social media.

Punjab's Lovely Professional University (LPU) suspended classes and postponed mid-term examinations after a protest over an alleged rape turned violent on Sunday with protesters clashing with the police and vandalism being reported.
Why the numbers stay high
Across India, sexual violence is a ​major issue, with more than 80 rapes reported to police every day, according to data from the National Crime Records Bureau.

Women's rights groups, including People Against Rape in India (PARI), have long argued that official crime statistics do not capture the full scale of sexual violence because many assaults go unreported.

The gang rape and murder of a student in New Delhi in 2012 sparked nationwide protests and led to sweeping legal reforms, including tougher penalties for offenders and the creation of fast-track courts.

But the changes have done little to reduce sexual violence. Women's rights groups say entrenched patriarchal attitudes, understaffed police forces and delays in the justice system leave many perpetrators believing they can avoid punishment.
Can tougher policing help?

"Women's safety is non-negotiable. Women must be safe on every street, at every hour," said Delhi Lieutenant Governor Taranjit Singh Sandhu, while ordering the creation of a dedicated "Pink Force" of women personnel to enhance the safety of women and children in education establishments, metro stations and other locations across New Delhi.

The Supreme Court has now stepped in. On September 28, it took up the recent sexual assault cases on its own initiative and said they raised serious concerns about the way authorities were protecting women in public spaces.
The apex court has directed Delhi Police to identify vulnerable locations, improve patrolling and conduct audits of lighting and CCTV coverage in parks and other public spaces.
The rape crisis in rural India is shrouded in silence
But Yashvardhan Azad, a retired senior police officer, says the problem starts well before the police are called.
"The failure is first the society where any woman going alone at night or with a friend is viewed with suspicion," Azad told DW. "The political climate in many states favour moral policing."

"Public places are neglected and badly lit. Police can never be everywhere. Most importantly, recent cases reveal the municipality's failure. Well-lit roads, better managed parks and trained guards are the answer, along with CCTVs," he said.
Kalpana Vishwanath of Jagori, a Delhi based women's rights group, says cities "must be designed and built to be inherently safe, inclusive and gender responsive."

"Evaluating public spaces on nine infrastructure and social parameters, including lighting, clear walkways, transit access, crowds, the presence of women and security personnel, and natural surveillance from vendors and shops, would make them safer and go a long way in curtailing sexual violence," Vishwanath told DW.
When reporting a crime isn't enough

Criminal lawyer says police cannot be everywhere at all times but the failures continue once a case reaches them for investigation, with seizures improperly made and witness statements badly recorded.
"Many times, the police refuse to register a case because they are inclined to disbelieve the woman at the very beginning," John told DW.

John also points to delays in forensic examination, emphasising that India has just seven Central Forensic Science Laboratories, alongside 32 state and 97 regional labs, adding to the time needed to process crucial evidence, often leading to acquittals or overturned rulings in higher courts.
The Supreme Court has given Delhi Police four weeks to complete audits and put stepped up patrols in place.

Whether that restores the confidence students describe losing will be tested well beyond the deadline, in the public spaces where many women continue to weigh every journey against concerns for their safety.
Is violence against women an epidemic no one cares about?

articles.title: British Sikh activist released from Delhi jail after nine-year detention
articles.summary:
Indian government issued with warning it would be in contempt of court if it failed to release Jagtar Singh Johal

The British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal has been released from a Delhi…

blocks.text: The British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal has been released from a Delhi prison after the Indian high court warned the government it would be found in contempt of court if it continued to attempt to keep him in jail despite an 18 September court order releasing him on bail. Johal has been incarcerated for nine years without any full trial.
The court order was issued after Johal’s lawyers issued a writ of habeas corpus alleging he was being detained against the express direction of the court.

Johal’s nine-year detention on alleged terrorist offences, has been a cause of diplomatic tension between the UK and India, but campaigners have claimed the British government has not been active enough to secure his release or, alternatively, a full trial.

The campaign group Reprieve says his case has never come to full trial largely because of the inability of the Indian government to assemble credible witnesses to back their claim that Johal transported £3,000 to France to fund a multinational extremist plot involving targeted killings in the Punjab in 2016-17.

On Thursday morning, the high court in Delhi instructed the Indian government to release Johal by 2.30pm Indian time, giving government officials three hours to comply or find themselves risking contempt proceedings.

Documents shown to the court by Johal’s lawyers on behalf of his father-in-law as petitioner revealed that messages from the prison to the Ministry of Home Affairs seeking permission for his release had been left unanswered.

His lawyers in their petition stated he had met all the bail conditions yet “the detainee has nevertheless not been released, and is being held in custody without the authority of any court, pending a ‘clarification’ sought by the jail from the Ministry of Home Affairs”.

The petition added that no clarification from the ministry had been forthcoming, explaining: “Every day of such detention is a continuing violation of the detainee’s fundamental rights under article 21 of the constitution of India.”

Johal has been detained by Indian authorities since 4 November 2017. He is facing eight charges of terrorism in the federal court, but had been cleared of largely similar charges by a Punjab court. He claims any initial confessions he gave were extracted under torture.

The bail terms last week imposed 11 conditions, including surrender of passport, a personal bond of 500,000 Indian rupees (£3,930) with two sureties, fortnightly reporting to the investigating officer, prior intimation of any change of residence and a ban on travelling to the Punjab. He was also restricted from talking to media about the case directly or indirectly.
In letters from the Delhi jail to the ministry seeking clarification on his release, the jail authorities said there were no further grounds for his detention.
They pointed out release warrants were issued on Monday after all the court’s bail conditions had been met, and any further detention without a court order amounted to administrative detention.
The Indian government has alleged the Khalistan Liberation Force undertook the killings and Johal had “complete knowledge of the conspiracy” and was a KLF member.
The UK Foreign Office is understood to have been supporting recent calls for his release on bail after last week’s court order, as have two campaign groups in the UK Redress and Reprieve.

articles.title: Young poomsae guns Candelaria, Yape add silver, bronze to PH haul in Asian Games
articles.summary: Only 18 years old, Juliana Candelaria delivers the highest finish by a Filipino taekwondo athlete in the Asian Games in two decades with a silver, while Jeus Yape contributes a bronze

blocks.text: MEDALISTS. Taekwondo athletes Juliana Candelaria and Jeus Yape of the Philippines flash their poomsae medals in the 2026 Asian Games.
PSC-POC Media Pool
Only 18 years old, Juliana Candelaria delivers the highest finish by a Filipino taekwondo athlete in the Asian Games in two decades with a silver, while Jeus Yape contributes a bronze

MANILA, Philippines – Two young taekwondo standouts aided the Philippines’ medal cause in the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, as Juliana Mykhail Candelaria and Jeus Gabriel Derick Yape won a pair of poomsae medals.
Candelaria snagged silver in the women’s individual poomsae, while Yape bagged bronze in the men’s individual poomsae at Toyohashi Gymnasium on Thursday, October 1.

Only 18 years old, Candelaria delivered the highest finish by a Filipino taekwondo athlete in the Asian Games in two decades, or since Tshomlee Go and Toni Rivero won silver apiece in the 2006 edition in Doha, Qatar.

“I feel great about everything. I’m super, duper thankful for the opportunity. At my age, oh my gosh!” Candelaria told One Sports in a mix of English and Filipino. “I’m so hyped and so happy for everyone who competed.”
Candelaria netted an average of 9.13 points for the silver as she finished behind South Korea’s Jung Ha-eun, who struck gold with 9.31 points.
“It’s such an amazing achievement for me. It’s my first Asian Games, so super, duper thankful for everything.”
Yape, meanwhile, finished third with 9.09 points, sharing the podium with South Korea’s gold winner Yun Kyu-sung (9.38) and Thailand’s silver medalist Navin Pinthasute (9.28).
“I’m happy with my performance. I did my best, and I gave it my all,” Yape told One Sports.
Singapore’s Zong Han Darren Yap also won bronze as the fourth placer with 9.04 points.

The podium finishes by Candelaria and Yape bode well for the rest of the Philippine taekwondo team, with the likes of three-time Southeast Asian Games titlist Kurt Barbosa and world junior champion Tachiana Mangin also eyeing medals. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Ukraine persists with Russian oil refinery strikes, defying Trump on fuel price warnings
articles.summary: Kyiv’s long-range strikes are headache for Trump before crucial midterms, while analysts’ claim war in Iran is responsible for rising prices

blocks.text: Ukraine is pressing on with strikes on Russian oil refineries, defying Donald Trump, who blames the attacks for exacerbating a global diesel shortage and pushing up fuel prices.

Kyiv struck an oil facility in Russia’s southern Samara region overnight, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday in a statement on social media. The Ukrainian president added that a Russian vessel in the Black Sea was hit, as well as a launch and storage site for attack drones in the Oryol region.

Trump has urged Zelenskyy in a private phone call to halt attacks on Russian refineries and repeatedly suggested in public that Ukraine’s strikes are to blame for the squeeze on global fuel supplies. “Diesel is really hurt much more, not by the Middle East, but by what’s going on in Russia, because those diesel refineries are being knocked out at a pretty alarming rate,” Trump said on Wednesday.

Diesel prices in the US have risen to record highs in recent weeks, adding to cost of living pressures that have helped push Trump’s approval ratings to a career low before next month’s crucial midterm elections.
Energy analysts, however, have pointed to the war in Iran and wider disruption to global oil markets as the leading drivers of the price increases.

Ukraine’s long-range strikes on Russian refineries have nevertheless emerged as an additional headache for Trump, with the attacks also contributing to tighter diesel supplies at a politically sensitive moment for the US president.

Ukraine’s campaign in recent months has knocked out more than 45% of Russia’s refining capacity, according to Ukrainian estimates, prompting fuel rationing in some regions and long queues at petrol stations.
Earlier this week, Russia – traditionally the world’s second-largest diesel exporter – extended its ban on diesel exports until the end of October, adding further pressure to a global supply crunch.

Mykola Bielieskov, a military analyst at Ukraine’s government-run National Institute for Strategic Studies, said it was unlikely Kyiv would stop targeting Russian oil infrastructure as long as Moscow continued its daily attacks on Ukraine. “There is no rationale for Ukraine to continue exercising restraint while it is being bombarded and major urban areas are under constant attack,” he said.
“We need to deprive Russia of revenue,” he added.
Zelenskyy has been pushing for a US-brokered energy ceasefire with Russia, but Putin has shown little interest in the proposal, instead vowing to intensify strikes on Ukraine.

Meanwhile, Russia has continued its deadly missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities, targeting energy infrastructure, commercial warehouses and other businesses in an apparent effort to cripple the country’s economy and render Kyiv increasingly uninhabitable.
A Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv on Thursday morning, but no one was injured because the children were sheltering in the basement, mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
A key bridge in the Ukrainian capital was also hit, forcing authorities to suspend metro services and other public transport.

Kyiv has experienced near round-the-clock Russian attacks in recent weeks, at times increasingly resembling a frontline city in what many see as the most challenging period for the capital since the early days of the full-scale invasion.

blocks.caption: Emergency workers attend a damaged school in Kyiv after Russian drone strike. The children were sheltering in the basement. Photograph: Gleb Garanich/Reuters

blocks.text: Russia’s newer jet-powered drones have proved particularly difficult for Ukrainian air defences to intercept, with success rates significantly lower than for the slower Shahed-type drones.

The sustained attacks have revived fears of another winter with prolonged power and heating outages, after similar strikes last year left parts of Ukraine without electricity during temperatures that fell as low as -20C.

articles.title: AMLC: Freeze order issued for 'prominent lawmaker' tagged in flood control scam
articles.summary: The Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) on Thursday said that it has secured a freeze order against a “prominent lawmaker” in connection with the flood control scam. In a statement, the AMLC said…

blocks.text: Published October 1, 2026 7:58pm
The Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) on Thursday said that it has secured a freeze order against a “prominent lawmaker” in connection with the flood control scam.
In a statement, the AMLC said that the Court of Appeals (CA) issued a freeze order after finding probable cause that the assets were related to plunder.

The Council said that the freeze order covered “assets linked to a prominent lawmaker, a corporation, and several associated individuals and entities in connection with alleged anomalies involving flood control projects and a broader government budget kickback scheme.”
The financial investigation showed that the individuals had no apparent operating revenues to support the scale of the investments.

According to the AMLC, the money involved in the investments was also moved through multiple layers with the use of intermediaries, corporations, bank accounts, a money service business, and a virtual asset platform.

“The use of multiple recipients and financial channels complicated the tracing of the funds and increased their transactional distance from their alleged source. The AMLC traced these transactions to funds allegedly associated with corruption and plunder cases involving the lawmaker,” the Council said.
The CA’s freeze order covered 86 bank accounts, four investment accounts, one insurance policy, and 25 virtual asset wallets.
The AMLC said that the probe showed the increasing use of financial technology used to move suspected illicit funds.
In the lawmaker’s case, the allegedly illicit funds were funneled through virtual asset service providers and multiple virtual asset wallets.

“The AMLC will continue working closely with partner agencies and financial service providers to identify, trace, restrain, and recover suspected illicit assets, while preventing the misuse of both traditional and emerging financial channels for corruption, money laundering, and other unlawful activities,” the Council said.

There are several lawmakers involved in the flood control scheme, with one senator already being detained as he faced plunder charges. Sen. Jinggoy Estrada is currently detained at the Quezon City Jail for allegedly receiving kickbacks.

Meanwhile, former House lawmaker Zaldy Co has been on the run from Philippine authorities after he was tagged as a mastermind in the flood control scheme. Estrada and Co are only two of the lawmakers named in connection with the flood control scheme. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: ‘Mabuting dumaan sa legal’: Mary Jane Veloso gives advice to future OFWs
articles.summary: ‘Sana po 'tong pag-share ko po ng aking kaso ay maging inspirasyon po sa iba na para po hindi na po sila matulad sa akin, para wala na pong pangalawang Mary Jane na makakaranas ng ganito,’ she says

blocks.text: AN OFW'S PLIGHT. Former overseas Filipino worker Mary Jane Veloso narrates her experiences during a press conference at the Department of Justice on October 1, 2026.
Rappler
‘Sana po 'tong pag-share ko po ng aking kaso ay maging inspirasyon po sa iba na para po hindi na po sila matulad sa akin, para wala na pong pangalawang Mary Jane na makakaranas ng ganito,’ she says

items: Mary Jane Veloso, a former overseas Filipino worker, advises potential OFWs to avoid illegal recruiters.
After her recent release, Veloso plans to look into livelihood opportunities and continue her education.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Mary Jane Veloso told those who want to become overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) to avoid illegal recruiters and ensure that they undergo the legal process for working abroad.
Veloso, a 41-year-old former OFW, gave the advice in a press conference at the Department of Justice (DOJ) in Manila on Thursday, October 1, days after her release from prison.

blocks.caption: ‘Mabuting dumaan sa legal’: Mary Jane Veloso gives advice to future OFWs

blocks.text: “Wala pong masama na mangarap. Wala pong masama na gusto natin maiahon ang ating mga pamilya sa hirap. Pero kung ako po, mabuti pong dumaan tayo sa legal na paraan,” she said.
(There’s nothing wrong with having a dream. There’s nothing wrong with having the desire to lift your family out of poverty. But for me, it’s better that we undergo the legal process.)

Veloso, who was supposed to work as an OFW in Malaysia, was arrested in Indonesia in 2010 as she was allegedly duped by recruiters into becoming a drug mule. (READ: What you should know about the case of Mary Jane Veloso)
Indonesian airport authorities found 2.6 kilograms of heroin hidden inside the lining of her suitcase, which was allegedly given to her by her recruiters.
“Huwag po natin hayaan na maengganyo po tayo dahil po mayroong free visa, na kesyo ‘pag free visa madali lang makahanap ng trabaho, mabilis lang makaalis,” Veloso said.
(Let’s not be blinded by the offer of a free visa, thinking that would make it easy to find a job and quickly leave the country.)

To prevent getting into danger, she reminded Filipinos to turn to the Department of Migrant Workers, which can help in giving instructions and information on legitimate job offers in their target country.

“Sana po ‘tong pag-share ko po ng aking kaso ay maging inspirasyon po sa iba na para po hindi na po sila matulad sa akin, para wala na pong pangalawang Mary Jane na makakaranas ng ganito,” Veloso said.
(I hope that in sharing my case, it would inspire others so that they wouldn’t end up like me, so that there would be no second Mary Jane.)
Indonesia granted Veloso a last-minute reprieve in 2015, allowing her to narrowly escape execution for drug trafficking.

In December 2024, Veloso was repatriated to the Philippines, but was still detained at the Correctional Institution for Women (CIW) in Mandaluyong City. Her life was spared at that point because the country has no death penalty.
It took a year and nine months before President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. pardoned the Filipina. She walked free and returned to her home province of Nueva Ecija last Saturday, September 26.

Under local anti-human trafficking laws, the Philippines followed the principle of “non-punishment” for human trafficking victims, which was applicable also to Veloso’s case, according to Justice Undersecretary Nicholas Felix Ty.

And while this was successfully applied to her case, Ty said this should not be seen by Filipinos as a signal to be deceived in other countries and think they will be saved because they are supposedly human trafficking victims.

“We are really happy that Mary Jane returned home, but this should not be seen as a reason for others to follow her path. Let us not forget that before we reached this day, Mary Jane went through so much. And it was not easy to bring her home and for her to be pardoned,” he said in Filipino.
According to the DOJ, it officially recommended to Marcos on May 12 that he exercise his constitutional authority to grant executive clemency to Veloso.

blocks.caption: ‘Mabuting dumaan sa legal’: Mary Jane Veloso gives advice to future OFWs

blocks.text: But discussions on the pardon, and in effect, the release of Veloso, had already started in 2024 following her repatriation, said Justice Undersecretary Deo Marco.
Among the considerations taken into account were the continued enforcement of Veloso’s sentence, the circumstances of her case, and the possible perspective of Indonesia.

blocks.caption: ‘Mabuting dumaan sa legal’: Mary Jane Veloso gives advice to future OFWs

blocks.text: Marco said that after Veloso’s transfer in 2024, it was already reported that Indonesia would respect Marcos’ decision regarding her case. (READ: In unique deal, Indonesia gives Marcos discretion to pardon Mary Jane Veloso)

A day after Veloso’s release, the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) provided P30,000 as cash aid to Veloso, and another P20,000 to her parents. Her two sons will also be given P10,000 each.
According to the DSWD, Veloso expressed interest in setting up a sari-sari store when she was assessed for the agency’s livelihood assistance program.

But Veloso also said on Thursday that she really wants to have capital to buy farmland since Nueva Ecija is an agricultural province, adding that she still lacks the skills to sell clothing or go into a retail business.
She also wants to finish junior high school through the Department of Education’s Alternative Learning System, which she started while inside the CIW.
As she returns to ordinary life with her family, Veloso said she would still try to help others.

“Mayroon na po tayong social media din po ngayon. Kaya kahit nasa bahay, kung gusto mo talagang magbigay ng support sa kanila para hindi sila mapahamak, kaya naman po nating gawin ‘yon,” she told reporters.
(We have social media now. Even if you’re just staying at home, if you really want to give support to others so that they won’t be put in danger, I think I can do that.) – Rappler.com

articles.title: Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names
articles.summary: The president wants AI to be called super intelligence - or SI - the same initials used by Slovenian domains.

blocks.text: President Donald Trump's push to rename AI may be behind an "unprecedented" rise in registrations for domain names in Slovenia, according to its official national registry.
The president wants AI to be called super intelligence - or SI - the same initials used by Slovenian websites.
Register.si spokesperson Klara Herman said 44,000 web addresses with the .si suffix had been registered in September, compared to less than 2,000 in August - an increase of more than 2,100%.
She said the scale of activity in late September was "unprecedented" compared to the previous 12 months.
President Trump called for the technology to be renamed during his speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on 11 September.
"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said.
"It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful... welcome to the new world of super intelligence."
Internet domains are the unique human-readable addresses people type into their web browsers to access websites - like bbc.co.uk.

Herman said registrations for .si web addresses in September stood out "very clearly" against the other months in the year, although she was "cautious" about attributing the entire increase to only President Trump's comments.
She said on 30 September alone, 11,000 new registrations were recorded.
One possible explanation for the purchases is cyber-squatting - where people speculatively register specific domain names in case they increase in value later on and can be sold for a profit.
For example, in 1997 Rick Schwartz, known as "The Domain King", bought the domain name men.com for $15,000 (£11,300). He sold it for $1.32 million seven years later.
On Tuesday, President Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the people "building America's Golden Age".
He signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and they should no longer acknowledge the use of the term AI.
SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.
Images of the signatures for the order were mocked online, external however - when it was discovered "United States" had been spelt incorrectly underneath President Trump's signature.

articles.title: Sara Duterte declared 2 Davao City properties in SALN — defense
articles.summary: Defense spokesperson Michael Poa says the defense was also surprised that the prosecution dropped former senator Antonio Trillanes IV from its list of witnesses

blocks.text: SARA. Accompanied by her brother, Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo Duterte, Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Quezon City RTC on September 11, 2026, to attend arraignment proceedings for a grave threat case.
Jire Carreon/Rappler
Defense spokesperson Michael Poa says the defense was also surprised that the prosecution dropped former senator Antonio Trillanes IV from its list of witnesses

items: The defense team of Vice President Sara Duterte claims that the two Davao City properties in question were declared in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth, despite prosecution witnesses asserting otherwise.

During the impeachment trial, the prosecution presented witnesses from the Land Registration Authority to argue that the properties were undeclared, but the defense challenged their credibility due to lack of personal knowledge regarding Duterte's SALN.

The defense also expressed surprise at the prosecution's decision to drop former senator Antonio Trillanes IV from their witness list, stating that it is within the prosecution's prerogative to choose their witnesses.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The defense team of Sara Duterte insisted on Thursday, October 1, that the Vice President had declared in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) the two Davao City properties currently being scrutinized by the prosecution in the impeachment trial.

“Are you saying that the subject properties are all stated in the SALN of the Vice President? Because it seems to be that the prosecution is saying that the subject properties were not declared. Please clarify,” Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo asked in a mix of English and Filipino.

“That is the position, our position: that the properties that the two witnesses [who] testified to today are in fact declared in the SALN of the Vice President,” defense lawyer Lindon Miguel Bacquel said in response.
On the trial’s 32nd day, the House prosecution team presented two witnesses from the Land Registration Authority to prove that Duterte had alleged undeclared properties in her SALN.

Davao City Register of Deeds IV Kathy Florence Baldonado testified that a lot in Matina, Davao City, was sold to the Vice President’s husband, lawyer Manases Carpio, for P6 million in July 2024. The second witness, Samal City Deputy Register of Deeds III Marco Pineda, testified that Carpio also bought a property on the island for P3 million in 2018.
However, the two properties do not match any of the entries in Duterte’s SALN.
Bacquel said the Matina property was listed as a residential lot in Barangay 74-A, while the other one was listed as a residential lot in Barangay Matanos, Kaputian District.
Before the direct examination of the two witnesses, the defense objected to their presentation. They argued that witnesses must have personal knowledge of the matters they are testifying on.

Bacquel also poked holes in the witnesses’ testimony. During his cross-examination, the defense lawyer elicited that neither Baldonado nor Pineda had personal knowledge of the Vice President’s properties, liabilities, business interests, and net worth listed in her SALN.
“And you cannot testify on the completeness or incompleteness to disclosure in the SALN because you had no personal knowledge, tama po (correct)?” the defense lawyer asked.
“Tama po (Correct),” Baldonado responded.

blocks.caption: Sara Duterte declared 2 Davao City properties in SALN — defense

blocks.text: Meanwhile, defense spokesperson Michael Poa, during a press briefing on Thursday, revealed that even the defense was surprised that the prosecution dropped former senator Antonio Trillanes IV from its list of witnesses.

“Actually, we also didn’t expect that. But, as I always say, it’s always a prerogative of the prosecution at this point whom they will call as witnesses, whom they will drop from their list for whatever reason,” Poa said in a mix of English and Filipino.
“But I have to clarify that that’s not an issue. It’s really within their prerogative,” he added.

The defense counsel added they were actually ready to cross-examine Trillanes. He also clarified that they were not “relieved” because of Trillanes’ removal, because the defense was already prepared based on the initial list of witnesses submitted.
“Because it’s really the time of the prosecution now to present their witnesses. So, we really just react to their presentation,” Poa added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Explosions heard in Ethiopia's capital after drone flights banned
articles.summary: It comes a week after fighting erupted north of the capital between the army and a new alliance of armed groups.

blocks.text: Explosions were heard overnight in Ethiopia's capital, some in the area of the military headquarters in the west and another in the south of the city, residents and diplomatic sources say.

The blasts came hours after drone flights were banned over Addis Ababa and a week after fighting erupted in the north between the army and a newly launched alliance of armed groups including forces from the Tigray region.
A source linked to the opposition fighters told the Reuters news agency they were behind what they said were drone strikes.
"It was very loud. It was strong enough to set off car alarms," a resident in a southern area of the city, near the base of the secret service, told BBC Amharic.
He estimated that he heard the explosion in the Gotera neighbourhood some time around 00:30 local time (21:30 GMT).
Another resident told the BBC that he and his friends were playing games when they heard an explosion.
He lives in the western suburb of Torhayloch, a neighbourhood close to the military headquarters.
There were no official reports confirming the cause of the explosions, the exact locations affected or whether there were any casualties or damage.
The office of Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, the defence ministry as well as the federal and Addis Ababa police have not responded to BBC requests for comment.

articles.title: Weakened US fuel-efficiency rules and promises of cheaper cars could see drivers pay higher running costs while also increasing carbon emissions.
articles.summary: Weakened US fuel-efficiency rules and promises of cheaper cars could yet see drivers pay higher running costs while increasing planet-heating emissions.

image.caption: Gas prices are on the rise as Trump moves to make cars less fuel efficientImage: Mario Tama/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: As part of its "Freedom Means More Affordable Cars" initiative, the US Department of Transportation this week rolled back fuel efficiency rules under the guise of lowering vehicle prices.

The Trump administration's transport agency says US taxpayers will save $138 billion (€122 billion) over the next five years — new vehicles will be $1,300 cheaper on average — since automakers will no longer have to invest in more fuel-efficient fleets.
But this does not account for soaring gas prices as Middle East conflicts choke global supply.

"Any savings on the front end get eaten up and spat out by excess costs of fuel … Fuel economy standards have saved drivers hundreds of billions of dollars," said Democratic Senator Sheldon Whitehouse in a social media post.

Under the revised Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) rules, vehicle fleets only require an average fuel efficiency of about 35 miles per gallon (14.7km per liter) by 2031, down around one-third from 50 miles per gallon.

Implemented by the Biden administration in 2024, the updated efficiency rules aimed to incentivize the production of low emission electric vehicles and hybrids. The US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) estimates the standards would have saved 70 billion gallons (265 billion litres) of fuel over 25 years.

blocks.caption: Drivers in the US will be pumping more gas under weakened fuel efficiency rules Image: Brandon Bell/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: Meanwhile, nonprofit advocacy group, the Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS) says an earlier version of CAFE regulations has saved US consumers have saved about $321 billion at the gas pump since 2010.
Rollbacks set to increase planet-heating emissions

The world's biggest petrol consumer, the US burns through 20 million barrels of oil per day, which is 20% of global consumption, notes Dan Becker, director of the Safe Climate Transport Campaign at the US-based nonprofit environmental group Center for Biological Diversity.
"Transportation is the biggest consumer of that oil, making strong auto standards the most effective way to cut pollution and oil use," Becker said in a statement.

The rules that have been diluted this week would have prevented more than 710 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions by 2050 — the equivalent of running 165 million gas-powered passenger vehicles for a year.

"With transportation representing nearly 28% of US greenhouse emissions, rolling back fuel economy standards is a dangerous setback for near-term climate goals," said Ben Scott, head of Energy Demand at UK-based climate think tank, Carbon Tracker.
"It risks keeping inefficient combustion engines on the road much longer than climate science demands," he told DW.

But following the Trump administration’s elimination of greenhouse gas emissions standards for light- and heavy-duty vehicles last year, Dave Cooke, senior vehicles analyst for the UCS Clean Transportation Program, said the rollbacks merely compound "a much more significant step backwards."
He said the trend sends "a specific signal to automakers," adding that "the United States is seeking to maximize oil usage to increase oil company profits."
This will be to the detriment of climate targets, with high-polluting oil contributing one-third of global fossil fuel emissions that continue to rise — along with temperatures.
The world just had the hottest August on record as severe heatwaves in Europe caused over 16,000 excess deaths in Germany alone.
US turns its back on EVs
Can US transport still transition to clean energy?
Sales of low emission EVs are down in the US in 2026, especially after president Trump scrapped the $7,500 tax credit for new electric vehicles.
American automakers also continue to push back against regulations that would incentivize a switch to EVs, arguing there is a lack of consumer demand.

"It's highly unlikely that the United States will suddenly become awash in electric options when neither the auto industry nor regulators seem interested in providing such choices for consumers," said Cooke.
But Ben Scott believes that while softening US fuel economy standards "will create temporary headwinds", it won't stall an inevitable transition to electric vehicles.

"With EVs delivering vastly lower running costs, electrification becomes a clear-cut economic choice," he said of cars running on "cheaper, domestically secure energy that will drive the transition forward, regardless of short-term politics."
As less efficient cars and trucks consume more oil that's more expensive and in shorter supply, "the fragility of oil-dependent transport" is set to be exposed, he said.
