Without naming the party directly, the signatories of the letter wrote that they believe that the greatest enemy of Jewish life is the Alternative for Germany (AfD): "At a time when an in-parts openly fascistic political party is marching towards power across Germany, it is an abdication of responsibility on the part of mainstream media and elements of our own community to continue to pretend that the Left presents the largest threat to Jewish safety."

In light of this, the letter states: "The constant accusations of antisemitism against the Left are not only cynical political weaponization, but they also conflate nearly any criticism of Israel with antisemitism."
Elif Eralp: From daughter of refugees to Berlin mayor?

The Left Party is the only party in the German parliament that opposes arms deliveries to Israel due to the military operation in the Gaza Strip following the terrorist attack by the radical Islamist group Hamas on October 7, 2023. Based on a resolution passed at its party convention, the Left Party classifies the ensuing war as a genocide.
Elif Eralp wants to build bridges

Human rights organizations and a United Nations (UN) commission have also classified Israel's actions in Gaza against the Palestinian people as a genocide. The Israeli government under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, however, has invoked Israel's right to self-defense.

The intensifying debate over antisemitism within the Left Party is complicating the formation of a government in Berlin. At a party congress convened on short notice, Elif Eralp, the potential future mayor of Berlin, emphasized that her party has a duty to bring people together and build bridges.
"And in doing so," Eralp said, "it must be absolutely clear that there must never be any calls for violence, and that statements that frighten Jewish people must never be made from our platforms."
With these remarks, Eralp once again criticized the antisemitic rapper's performance during the Berlin election campaign. Jewish people must be able to feel safe in Berlin, said Eralp.
"I will strengthen Berlin's diverse Jewish community and combat antisemitism. And Palestinian and Muslim people must also feel seen and safe," Eralp said.

blocks.caption: Scott Grabell, an artist originally from New York, rejects sweeping accusations of antisemitism against the Left PartyImage: DW

blocks.text: Outside the building where the special party convention was held, about 20 Jewish people expressed their solidarity with the party. A poster in Hebrew and German lay at their feet, reading, "Mazel Tov to the Left," congratulating the party on its September 20 election victory in Berlin.
One of the demonstrators was Scott Grabell, an artist originally from New York.

"Antisemitism is real — we know that," Grabell told DW. "But three years of genocide are also real, as are illegal occupation, forced destruction and displacement in the West Bank — that, too, is real."

Grabell emphasized that they were there to support the Left Party in its efforts to advance progressive policies. "We also want to show the diversity of Jewish life in German society. Everyone talks about the different sides — we are also part of Jewish life."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: ‘We want justice’: series of rapes trigger mass protests at Indian universities
articles.summary:
Women say nothing has changed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya bus rape case 14 years ago

The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners. “Girls don’t need curfews,…
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Aakash Hassan in Delhi

blocks.text: The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners. “Girls don’t need curfews, rapists need consequences,” read one. “Lock your dicks rather than your women at home,” read another.

As hundreds of women walked from the gates of their university campus into the streets of Delhi – where sexual harassment, assault, catcalling and molestation are a constant, daily threat – they shouted together in a chorus of rage and defiance: “We want justice.”

The fury that has erupted on India’s university campuses over the past week has been double-edged. The trigger was a series of brutal rapes that have taken place in Delhi in recent weeks, including the alleged gang-rape of a 17-year-old in a public park close to Delhi University by three men who posed as police officers.

Just a week earlier, another 17-year-old was gang-raped and murdered in Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar neighbourhood after she went to meet friends. The accused allegedly raped her, stabbed her to death and dumped her body in a field, where it was discovered days later half eaten by dogs.
Rapes of an 11-year-old and a six-year-old were reported in the same month. Last month, a 16-year-old was allegedly raped by a bus driver and conductor after she boarded a sleeper bus in Delhi.

Women who have taken part in protests on Delhi university campuses have condemned these alleged violent rapes on minors as disgusting and unforgivable – but they have also been at pains to emphasise that they are not out of the ordinary.

Fourteen years have passed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya rape case, when a woman was gang-raped on a bus and died from her injuries. But while it provoked international outrage and a slew of legislation and government promises, women say nothing has changed; for them, India’s streets, particularly in Delhi, remain as unsafe as ever. According to statistics, a women is raped in India every 20 minutes – though the real scale is believed to be far worse due to chronic under-reporting.
This week, the supreme court said the five successive rape cases “starkly underlined a systematic failure” and it could not help but “draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012”.

Vaishnavi Dhruw, 21, a history student at Delhi University, was among the female protesters at the “smash the patriarchy” protest march on Wednesday afternoon. “I don’t know a single woman who lives in this city and feels safe,” she said.

blocks.caption: Students’ Federation of India (SFI) members protest over the alleged rape of a 17-year-old girl. Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPA

blocks.text: While some of the key demands of the protest have been better lighting and policing, Dhruw emphasised that for anything to change, the country required a deep societal shift where men no longer felt they had ownership over women’s bodies.

“We are not marching for safety, we are here to protest for our freedom, for the most basic right to walk in our own streets,” she said. “Again and again, women are told to stay indoors, to not go out at night, to cover ourselves, to protect ourselves. When will society tell men in our country not to rape?”

Much of the anger driving the protests has also been prompted by the response by the authorities to the rapes, which women say once again has only been to police their freedoms. Women in Delhi were told to stay out of parks at night, and classes were temporarily halted at one of Delhi’s most prestigious female colleges. Many hostels where female students stay impose strict curfews preventing them from going out at night.

“Instead of going after criminals, you’re going to tell women to sit at home,” said Aranya Rathore, 25, a student at Delhi University. “A demand for more surveillance is not a solution. In fact, it’s going to curtail our freedom more.”

Female students say a lot of their time is taken up by safety logistics – from wearing modest clothes to reorganising their days to ensure they do not travel alone or at night and always having a trackable live location on their phones. There is widespread awareness that should anything happen, the onus of blame – both within the family home and more widely in society – tends to fall on women. As one poster at Wednesday’s march pointed out, “no one ever asks what the rapist was wearing”.

Yet despite their best efforts, many women said it was almost impossible to avoid harassment. Ananya Wig, a 26-year-old graduate of Delhi University and the founder of Her Huq, a gender equality initiative, said she had experienced harassment both around university campuses and in public spaces.

She recounted an incident where a driver rolled down his car window and began masturbating as she and female friends got off a rickshaw and walked through the college gates. “This wasn’t at night, it was in the middle of the day,” she said. “I’ve always lived in Delhi and the city has not changed.”

The protests have brought into focus a dilemma faced by many Indian women, who are being educated in greater numbers than any time in the country’s history and have better job opportunities than ever before, but still have to navigate the constant debilitating threats to their safety and the conservative pressures from their families.

“I know so many girls, not just 10 years ago but even today, who end up choosing educational institutions and jobs and other employment opportunities depending on how close they are from their home,” said Wig. “Not on the basis of their marks, not on the basis of their aspirations, but simply, ‘OK, the shorter the distance is, the more likely it is that I will be safe’.”

Many of the Delhi University students who took part in the marches said that sexual harassment had become prevalent on campus, and have demanded better accountability mechanisms for reporting assault. The university has not responded.

Devyani Sarkar, 24, who is studying for a master’s in English, said: “Delhi University is one of the most prestigious universities in India right now but there are various cases of women being assaulted by professors, sometimes unfortunately also for grades. It’s despicable, but it’s also a living truth.”

Many on the marches said it was no coincidence that they were taking place in the aftermath of India’s “cockroach” movement, in which hundreds of thousands of young Gen Z Indians took to the streets over education reform.
“My generation is not afraid to stand up and protest. We know that society has to change,” said 17-year-old Subhani. “The days of women being silent is over.”

articles.title: Passengers describe stabbing on Israel-bound plane
articles.summary: Passengers on the Flydubai flight bound for Israel filmed the moments following the stabbing.

blocks.text: A pilot on an Israel-bound Flydubai flight stabbed another pilot and "apparently tried to crash the plane", Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said.
The plane was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv when it plummeted 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes, before being diverted to Saudi Arabia.
Eyewitnesses inside the plane described the moment the incident happened, with one man calling for help in a video shared on social media.
Follow this story live.

articles.title: Ethiopia fighting escalates in Tigray killing 52 civilians, medic tells the BBC
articles.summary: The deadly fighting has also spread to neighbouring regions, stranding tourists in Lalibela.
articles.byline: Michael Teferi, Lion Tsigab, Lucy Fleming

blocks.text: At least 52 civilians have been killed during three days of heavy fighting around Alamata in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, hospital sources have told the BBC.

It appears government troops have taken control of the town from regional fighters and intend to push north towards Mekelle, the region's main city. Social media clips show army tanks on Alamata's streets.
Clashes broke out last week after months of tension between the government and the party that controls Tigray, with both accusing each other of violating a 2022 deal that ended a two-year civil war.
Fighting has also affected neighbouring regions with 33 tourists stranded for the last week in Lalibela, a Unesco world heritage site.

"We have heard fighting, gunfire and artillery cannons firing throughout the week," a British tourist, who asked not to be named, told the BBC's Newsday programme about clashes near Lalibela in the Amhara region.
He said there was a large military presence in Lalibela, famous for being home to 13th Century churches hewn from rock and a holy site for millions of Orthodox Christians.

Most visitors to the tourist hub had been unable to leave since the airport closed to commercial flights last Wednesday, though he said 14 Israeli tourists had been evacuated by military helicopter on Monday.
The fighting around Lalibela has involved the army and an Amhara militia that has allied with Tigrayan fighters.
Earlier in September, they joined forces with other Ethiopian armed movements to form a seven-member alliance with the stated intention of removing the government in the capital, Addis Ababa.
There is also a fear that neighbouring Eritrea could be drawn into the conflict - as the government accuses Asmara of supporting the armed groups, something it denies.
The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas and it is difficult to find out what is happening because communications to the region have been cut.
The two sides disagree over who started the latest fighting.

The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray, says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in the region.
TPLF fighters are also fighting in the Afar region, in a strategic area which connects landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti and its ports.
Over the last few days, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said more than 700 wounded people had been admitted to hospitals it supports in Tigray.

The doctor at Alamata General Hospital, who requested anonymity, told the BBC the fighting in and around the town had taken place between Saturday and Monday, and involved heavy explosives and artillery, some of which landed in residential homes.
Those killed in the crossfire included children as young as three days old, mothers and cattle herders.
Twelve people had died in a single strike on the town's marketplace, the medic said.
Since the fighting erupted, banking services in Tigray have been suspended by the government. Access to the internet has also been cut - though it is not clear who ordered the closure.
A separate source in Alamata told the BBC there was a worsening humanitarian crisis in the area, as the town swelled with people fleeing fighting.
"All the residents of the surrounding areas entered the town of Alamata by walking on foot for as long as an hour, hoping the town would be safe.
"Unfortunately, everything is blocked - no banking service, no money transfer, no power, no internet, no phone. Hence people are in crisis, simply suffering, everyone is desperate and frustrated."
The British tourist in Lalibela said online banking was working in Lalibela but there was a shortage of physical cash.
He said the situation around the town had calmed down in the last two days and there were indications the airport, which was still being used by the military, might reopen on Thursday.
"The local people, they are still scared of what might happen. The military presence here in the town has remained and a larger military force has been seen leaving the town heading north," he said.
When the airport was first closed, 53 tourists had been in the town, he explained.
But some had since been evacuated, including the 14 Israelis airlifted out on Monday while another five had left the day before via an NGO convoy, despite advice not to travel by road.
Of the remaining tourists in Lalibela, the largest group were Americans, with Israelis, Britons, South Korean, South Africans, an Ethiopian-New Zealander and a Mexican also stranded, he said.
Meanwhile, for those cut off in Tigray because of the telecoms shutdown, the Tigray Broadcasting Service (TBS), based in Addis Ababa, has started an initiative to help reconnect families.
The broadcaster has said it will collect video messages via its Telegram channel from people outside the region and air them via satellite TV.
While limited to greetings and updates, this will provide a rare lifeline for families separated by the blackout.
The clampdown on Tigray's banking services is also affecting Tigrayans who are not physically in the region.
Customers have told the BBC that bank accounts opened in Tigray have been frozen or restricted.

"I boarded public transport from Addis Ababa to Adama and tried to pay using a mobile transfer, but it didn't work," said a former Mekelle resident who moved to the capital two months ago because of growing tensions in Tigray.
"It has created havoc for many people like me who escaped the situation in Tigray," he told the BBC's Tigrinya service.
"Many Tigrayans are now in trouble."
Additional reporting by Yemane Nagish

articles.title: South African leader urges men to speak up on gender-based violence after series of killings
articles.summary:
President announces measures amid anger at authorities over recent murders of women

South Africa’s president has called on men to take more responsibility for violence against women as he…

blocks.text: South Africa’s president has called on men to take more responsibility for violence against women as he announced measures to tackle the problem, amid anger at authorities over a recent wave of murders.

Cyril Ramaphosa acknowledged that not enough had been done to protect women. He said police would be reviewing unsolved murders, attempted murders and serious sexual offences against women and children, as well as producing a funded plan to reduce the forensic backlog for such cases, both within 60 days.

In a televised speech on Tuesday night, the president said local governments would have five months to address issues that compromised women’s safety, from broken streetlights to overgrown public spaces and abandoned buildings. He added that he had tasked five ministers to come up with a plan within 60 days to reduce alcohol-fuelled violence.

blocks.caption: Cyril Ramaphosa acknowledged that not enough had been done to protect women. Photograph: Jairus Mmutle/South African Communications and Information Services/AP

blocks.text: “Alcohol does not cause gender-based violence and it can never excuse it. Responsibility always lies with the perpetrator,” Ramaphosa said. “But harmful alcohol use is a significant aggravating factor in interpersonal violence and it must be addressed as part of our wider prevention effort.
“Women should not have to live in fear because government has failed to repair a light, clear a public space, process evidence or enforce a law.”

South Africa has been gripped by grief and fury after the discovery of 11 women’s bodies dumped across Ekurhuleni, the municipality adjoining Johannesburg to the east, since 15 July. Eight of the women were found in the last three weeks, including Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo, who was discovered on 12 September after she went missing when she went for a run after work.

blocks.caption: People take part in a memorial run in honour of Elizabeth ‘Tsontso’ Moselakgomo. Photograph: Alet Pretorius/Reuters

blocks.text: Ramaphosa said suspects had been arrested in connection with three of the killings and that the other cases would not be left to go cold. He added that police had not found evidence that a serial killer was responsible for all 11 killings, but that all possibilities were still being investigated.

He directly addressed South African men, urging them to challenge relatives, friends and colleagues who harassed, humiliated or abused women. “It is time for good men to stop being silent men,” he said.

“For too long, gender-based violence has been treated as a woman’s problem to solve. Women march, the women of our country organise, they speak out, they protest, they confront and they comfort survivors,” Ramaphosa said.
“Women change their routes home. Avoid going out at night and warn one another about dangerous places and dangerous men. We have placed the burden of male violence on women. That must change.”
Activists expressed their frustration that solid policy actions had not been taken years ago and scepticism that the measures Ramaphosa had announced would work.

Shenilla Mohamed, the executive director of Amnesty International South Africa, said: “These are not new issues and as a country we have been talking about ways to tackle the high numbers of [gender-based violence and femicide], especially since 2019 when women took to the streets to protest, and yet here we are again in the face of continued attacks against women.
“Amnesty International South Africa also notes the timelines put in place by the president, but this will only mean something if it results in action, and if there are consequences for inaction.”

Mpiwa Mangwiro-Tsanga and Bafana Khumalo, of Sonke Gender Justice, an NGO, said: “Our concern … is that the response remains heavily weighted towards what happens after violence has already occurred.”

They added: “Investigating unresolved cases, processing forensic evidence and repairing unsafe public spaces are necessary, but they do not constitute a comprehensive prevention strategy. It is concerning that the president is asking municipalities to do what is actually their mandate and yet they do not deliver on these.”

articles.title: Manchester City Premier League charges: What do they mean?
articles.summary: Since being bought by the UAE in 2008, Manchester City have become one of the world's most successful football clubs. A raft of serious financial charges threatens to undermine this and bring chaos…

image.caption: Sheikh Mansour, as he is widely known, fronted the deal to buy City for the UAE nearly 20 years agoImage: Martin Rickett/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Manchester City have won the Premier League eight times over the last 14 years. But whether those titles will remain is one of a plethora of issues at stake after England's top division charged one of its most high profile clubs with more than 100 breaches of its financial regulations.

On Tuesday, the Premier League announced that an independent commission had found City had drawn up "sham contracts" as well as "relying on sham agreements to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs". These contracts, dubious sponsorships and a number of other methods were, according to the commission's report, used to inflate the club's revenue to the tune of about £900 million (€1.05 billion) over the period between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.
The case has been ongoing for eight years after initial revelations from Germany's Der Spiegel and Rui Pinto of the 'Football Leaks' website. City continue to deny any wrongdoing.

"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case," read a City statement. "Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe."
What was the Premier League verdict on the Manchester City charges?

The 750-page report was damning, accusing City of inflating contracts and sponsorship deals, running secondary contracts off book, making "concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the Premier League investigation" and signing off inflated image rights deals to artificially boost their earnings. All this enabled them to pass both Premier League and UEFA financial spending limits, states the report.

The Premier League's chief ­executive, Richard Masters, described the case "as the most significant in Premier League history," adding that the club "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade."

Though the Premier League, the most commercially successful football league in the world, has drawn some praise for its actions, others point to the fact that it took Pinto leaking emails and media reports to force any action. The report shows that City, who had won the league once in 71 years before being taken over by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in 2008, were consistently posting revenues way higher than any of their more established and successful rivals.
Who are the key figures at Manchester City?

In this context, its the owners. The Abu Dhabi United Group, essentially an investment vehicle for the UAE royal family, bought the club in 2008. The takeover was fronted by Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, know simply as Sheikh Mansour. He is a member of the ruling Al Nahyan family and the UAE's vice president and deputy prime minister. Khaldoon Al Mubarak, who also holds a number of government positions in the UAE, was brought in as chairman.

Nation state ownership of this type is controversial in European football and City's owners have long been criticized for the country's human rights record and using the club for sportswashing. Similar criticisms have been made of European champions Paris Saint-Germain (Qatar) and City's Premier League rivals Newcastle United (Saudi Arabia).

blocks.caption: As well as huge domestic success, City won the Champions League under Pep Guardiola in 2022-23Image: Jose Breton/NurPhoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: City's CEO, Ferran Soriano, joined in 2012 as City expanded their ownership into foreign leagues, buying up clubs in the US, Japan and Australia. He replaced former head coach Roberto Mancini with fellow Spaniard Manuel Pellegrini before former Bayern Munich and Barcelona coach Pep Guardiola took over in 2016, ushering in the club's most successful period.
How did Manchester City's system work?

The club immediately started splashing out on big money transfers on the arrival of UAE investment. At that point, neither UEFA nor the Premier League had the tight financial rules they now have. UEFA's Financial Fair Play (FFP) rules were brought in for the 2011-12 season while the Premier League followed with its Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR) in 2013-14.

City's free spending and relative lack of commercial income meant they were likely to fall foul of such rules. The club were handed a conditional €60 million UEFA fine for losses in the 2011-12 and 2012-13 seasons. They would later be banned from the Champions League on similar grounds in 2020 before being reinstated on appeal.

In an attempt to try and comply with such financial rules, City set up a system they called 'Project Longbow' in 2012. The commission said much of this was genuine but one arm of it was an agreement with a a third party called Fordham which was, according to the ruling, "little more than a front." Essentially, it reads, the club's UAE owners "would be used (and were used) to enable Fordham to acquire from the club (at a sizeable, artificially-inflated price) the club's entitlement to benefit financially from its players' image rights."

In other words, City's owners were pumping money in to their own club through vastly inflated sponsorship and image rights deals so their income looked higher and they could spend more, particularly on player transfers and wages. The report also claims that City paid three individuals, whose names are redacted, through a third party to keep them off the books.
What happens next?

That's the question on everyone's lips. As yet, no sanctions have been laid against City and the appeal will likely drag proceedings out even longer. Meanwhile the club, who are top of the Premier League, face Liverpool on October 11, after the international break.

While there is no precedent for such a tranche of charges, clubs have fallen foul of the Premier League's PSR regulations before. Everton were handed a 10-point penalty for a £19.5-million(€22.8 million) breach over a period ending with the 2021-22 season. This was based on a Premier League tariff of six points for the initial breach, plus an additional point for every £5 million the club overspent. Given that City's overspending is close to a billion pounds, applying that would certainly relegate them, though the division below, the Championship, is not operated by the Premier League.

For now, it looks like City and the league will play on under a cloud. But if the verdict remains after appeal, clubs and individuals whose careers and honors stand to be impacted, will likely come forward and litigate. City themselves could be relegated, docked points over successive seasons, face transfer bans or any combination of those things. The titles won in the relevant period could also be stripped.

articles.title: Servers at Munich's iconic Oktoberfest call for more respect
articles.summary: Oktoberfest is famous the world over for beer, brass band music and Bavarian traditions. But staff at the Wiesn are also reporting incidents of racism and sexism. They're taking a stand against…

image.caption: Oktoberfest staff work hard to serve the millions of people from all over the world that come to Munich for the folk festivalImage: Matthias Schrader/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "The first week went by peacefully," Oktoberfest Director Christian Scharpf said at the festival's half-way point. Munich's Deputy Mayor Verena Dietl praised the "good, harmonious atmosphere."
The city's police force also delivered a positive report half-way through the event in Munich.

But if you take a closer look, all is not peachy at the Wiesn. Service personnel are among those painting a very different picture. And they're the ones at the heart of the action. The situations they encounter often go unreported and don't appear in the statistics, but sometimes, a line is crossed, with racist, discriminatory comments, for example.
In response, a group of service staff have launched an initiative calling for "mutual respect at the Wiesn."
In a video posted on Instagram and TikTok, staff say: "For years, we've been observing how it's suddenly acceptable to say certain things again, and that there's less of an outcry."

Service personnel say the election successes of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt, coupled with their personal experiences at Oktoberfest, were a catalyst for setting up the initiative. To them, the current climate is an indication that right-wing views are gaining social acceptance.
Hence the name of the initiative: "Staff Against the Right".
Security at Oktoberfest

In an interview with Bavaria's public broadcaster, Bayerischer Rundfunk, a spokesperson for vendors at Oktoberfest insisted that "the entire Oktoberfest family has always rejected and continues to reject any form of discrimination, racism and sexism in the strongest possible terms".
But supporters of this latest initiative want to see more being done to address the problem.
There's certainly no shortage of surveillance: Oktoberfest is monitored by 56 police CCTV cameras and patrolled by around 600 police officers and thousands of private security staff.

Halfway through the festival, police had recorded around 470 offenses; reports were also filed for assault, sexual harassment and upskirting ― secretly filming or taking photographs up someone's skirt.

Munich's Oktoberfest is the world's largest folk festival and attracts millions of visitors from all over the world every year. At the halfway point, organizers estimated visitor numbers at around 3.8 million people. Oktoberfest ends on October 4 after 16 days of revelry.
This article was translated from German and edited by Soliman Lawrence.
Just how international is Munich's Oktoberfest?

articles.title: MI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universities
articles.summary: Institutions have for years turned to China for funding opportunities but national security concerns are mounting

blocks.text: The security alert issued by MI5 regarding a Chinese state-owned conglomerate accused of conducting espionage in the UK reveals the extent to which British intelligence remains concerned about Beijing’s influence, and risks casting a shadow over UK-China cooperation at a time when the bilateral relationship is enjoying a revival.

The UK’s domestic security service on Wednesday warned researchers and academics to cease work with the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT), an organisation MI5 described as a “significant threat”.

The CAGT, which is also known as the China General Technology Research Institute, is accused of paying UK academics working in sensitive fields such as artificial intelligence and cybersecurity for “research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage”. The MSS is China’s Ministry of State Security, its intelligence agency.
China’s approach to intelligence gathering involves hoovering up vast amounts of data, often from unsuspecting individuals who believe they are participating in normal research or consultancy work.
This year the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre warned businesses about Beijing-backed attempts to hack into everyday devices such as wifi routers.
Last year, MI5 issued another China-related security alert, warning parliamentarians about approaches from two LinkedIn profiles thought to be linked to Chinese intelligence.

Wednesday’s alert said academic institutions or researchers should be aware of the 2023 National Security Act, which makes it an offence to engage in conduct that is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence agency. The warning is likely to send a chill through the UK’s cash-strapped higher education institutions, which have for years turned to China for funding and collaboration opportunities.

The UK is one of the leading countries to partner with China’s higher education sector. In May, China’s education ministry announced 219 new transnational education partnerships, with more than a fifth of the approvals being with British universities. That puts the UK at the top of the list of partner countries, ahead of Russia, France and Italy.
Chinese students are also the largest group of non-EU international students in the UK, generating about £600m a year for the higher education sector.

There has been growing concern in the UK that partnerships with China pose a risk to national security. The 2023 Intelligence and Security Committee report on China said UK academic institutions “provide a rich feeding ground for China to achieve both political influence and economic advantage” and flagged the risk of China “directing or stealing UK academic research.

In this case, MI5 said that more than 100 academics linked to the UK had contributed to projects funded by the MSS via the front company. The areas of interest were AI, cybersecurity and steganography, the embedding of hidden data in pictures online.

Sam Goodman, senior policy director at the China Strategic Risks Institute, said UK academics were “between a rock and a hard place” when trying to navigate areas of advanced interest that could be of interest to Chinese intelligence. “There is a lack of a coherent steer from government on something like AI. It isn’t particularly clear on AI at this juncture what levels of collaboration we can have with the Chinese,” Goodman said.
after newsletter promotion
Analysts say the UK should do more to highlight which areas are of potentially dual-use interest to Chinese intelligence and provide more guidance to universities and academics.

“It’s all very well issuing these warnings,” says Charles Parton, a senior fellow at the Royal United Services Institute. “Actually far more important, surely, is a consideration of which technologies can be cooperated with China, and which can’t.” He said naming specific Chinese companies as a risk would not help UK researchers to do due diligence on every potential partnership. “The Chinese are not stupid. If they want to hide the origin of someone, they’ll do it,” Parton said.
Meia Nouwens, a senior fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said more clarity was needed on the UK side to help guide researchers working in sensitive fields.

Nouwens said: “A problem has been that in the past there hasn’t been a great deal of discussion of what areas of research constitute a national security risk. Without understanding the limits are of what the UK seeks to protect, it is impossible to have a conversation about managing risk.”

The MI5 alert specifically accused the CAGT of being a front for China’s intelligence. But any research institution in China is ultimately controlled by the Chinese Communist party. “Research institutes that are conducting research on areas of strategic interest for China such as technology will have oversight from the party-state,” Nouwens notes.

That does not mean any collaboration with Chinese educational institutions is inherently dangerous, but it does mean UK academics working in sensitive fields will feel increasingly uneasy about working with a country that has financially underpinned the UK’s higher education sector for decades.

articles.title: MI5 issues spy alert to UK universities over Chinese front company stealing research
articles.summary: Security service says academics should stop taking grants from and working with firm backed by China’s intelligence service
articles.byline: Vikram Dodd Police and crime correspondent

blocks.text: China’s intelligence service used a front company to pay grants to British universities and steal crucial research about technology projects, MI5 said on Wednesday in a rare public espionage warning.

Britain’s domestic security service said researchers and academics should cease work with the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI), sometimes also known as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT). MI5 believes it poses a “significant threat”.

The Chinese organisation has given money to 100 or more academics at a string of universities across the UK, in return getting access to the research, which it is alleged found its way back to China’s intelligence service.

MI5 is now prepared to say publicly that the CGTRI is a front for Chinese intelligence, namely the Chinese ministry of state security (MSS). It said continued collaboration could be prosecuted under the National Security Act 2023.

Areas of research targeted include AI, cybersecurity, covert communications, and the embedding of data in pictures online called steganography. MI5 believes it has clear evidence of sensitive information being passed back to Chinese intelligence. The Guardian understands that as well as research money, some British-based academics were given awards, as in honours, by the Chinese.
Successive British governments have courted Chinese investment and encouraged cooperation.

In the alert issued on Wednesday, the Security Service said: “MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage.”
It said that the CGTRI had “very strong ties to the … MSS, China’s civilian intelligence and security service”.
It added: “Many academic institutions and individuals will to date have engaged with CGTRI in good faith given CGTRI’s obfuscated links to MSS.

“UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions. Further, academics are advised to establish the ultimate funding source when conducting any research collaboration with Chinese institutions, to ensure CGTRI is not involved.”
The alert warns of “potential criminal consequences”, in a section issued after consultation with the Crown Prosecution Service, which authorises criminal prosecutions in England and Wales.

“Through this espionage alert, MI5 has placed the fact that CGTRI has very strong ties to MSS in the public domain,” it states. “Going forward, academic institutions, staff and researchers should ensure they are aware of the National Security Act 2023, particularly offences under section 3 (assisting a foreign intelligence service) and section 17 (obtaining a material benefit from a foreign intelligence service).

“Under section 3, an offence is committed if the person a) engages in conduct that is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out UK-related activities, and b) knows, or having regard to other matters known to them ought reasonably to know, that their conduct is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out UK-related activities.”

Such is the scale of Chinese state espionage targeting the UK that MI5 has decided on a deterrence strategy via a public alert such as this, rather than pursuing every single case. It hopes universities will heed the warning and immediately cease their work with the CGTRI.

The Guardian understands that in one case uncovered by MI5, Chinese intelligence officers posed as researchers at a British university, thereby making it easier to pass material of potential value back to Beijing.
In another case, Chinese intelligence gained access to cutting-edge British research on scraping social media (searching and retaining useful information from social media sites).
after newsletter promotion
The National Security and Investment Act 2021 could prevent a state such as China, assessed as having hostile intent towards the UK, from buying access to the technology on a commercial basis.

The security minister, Dan Jarvis, demanded universities end ties to the CGTRI. He said: “This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security and that of our allies.

“I have written to all university vice-chancellors to ensure they support their staff to end all arrangements with this company, preventing further benefit to the Chinese intelligence services and ensuring compliance with the National Security Act.”

He added: “International partnerships are vital to ensure our universities and research institutes continue to thrive, but we will take robust action to defend against the threats we face. That means supporting our police and intelligence services to expose and disrupt harmful activity, using the full force of the law.”

Responding to the MI5 alert, Vivienne Stern, the chief executive of Universities UK, which represents 142 institutions across the UK, said universities took their responsibilities around research security and national security extremely seriously.

“The sector has made significant investments in recent years to strengthen due diligence, risk assessment and research security processes, while continuing to support the international collaboration that is essential to world-leading research and innovation,” she said.

“Close engagement between government and the higher education sector is vital to ensuring that universities and the country continue to benefit from international collaboration while effectively managing national security risks.”

Libby Hackett, the chief executive of the Russell Group of research-intensive universities, said: “All our universities take national security responsibilities very seriously. Working closely with government departments and the security services enables universities to take swift action to protect UK interests – and we will continue to do so in the face of new and emerging threats”.
The Chinese embassy has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Burundi agrees to receive ‘third-country’ migrant deportees from US
articles.summary:
Burundi joins several other African nations in accepting people deported under Trump’s hardline policy

Burundi has agreed to join a…

blocks.text: Burundi has agreed to join a clutch of ⁠other African nations in receiving migrants from other countries deported from the US under ⁠Donald Trump’s hardline ⁠immigration ​policy.

However, the authorities in Bujumbura, the country’s economic capital, said Burundi will only accept those not accused of crime or terrorism links, said ⁠Nancy Ninette Mutoni, a spokesperson for the country’s president, Évariste Ndayishimiye. Tuesday’s announcement gave no details of numbers, timing or financial ⁠details.

Washington has sent so-called “third-country deportees” to some half ​a dozen African nations ‌as well as many other countries, often where they have no ties, have never been and find themselves detained indefinitely, under opaque deals ‌that Senate Democrats say have cost tens of millions of ‌dollars.

In many cases, deportees had secured legal protections from immigration courts in the US against repatriation. But rights groups say the third-country deals allow the US to circumvent those protections.

Mutoni said preparations were underway to arrange accommodation, ‌living conditions and integration into local communities in Burundi. “Receiving them requires serious planning – where they will stay, what they ​will eat and how they will live alongside the local population,” she said.
“If they choose to join Burundian citizens and make a valuable contribution to national development, the law ⁠will be respected,” she said, regarding potential citizenship.
Burundi aimed ​to both ​strengthen diplomatic relations and provide ​hospitality to people in need, the spokesperson ​added.
The US ‌state department ​did not ​immediately respond to requests for comment while a spokesperson for the Burundi foreign ministry said details of the agreement were not yet available.

articles.title: Bosnia elections: Polls overshadowed by exhaustion, exodus and geopolitics as ethnic politics eclipse real problems
articles.summary: Bosnia goes to the polls on October 4 to elect several parliaments and presidents. While voters worry about the economy and emigration, the campaign is focused on ethnicity, exposing the country's…

image.caption: General elections are being held in Bosnia and Herzegovina on October 4Image: Denis Zuberi/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Picture a country that has lost nearly one in six of its citizens — roughly 600,000 people —through emigration in just ten years.
A country that has conducted only a single census since being ravaged by war in the 1990s, counting just over 3.5 million people in 2013.

A country where young people aged 20 to 29 are leaving faster than any other age group and where demographers warn of a looming population collapse because the birth rate has trailed the mortality rate every year since 2009.
This is Bosnia and Herzegovina.

But when voters here go to the polls on October 4 to elect people to the most powerful positions at both state and entity levels, the focus of the election campaign will not be on how to stop the country hemorrhaging citizens. It will — once again and for the umpteenth time — be about who is Serb, who is Bosniak, who is Croat and who supposedly threatens whom.
That fact alone says more about the state of Bosnian politics than any opinion poll could.
A complicated electoral system

After the brutal 1992-95 Bosnian War, Bosnia and Herzegovina was left divided by the Dayton Peace Agreement — a compromise that stopped the killing but built ethnicity into the state's architecture as a permanent rather than a temporary fix.
Three decades on, that architecture hasn't changed, and progress has stalled completely.
The complicated constitution drafted at Dayton produced an equally complicated electoral system.

Bosnia is divided into two entities, the Serb-majority Republika Srpska and the Bosniak-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Brcko District. It has a total of 14 governments and parliaments at state, entity and cantonal level — a lot for such a small country.

On October 4, voters will elect a new presidency at state level. The presidency in Bosnia comprises three people. Each of the three ethnic groups elects its own representative: a Serb chosen in Republika Srpska, and a Bosniak and a Croat chosen in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

blocks.caption: Research shows that ethnic identity remains the single strongest predictor of how people in Bosnia voteImage: Dragan Maksimović/DW

blocks.text: On top of that, voters will be electing a new president in Republika Srpska and lawmakers for both the state-level and entity parliaments, while the Federation's president and the remaining parliamentary chambers are filled after the vote through ethnic quotas.
Voting along ethnic lines
Bosnia today operates as a patchwork of parallel, ethnically defined power structures whose chief skill is blocking one another. And that isn't a design flaw, it's the design.

"Many citizens will keep voting for parties that represent their own people, because political elites constantly manufacture a sense of threat and fear, turning elections into a referendum on national survival," political scientist Mladen Bubonjic told DW.

This is far removed from the issues affecting voters in their day-to-day lives: high prices, low wages and pensions, unaffordable housing, precarious jobs, corruption, poor public services and the steady drain of people leaving the country.
Same script, new faces
Poll after poll shows that voters don't believe campaign promises, and their answers in such polls tend to boil down to the same thing: "Nothing has changed in 30 years."

blocks.caption: Voters will elect the members of the presidency and parliaments in the two entities that make up the country and at cantonal level. Pictured here: the buildings of the Council of Ministers and Bosnian parliament in Sarajevo Image: Dragan Maksimović/DW

blocks.text: That sentence could have been spoken a decade ago, or even two decades ago. And that's precisely the problem: Bosnian politics isn't stuck by accident, it's stuck by design, because the system rewards whoever keeps the divisions alive and punishes anyone who tries to make meaningful change.

Elections in Bosnia have never simply been about getting better roads or cheaper electricity. They function as an act of tribal defense, and every side knows it and cultivates it. Research consistently shows that ethnic identity remains the single strongest predictor of how people vote, far outweighing economic self-interest.

This campaign, too, has been dominated by identity politics and institutional paralysis rather than any real debate over jobs or prices. This means voters are choosing fear, because no one is seriously offering them a real alternative.

"Unfortunately, out of a decades-old habit, ethnic tensions keep rallying citizens around ideological and identity issues. Corruption, poverty and demographic collapse have all been absorbed into political identities," political analyst Tanja Topic told DW.
What voters actually want fixed

But step off the political stage and onto the street and people's priorities sound the same as they do in any other country: They want jobs, a paycheck that covers the bills, an affordable home, healthcare that actually works and a government that doesn't steal.

blocks.caption: Voters would like to see politicians tackling a range of subjects such as high prices, low wages and pensions, housing, public services and emigrationImage: Dragan Maksimovic/DW

blocks.text: People blame corruption as the reason reforms stall before they are completed, and young people choose to leave the country rather than cast a ballot.
The real fight is over identity and wartime history, not economic hardship. Migration gets mentioned mostly as an alarming statistic, rarely as an issue anyone is racing to solve.

"The Bosnian triangle, dominated by three ethnic principles, is disastrous for all of Bosnia's citizens. But if you don't vote along those lines, you get branded a traitor to your own people. Which is disastrous for the country's progress," Vehid Sehic, a political analyst from Tuzla, told DW.
EU accession recedes further into the distance
Bosnia has been an EU candidate since 2022. In 2024, it got the green light to open accession talks. In practice, however, progress along that path has all but ground to a halt.

An independent analysis shows that, according to the EU's own progress reports, Bosnia's readiness score dropped from 4.14 to 2.91 out of ten in a single year — the steepest fall of any candidate country.
Bosnia still hasn't appointed a chief negotiator for EU accession talks, and of the 113 reforms required for EU accession, not one has been implemented.

blocks.caption: Bosnia has been an EU candidate since 2022, but implementation of the necessary reforms required for accession has stagnated. Pictured here: EU High Representative Kaja Kallas (left) and Chairwoman of the Council of Ministers of Bosnia, Borjana KristoImage: Council of Ministers of BiH

blocks.text: For ordinary citizens, EU membership is no longer a burning question. It has curdled into a tired, accepted truth that when politicians speak of the "European path," it amounts to little more than ink on paper.
Geopolitical backdrop

Bosnia's elections, alongside Serbia's on October 25, are taking place at a time when the Western Balkans has once again become a stage for intense rivalry between Russia, the European Union and the United States.
Against this backdrop, political forces across Bosnia are already looking for allies abroad.

Bosnia is heading into this election as a country that has spent three decades spinning in place, at the exact moment its internal paralysis has turned it into a playing field for other people's geopolitical bets.
Meanwhile, the 600,000 people who have already left in search of a normal life have effectively answered the question of whether they think anything is about to change.

articles.title: Top Trump figures push to direct human rights funding to rightwing causes
articles.summary:
Support for white Afrikaners, anti-communism and others reveals how US redefining what qualifies as human rights

With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is…
articles.byline: Andrew Roth and Joseph Gedeon in Washington

blocks.text: With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a massive $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court, and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilisational norms”.

Critics have focused on 43 awards of a combined $176.9m that will bolster rightwing and conservative causes around the world while likely angering US allies over interference in internal politics. The Guardian has seen a sample of the controversial grants, which makes up most of the $205m in funding that Congress has appropriated for the entire human rights and democracy fund (HRDF).

Sources with knowledge of the grant process have told the Guardian that the awards were personally lobbied for by members of the Trump administration, and reflect interests that include JD Vance’s warnings of the collapse of traditional western values in Europe, and Stephen Miller’s push against immigration and to support white minorities in countries like South Africa.

“The story for me is the high-level – including White House-directed – attention on these programs,” said a person familiar with the discussions over the democracy awards. “These awards have been briefed at the highest levels of the department and have buy-in from the White House.”

The proposed awards represent a significant shift in US support for dissidents, human-rights defenders and civil-society groups under authoritarian governments. The new slate includes projects in wealthy nations, and focused on opposition to regulation, Brexit, migration, anti-communism, Christian protection and opposition to “gender ideology”, offering a window into how the Trump administration is redefining what qualifies as human rights and merits tens of millions of dollars in US foreign assistance.

“Congress appropriated money for the democracy fund on a bipartisan basis to support defenders of human rights, to assist victims of human rights violations and to instead promote the growth of democracy abroad,” said senator Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the US Senate committee on foreign relations.

“The Trump administration’s proposals would use taxpayer funds to promote far-right organizations and programs in established democracies. This is a waste of resources and undermines United States values and relations with democratic partners, including allies in Europe.”

The largest award of $40m was directed to a consortium led by the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation (VOC), an anti-communist non-profit that has received far smaller grants in the past. A state department vetting document seen by the Guardian records $96,997 in previous contracts in the last five years between the foundation and the department, all in the 2022 fiscal year, and notes that it had been vetted in 2019 in connection with tickets to the foundation’s gala. The vetting document also identifies Andrew Bremberg, a former Trump White House domestic policy adviser and US ambassador to the UN European office, as a “senior leader” of the foundation.

In July, ProPublica reported that Samuel Samson, a 27-year-old deputy assistant secretary overseeing the new grants, was linked to senior members of VOC through his studies at the Christian conservative Hillsdale College graduate program. (A state department official then told the outlet that the relationship had nothing to do with the grant).

Samson has described the US and Europe as partners in a shared civilizational struggle. Samson toured Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia last December – all countries that were floated to receive a $2m grant to counter migration weaponized by Russia and Belarus, and criticized NGOs that previous administrations had worked with for promoting what he called radical concepts, including gender theory and DEI.

The state department did not comment on individual grants but told the Guardian the programs were still in “active deliberation”, that awardees would meet guidelines for federal grants, and that all programming would undergo a “standard and rigorous vetting process by grant professionals.”

“Our programming in Europe aims to support our European allies in defending those rights and principles, along with their civilizational self-confidence and sovereignty from those who seek to undermine them,” a state department official said. “The national security strategy highlights our priorities in Europe which includes advancing political liberty, promoting free speech, and collaborating with European partners to jointly support European revitalization and civilizational self-confidence.”

Under the legislation authorizing the fund, the money must be assigned by 30 September, the end of the fiscal year, when unobligated funds typically lapse. Shaheen, the ranking member of the Senate foreign relations committee, has put a partial “hold” on giving the grants to some of the controversial awardees – setting up a showdown with the State Department with just hours left for the money to be obligated.
ProPublica first reported that Trump officials had drawn up at least a dozen no-bid grants aimed at rightwing and anti-immigration causes in Europe and advocates for white South Africans.
The document now shows how much of the fund the plan takes up, and which awards have since been dropped.

A $1m award titled “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court. The Trump administration sanctioned Justice Alexandre de Moraes last year after lobbying by Eduardo Bolsonaro, son of the former president.

A program titled “Promoting Western Civilization Allies” would be limited to implementers who do not subscribe to “ideologically weaponized accounts of human rights, such as gender ideology”, according to the document, and will receive $2m. It names possible recipients in Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and the Balkans with “anti-communist” and “natural rights” approaches.

One award was allocated to document “democratic backsliding” in Europe tied to “mass and illegal migration” and legislation by “supra-national entities”, while a $1m journalism consortium would push back against designations of “trusted” media outlets. The list also includes $2m for early-warning networks protecting Christians in Nigeria.

And a $3m no-bid award would go to the Jobs Foundation, a UK group run by Matthew Elliott, who led the Vote Leave campaign. The grant, titled “Countering Overregulation to Advance American Investment”, would promote a “common good capitalism index” and pro-business policy, including how the foundation promoted Brexit as a chance to cut the UK’s climate regulations.

The document also shows that a proposed $5m no-bid grant to the Free Speech Union, the British group founded by Toby Young, has been marked “withdrawn”. When the award was first reported in July, Young said the group had never applied for or received US government money (though Trump officials had reportedly met with the group during a European tour late last year).

The grant would have paid the group to campaign against online safety and hate speech laws, including Britain’s Online Safety Act, a law passed under the Conservatives in 2023. Meant to protect children from harmful content and is enforced by Ofcom, its age-verification rules – which took effect last year – have drawn constant criticism from the Trump administration, which cast them as censorship.

The Free Speech Union is the second British group to drop off the list. A $7m no-bid award to 878, a thinktank whose stated missions include restoring Judeo-Christian culture and “ending mass migration and deporting illegal immigrants”, was abandoned in July after pushback from Congress. It was founded by Jacob Rees-Mogg, who served as Brexit opportunities minister and business secretary before losing his seat at the 2024 election, and now presents on GB News.

The British awards would have sent $15m in US taxpayer money to groups run by two sitting Conservative peers and a former cabinet minister, on issues from online safety law to migration that are live in British politics.

articles.title: Russia launches largest attack on Ukraine energy infrastructure since spring
articles.summary: At least six people were killed and 33 others injured across the country in the overnight attacks, local authorities reported.

blocks.text: Russia has launched the largest attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure since the spring, primarily targeting Kyiv and the surrounding region, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi has said.
At least six people were killed and 33 others injured across the country in the overnight attacks, including a child in the Kyiv region, local authorities reported.
The strikes also impacted people's power supplies, with Ukraine's biggest private energy firm, DTEK, saying power to 8,000 homes had been restored following "a difficult night" for the capital.
The Russian defence ministry said one of its targets was the Trypilska power station, the largest supplier of electricity to Kyiv. This has not been confirmed by Ukrainian officials.
In a statement on Telegram, Koretskyi said: "Since the summer, there has effectively not been a single day without enemy attacks on our energy infrastructure.
"However, a mass and combined attack of this scale has occurred for the first time since the end of the last heating season."
Ukraine has been expecting another protracted Russian assault on the country's energy grid. It has happened every winter so far since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
In total 11 regions of the country were attacked overnight, with residential buildings, social infrastructure, civilian enterprises and railways also targeted, Koretskyi said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said there were strikes on critical infrastructure in the Zhytomyr, Mykolaiv, Kirovohrad and Rivne regions.
On Wednesday, some households in the Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Sumy, Kyiv and Kharkiv regions remained without power, Ukraine's energy ministry said.
State-owned grid operator Ukrenegro advised residents not to use powerful electrical appliances between the hours of 10:00 and 16:00 local time as electricity supplies were lower than usual.

In Kyiv, people woke to find the city blanketed by thick, acrid smoke after a night punctuated by the sound of explosions. An air raid alert was still on and the distant sound of air defence gunfire echoed through the murky atmosphere.
Residents in several districts were advised to close their windows until the smoke cleared.
Among those killed in the overnight strikes was a child whose body was found under the rubble of a house, Kyiv regional governor Timur Tkachenko said.

Kyiv Mayor Vitaly Klischko said three people were killed in total in the capital, including a Ukrainian utility company worker who was killed at a warehouse building. It is not clear if the three he mentioned included the child.
Two people were also killed in the north-eastern Sumy region, governor Oleh Hryhorov said, while another person was killed in the Mykolaiv region, acting regional governor Heorhiy Reshetilov said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

articles.title: Last UK and US troops leave Iraq as anti-Islamic State mission ends
articles.summary: The withdrawal of coalition forces, under a deal agreed two years ago, was a key demand of the Iraqi government.

blocks.text: The last British and American troops have left Iraq after a military presence of more than a decade in the country.
The exit of the remaining UK military personnel - around 100 - from Irbil, in the northern Kurdistan region, was co-ordinated over recent weeks with US forces, who also departed on Wednesday.
It follows an agreement between the US and the Iraqi government, signed two years ago, to withdraw foreign troops by the end of this month.

British and US forces have been present in Iraq since 2014, as part of the international coalition to help defeat the extremist Islamic State (IS) group. Their departure brings the mission, known as Operation Inherent Resolve, to an end.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said the end of the coalition's mission marked "Iraq's transition to a phase in which it assumes full responsibility for its security and stability".
Iraq is set to hold four "Sovereignty Days" as a national holiday to mark the withdrawal.

"Following more than a decade of operations, training and capacity building, Iraqi Security Forces (ISF) and the Kurdish Peshmerga have secured the enduring territorial defeat of Daesh in Iraq and are now well placed to take primary responsibility for the country's security," the UK Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in a statement, referring to IS by an Arabic acronym.
"With these objectives achieved, Iraq and its international partners can begin a new chapter focused on enduring security co-operation under Iraqi leadership."
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said the coalition's departure from Irbil marked "the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated [IS] in Iraq".

He added: "The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq's remaining security challenges, including [IS] remnants and Iran-aligned militias that undermine Iraqi sovereignty and regional stability, now rests with the government of Iraq."
The Iraqi government declared the military defeat of IS in 2017, but coalition forces remained to help prevent the group's resurgence.
A recent UN report estimated that sustained counter-terrorism pressure by Iraqi security forces had left IS with several hundred fighters who were "able to carry out unsophisticated operations only".
The Iraqi government also faces the challenge of Iranian-backed militias in the country.
Zaidi, who took office in May, has vowed to disarm them and bring all weapons under state control following the coalition's exit.
But several powerful factions have resisted his plans and could now see their influence grow without the US presence.
Since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran earlier this year, militias have been targeting the remaining US and UK forces stationed at Irbil air base.
Hundreds of Nato troops stationed in Baghdad left the country in March as tensions rose.
A BBC team visited the coalition base in Irbil in April this year, during a fragile ceasefire between the US and Iran.
They were forced to circle the base in an RAF transport aircraft while drones were being launched nearby.
At the height of the US bombing campaign against Iran, the coalition base was being targeted by up to 28 drones and missiles a day.

RAF Regiment Gunners, who were among the last British military personnel stationed there, had shot down more than 100 drones in the first six weeks of the war. Many of the attack drones were being launched by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq.
On Wednesday, signalling the end of the mission, the MoD paid tribute to UK personnel who had contributed to the counter-IS mission.

It said they had provided "valuable support, training and assistance" to more than 111,000 members of the Iraqi Security Forces, including more than 21,000 Peshmerga forces in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region.

It also said the RAF had conducted thousands of sorties, striking more than 2,300 IS targets. The RAF is expected to continue flying missions over neighbouring Syria, to prevent the remnants of IS from gaining a foothold.
The Pentagon said the US would continue to provide "targeted training and intelligence support" to its Iraqi partners.
US Central Command said the coalition's joint taskforce remained operational and was now based in Jordan.
US forces will also continue their mission against IS in Syria, where the UN estimates that the group has up to 3,000 fighters.
This is the third time US and UK forces have withdrawn from Iraq.
Tens of thousands of US and British troops were deployed to the country in 1991 following Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait.

They returned to Iraq in 2003, when US President George W Bush ordered Operation Iraqi Freedom to remove the dictator from power and eliminate weapons of mass destruction that turned out not to exist.
The fierce sectarian insurgency that engulfed Iraq following the invasion cost tens of thousands of lives, including those of nearly 4,500 US military personnel and 179 British military personnel.
US and UK forces left Iraq in 2011, only to return three years later, when IS threatened to take control of the country.

articles.title: AI tool that copied actor’s ‘lustrous’ voice violated his rights, says Tokyo court
articles.summary:
Kenjiro Tsuda wins case against TikTok account in landmark verdict to protect publicity rights

A court in Japan has ruled that the human…

blocks.text: A court in Japan has ruled that the human voice has legal protection after a landmark case involving a well-known actor and a TikTok account that he claimed had cloned his “lustrous” baritone voice in its AI-generated videos.

Tokyo district court said on Wednesday that voices should enjoy the same protection as publicity rights, at the end of a closely watched legal action brought against TikTok by Kenjiro Tsuda – best known for voicing the character Kento Nanami in the anime Jujutsu Kaisen.

But the court dismissed Tsuda’s request that the operator of TikTok remove the videos, noting that the user had deleted them soon after the suit was filed last November. “The unauthorised use of a performer’s voice … can be considered an infringement on publicity rights,” said the presiding judge, Aya Takahashi.

The lawsuit is believed to be the first in Japan seeking to defend an individual’s vocal identity against AI-generated copies. Japan’s voice actors, many of whom achieve star status through their “appearances” in anime, are increasingly worried that AI mimicry is threatening their livelihoods and the industry as a whole.
An actor’s voice “is the result of years of rigorous training and apprenticeship”, Yuko Sasaki, executive director of the Japan Actors Union said ahead of the ruling.

Tsuda, 55, claimed that the 188 TikTok videos uploaded on an anonymous account between July 2024 and September last year had been narrated by a “deep” and “lustrous” voice that could only be his. In response, the platform argued that the videos contained a “generic male voice” and that any perceived similarities to Tsuda’s voice were highly subjective.

The verdict is the first in which a Japanese court has declared that the human voice is protected under publicity rights, a reference to the ability to control and profit from aspects of an individual’s identity, in Tsuda’s case his distinctive voice.

The protection applies “if the purpose of using the voice is exclusively to take advantage of its commercial appeal”, Takahashi said, describing a voice to be “as symbolic of one’s personality as portraits are”.
The TikTok account, whose picture resembled Tsuda’s Jujutsu Kaisen character, combined images and AI-generated speech about urban legends, the occult and conspiracy theories.

At one point, the account had more than 200,000 subscribers and, according to the legal complaint, the clips would have earned its owner between ¥500,000 (£2,395) and ¥75,000 in monthly revenue, the Kyodo news agency said.
after newsletter promotion
Describing the content as “sordid”, Tsuda’s legal team claimed the account had only attracted attention because it had cloned the “attractive voice of a popular actor”.

TikTok said in a statement it would “respect the court’s judgment while considering what steps to take after scrutinising [the ruling’s] details”. It added: “We will continue to sincerely work on the balance between technology development and rights protection.”
In 2024, actors in Japan launched a campaign called “No More” to oppose the unauthorised use of their faces and voices in AI-generated content.
With reporting by Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Couple describes relief at rescue after whale destroys their yacht
articles.summary: Jeremy and Gemma Cooper were 500 miles off the coast of New Zealand when their yacht, the Tai Tam, collided with a sperm whale.

blocks.text: A sailor couple have spoken of their relief to be rescued after a sperm whale collided with their yacht.

Jeremy and Gemma Cooper told the BBC that they were 500 nautical miles off the coast of New Zealand when the boat, the Tai Tam, lurched port side and they knew they'd "been hit by something" - only to see a pod of six sperm whales swimming behind the boat.
As their boat took on water and eventually sank, the Coopers and two other sailors aboard the vessel evacuated to a life raft. Seventeen hours later they were rescued by a container ship.
The couple told the BBC that, despite their ordeal, they would be out on the water again soon.
Video produced by Lana Lam, edited by Alex Foster.

articles.title: Luxury prison in Indonesia demolished after public outcry
articles.summary: Indonesian lawmakers on Wednesday ordered the demolition of a controversial luxury compound inside a penitentiary near the capital.

blocks.text: A prison compound in Indonesia has been demolished after public outcry following the discovery of luxury apartments within the penitentiary.
Investigators reported finding luxury facilities in Cibinong Prison in Bogor, near Jakarta, allegedly used by favoured inmates during a surprise inspection on 23 September.

The units contained amenities including air conditioners, big-screen televisions, refrigerators, sofas and dining areas. Investigators also reported finding a gym, a golf simulator under construction and luxury vehicles in the complex.
Officials said the residences appeared to house inmates, although prison officials claim they were for staff.

The incident has drawn widespread public attention and renewed scrutiny of Indonesia's prisons, which have long faced allegations that wealthy or well-connected inmates can obtain preferential treatment through bribery.

articles.title: Flydubai pilot investigated over possible attempt to crash Tel Aviv-bound flight
articles.summary: Israeli media say authorities are investigating whether a Flydubai pilot tried to crash a Tel Aviv-bound plane before it diverted to Saudi Arabia.

image.caption: Image: Markus Mainka/picture alliance

blocks.text: Authorities are investigating whether a pilot on a Flydubai flight tried to crash the Israel-bound on Wednesday, according to Israeli media reports.
The plane lost thousands of meters of altitude in about a minute before making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, with Flydubai confirming that all passengers were safe.
What happened on the Flydubai flight?
Flydubai said flight FZ 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv experienced an "incident" while en route and landed safely at Tabuk Airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia. The aircraft was a Boeing 737 MAX 8.
"The aircraft has landed safely in Tabuk Airport and all passengers are safe and accounted for," a Flydubai spokesperson said.
Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 reported that authorities were investigating whether one of the pilots had deliberately tried to crash the aircraft, with the other pilot intervening to stop him.
Israeli media said one of the pilots suffered a stab wound. Initial reports had described the incident only as a fight between the two pilots.
According to reports, the captain was of Russian origin and the co-pilot Ukrainian.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

articles.title: Israel-bound passenger plane makes emergency landing in Saudi Arabia
articles.summary:
Israeli media say incident, which raised fears of possible hijacking, stemmed from feud between plane’s two pilots

A commercial plane travelling from Dubai in the United Arab Emirates to

blocks.text: A commercial plane travelling from Dubai in the United Arab Emirates to Israel has been forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, briefly raising concerns about a possible hijacking and prompting Israel to scramble warplanes.

Israeli media, citing security officials, said the incident on Wednesday stemmed from a feud between the plane’s two pilots, and everyone onboard was safe. The plane landed in Tabuk, a civilian and military base in the kingdom.
The FlyDubai plane had transmitted an emergency alert, according to publicly available flight tracking information.

About two and a half hours after departing from Dubai, it abruptly descended from 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet within a minute, before making an erratic circle close to the Jordanian border and landing in Tabuk about an hour later, according to FlightRadar24.
A regional official briefed on the incident said a fight broke out in the cockpit and apparently involved pilots. It was not immediately clear what had caused the fight, the official said.

A second official confirmed that Israel had scrambled warplanes, fearing a hijacking of a plane carrying dozens of its citizens. The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has warned in recent days of unspecified, escalated security threats.
Both officials spoke on condition of anonymity because the incident was still under investigation.
Netanyahu’s office later said the situation was under control and Israel was working to bring the passengers home.

Emergency landings for personnel reasons are rare yet not unheard of. In 2022, two Air France pilots were suspended after fighting in the cockpit on a Geneva-Paris flight, though it did not have to be diverted and landed as planned.
